The thirty-seventh chapter, titled "An Exposition of Prapatti,
Also Known as Nyāsa," which instantly destroys a multitude of sins numbering many tens of millions.
We meditate upon that divine splendor of the god Sudarśana.
Following the restatement of what has been said, Nārada asks about the purpose and other details regarding the sixteen arms of Sudarśana:
Nārada: [Question]...
O Blessed One, O Supreme Lord, O Master, you have explained everything regarding the *yantra* and the mantra of the *Saudarśana*, as well as your own. (37-1)
Furthermore, [he described] the majesty of the missiles, as well as their true nature, their characteristics, their propitiation, their application, and especially their inherent natures. (37–2)
In the description of the form, it was stated that he may have sixteen arms; tell me, when, by whom, for what purpose, and of what nature is that [form] to be made? (37-3)
The purpose of having sixteen arms is the prevention of great calamities and the like for kings; as Ahirbudhnya states:
"When kings are about to be overcome by enemies, [the Lord appears] endowed with power for them."
When the cities were set ablaze and the armies of the kings were put to flight.
When enjoyments are obstructed for those dwelling in their respective territories,
and when the kingdom is thus oppressed by enemy forces, O Great Sage— (37.5)
When stability is unattainable for a king whose enemies are not yet eliminated,
he should cause the sixteen-armed Sudarśana to be fashioned without obstruction.
A description of the form of the sixteen-armed Sudarśana: boundless, indefinable, beyond the reach of speech and mind;
red in color, with noble limbs, and clad in yellow silk garments. (37.7)
He was endowed with hair resembling a mass of lightning that stood upright,
and he was terrifying with his three fierce, rolling, tawny eyes.
His fangs were clearly visible as he bit his lower lip, emitting sparks of fire;
he was resplendent with a girdle of tinkling bells.
It was adorned with a sword blazing at its waist-hanging belt,
and it bore a garland of tinkling bells that resounded like a swarm of bees.
Likewise, [he wore] a divine garland hanging down to his feet, studded with pearls and gems,
while his lotus-like feet shone with tinkling anklets.
Adorned with necklaces, armlets, earrings, and crowns, and further embellished with various other wonderful ornaments made of jewels. (37.12)
He bears in sequence a discus, an axe, a spear, a staff, and a goad;
he holds weapons with a hundred faces, as well as a sword and a javelin.
With his eight other right hands, which are long and turned upward, and with his left hands, he holds in sequence a conch, a bow, a noose, a plow, and a vajra. (37.14)
He bore these terrifying maces, clubs, and spears,
and was enveloped by a great fury arising from his enemies who had taken refuge with him.
Bearing a terrifying face with a furrowed brow and knitted frown,
he stands in the distinguished posture of pratyālīḍha, garlanded in flames.

One should meditate upon Sudarśana as the Greatly Radiant One, whose nature is Time (Kālātman), who withdraws this entire world in the form of Kālāgnirudra; thus, through the aforementioned meditation on Sudarśana, there is the accomplishment of freedom from rivalry. (37–17)
By the mere meditation upon this, the king shall become free of rivals in an instant;
there shall be no appearance of those rivals anywhere upon the surface of the earth. (37-18)

Enemies perish wherever they may flee, for kings who do not propitiate the Sudarśana suffer defeat by their foes; even so, kings of immeasurable prowess [perish] if they fail to propitiate him. (37–19)
They are indeed overcome by rivals and become bereft of prosperity.
[However,] through yoga or ritual surrender (*nyāsa*), the propitiation of Sudarśana is a means for attaining fruits both in this world and the next;
whoever worships him with devotion according to the very path previously described— || 37–20 ||
O great sage, by means of both external and internal yoga, or through the practice of nyāsa, he becomes happy in this world and the next; of this there is no doubt.
(p. 356) Following the restatement of what has been said, Nārada asks about the nature of *prapatti* known as *nyāsa*: "The external and internal yoga of mine has been previously described."
The practice known as Nyāsa has been proclaimed; tell that to me, O Maheśvara.
Ahirbudhnya proclaims the supreme secret nature of Nyāsa:
"This Great Upaniṣad is the highest secret of the gods."
It immediately bestows desired objects and destroys all sins. || 37-23 ||
This must never be spoken to anyone who is not a devotee;
however, because you are my steadfast devotee, I shall speak it out of a desire for your welfare. (37.24)
Establishing that nyāsa is the means for attaining all fruits:
Whatever cannot be attained by one who desires objects of desire through other means, nor by the seeker of liberation through Sāṃkhya, Yoga, or devotion— [that is attained through nyāsa]. (37.25)
The supreme abode is attained, from which one does not return again;
that very state is obtained through renunciation alone, O great sage. (37.26)
And by that very means, the Supreme Self, the Puruṣottama, is realized.
O great sage, those who know the Vedas declare that this surrender has six limbs and is indeed sixfold. (37.27)
The resolve for conformity, the avoidance of opposition, the conviction that [the Lord] will protect, and likewise the choice of Him as protector. (37.28)
The sixfold taking of refuge consists in the wretchedness of surrendering oneself.
In the section on entrustment (*nyāsa*), it is stated that the word "refuge" (*śaraṇa*) denotes the means: "The word 'refuge' refers to both the means and the protector of the house. (37.29)
And now this [term] functions as a singular expression for the purpose of the means:
"I am characterized by surrender; I am the abode of offenses, destitute, and without refuge. (37–30)
The thought of praying, "May you alone be my means," is called taking refuge; let that be applied toward this God. (37.31)
Regarding the surrender to Sudarśana, the specific mantra is stated:
"O Lord, all-conquering, thousand-spoked, and invincible one!
I have taken refuge in You, the auspicious Śrīsudarśana. (37.32)
For one who has taken refuge with this mantra, there is the cessation of all evils that obstruct the arising of the fruit;
for one who has taken refuge with this very [mantra] unto the Lord Sudarśana, all those evils, which are its consequences, undoubtedly perish. (37–33)
O best among those who perform austerities, for one who has sought refuge, all austerities have been accomplished by him;
in an instant, all sacred fords, all sacrifices, and all gifts [have been attained].
p. 358) "By him [this] has been accomplished, and liberation is in his hand; of this there is no doubt.
Nārada asks about the nature of the attainment of asceticism, sacrifice, and so forth through mere *nyāsa*: [text follows].
How are austerities, sacrifices, sacred fords, and gifts of every kind [to be understood]? (37.35)
"O Lord, by the mere performance of that very nyāsa, [all things] are accomplished in that same way.
Regarding the statement that the nyāsa described thereafter possesses a power of austerity exceeding all other austerities,
Ahirbudhnya says:
Indeed, those austerities which have been enjoined for the sake of the supreme good (niḥśreyasa).
Among those ascetic practices, the renunciation (nyāsa) is declared to be the supreme austerity.

For one who has performed the internal renunciation of the self by means of the word "namas," the performance of sacrifices—such as those requiring fuel-sticks as their instruments—is rendered equivalent to a well-conducted sacrifice. || 37 || 37 ||
He who performed [the rite] with salutation (namas) is the one praised as the performer of a perfect sacrifice (svadhvara). This demonstrates the authority for the supreme nature of Nyāsa:
[one should worship] the Lord, who is to be known through one's own self, which has become the means of sacrifice. (37–38)
"We have heard that these were the first rites of dharma performed.
He who worships the God who assumes the form of sacrifice through his very self attains the equality of all sacrifices in the act of depositing [the self]. (37–39)
By that high-souled one, all sacrifices have been performed here.
For the sake of establishing the sacrificial nature of renunciation (*nyāsa*), there is a description of it as having the fullness of all sacrificial components:
"The body of this one who bears the form of sacrifice is considered to be the sacrificial altar. (37–40)
The mouth is the Āhavanīya fire, the heart is the Dakṣiṇā fire, and his stomach is declared by the Śruti to be the Gārhapatya fire. (37–41)

The sacrificer is proclaimed to be the principle of the mind (manas-tattva), and the intellect (buddhi) is proclaimed to be the wife. Those who are adversaries to one's own [self] are proclaimed to be the sacrificial animals (paśus). || 37-42 ||
The body hairs are said to be his sacrificial grass (barhis), and the vital breath is declared to be the oblation (havya).
The pressings (savana) are proclaimed as his head, middle body, limbs, and feet.
O great sage, his ten sacrificial implements are also his organs of knowledge and action; the sixteen officiating priests are the arms of this God. (37–44)
O Nārada, the resolve to protect his devotees is the initiation (dīkṣā) of the Lord;
the resonance of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas is considered his sound of ornaments.
The ornaments of this [sacrifice] are the members of the assembly; compassion is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of the Lord;
and likewise, the *juhū*, *dhruvā*, and *sruva* ladles, as well as the *prāśitraharaṇa* vessel.
The *mekṣaṇa* and the *upabhṛt*, the *veda*, the *iḍāpātrī*, as well as the wooden vessel (*dārupātra*), the *yoktra*, the *camasa*, and the *sṛṣṭi*. || 37-47 ||

The flour for the *udvapanī*, the vessel for clarified butter (*ājya-sthālī*), and likewise the wood-chipping tool (*vidhmapravraścana*)—these are employed in the ritual implements, such as the discus (*cakra*) and others, along with the *madantī* water. (37–48)
The conclusion regarding the state of having accomplished all that was to be done for one who has sought refuge is as follows:
"Having worshipped Him in this manner, with all his sins utterly destroyed and having performed hundreds of sacrifices, he shall become [liberated]; of this there is no doubt. (37–49)
p. 360) For those who do not propitiate Sudarśana according to the sequence described above, there is the attainment of afflictions;
thus is that Sudarśana endowed with many kinds of forms.
Having performed that [rite], but not having established [the deity] therein, neither kings nor even ministers [should proceed].
Their prosperity was instantly destroyed and they were humiliated by their enemies;
due to the absence of worship, they fell from their kingdom and suffered for a long time. (37-51)
For those who do not propitiate Sudarśana, the fault of killing a Brahmin and other such evils arises in their kingdom;
O great sage, the compassionate Ṛgvedic śruti declares regarding this: "One's own kingdom may become defiled by the faults of killing a Brahmin and the like. (1) 37–52.
For kings who do not propitiate the Sudarśana [discus], there is an absence of affection from their subjects;
for because they do not contemplate it, all those dwelling within its domain become disaffected when the great king has committed an offense. (37–53)
Due to the failure to propitiate Sudarśana, the subjects of the kingdom also experienced great suffering; moreover, those who lacked faith in this matter became miserable in this very life.
In this regard, two Vedic passages from the *Ṛgveda* should be understood: "He who [worships] with fuel, he who with oblations, he who with the Veda..."
The mortal who, performing the sacrifice well, offers oblations to Agni with reverence—his swift steeds hasten forward;
his glory is most resplendent. Neither distress caused by the gods nor that wrought by mortals from any quarter shall reach him. (Rigveda 8.19.6)
After death, they fall further and further down; they do not attain happiness anywhere. (37.54)
The conclusion regarding the attainment of all fruits through the propitiation of Sudarśana:
for those who have properly taken refuge in that form of sacrifice, the Lord has performed the initiation for the purpose of providing protection.
Extremely terrifying, endowed with sixteen arms, and intent upon the destruction of his own enemies' factions. || 37-55 ||
Having depicted on a cloth or fashioned from stone an image of the form described above— one who holds all weapons and is accompanied by personified missiles—
Or having fashioned his image out of metals. || 37-56 ||
The king who, having performed the consecration, worships the Lord of Sudarśana with devotion,
shall have his desires fulfilled in an instant.
And there shall be the destruction of its opposing factors. || 37-57 ||
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of Prapatti, Synonymous with Nyāsa," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
Chapter Thirty-Eight, titled "The Prescription of Methods for the Cessation of Diseases such as Fever," beginning from verse 2376:
A single meditation quickly destroys a multitude of sins numbering many millions.
We meditate upon that divine splendor of the god Sudarśana.
Following a restatement of what has been said, Nārada asks about the means for liberation from disease:
"The supreme protection of kings from their enemies has been explained by you."
In the same way, all human goals have been proclaimed by the Omniscient One. (38.1)
The means for achieving that and other matters have been set forth as an incidental discussion;
now, O Blessed One, explain this to me as I ask. (38.2)
For kings, their ministers, and likewise for other men as well, there are exceedingly cruel diseases that stand in opposition to the goals of human life. (38-3)
For they do indeed arise; by what means is their liberation accomplished?
Ahirbudhnya speaks on the causes of the arising and destruction of disease:
Well asked, O sage, by what diseases these unbearable afflictions arise. || 38-4 ||
Listen, I shall now tell you that by which they are destroyed:
during the dissolution of primordial nature (*prākṛta-pralaya*), when the entire world has reached its re-absorption, there is an absence of pleasure for the solitary Supreme Person. (38.5)
O great sage, when the lifespan of Brahmā has been exhausted and all things mobile and immobile have perished, when all beings have dissolved into the primordial source of existence; 38-6.
When the elemental [tanmātras], the senses, and the fiery [ego] have merged into the Great One (mahat), and that Great One has then passed into Prakṛti characterized by intellect (buddhi); || 38-7 ||
And so, when that [Prakṛti] has dissolved into the Puruṣa, the twenty-fifth principle, and when she too has dissolved into the lotus-eyed Puruṣa; || 38-8 ||
Having withdrawn everything into Himself, that very Supreme Person, the Lord, the lotus-eyed one, the Supreme Self who consists of the universe, [remains]. (38–9)
At that time, the eternal one did not find delight in being alone;
for the sake of divine play, he—the lotus-eyed one—again created this world for the sake of his sport. (38.10)
The manifestation of name-and-form:
he, the all-pervading one, first fashioned names and forms for everything;
the sport of the Supreme Self, by means of primordial nature (prakṛti) which serves as the instrument of his play.
The Lord [perceives] primordial nature, consisting of the three qualities, as the instrument for his divine play.
Having further created the notion of *māyā*, Janārdana took delight in it;
for she is the concealment of the true nature of both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*), and she is endowed with all the respective powers of all beings. (38.12)

Deluding both the individual soul and the Supreme, and likewise extending the notion of being an object of enjoyment toward herself, she exists for the purpose of concealing the true natures of the two. (38-13)
The transmigratory existence of the individual soul (jīva) results from its subjection to primordial nature (prakṛti); thus, this entire world wanders about rendered helpless by her.
Primordial nature is the cause of the delusion that the body is the self.
By that very [ignorance], a person first forms the notion of a self within the body.
That very [notion] is the cause of the cognition of ownership regarding one's own [possessions];
from that, one develops a sense of "mine" toward sons and others connected to the body,
which results in the strengthening of the latent impressions (vāsanā) arising from the notions of "I" and "mine."
Then his latent impressions (vāsanās) arise from egoism (ahaṃkāra) and from the sense of "mine" (mamata).
O Sage, [affections] are firmly bound for a long time toward the body, sons, and so forth;
through the medium of attachment and aversion, the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) arising from those [affections] become the cause of merit and demerit.
Therefore, [this applies] toward one's own body, sons, and others who are benefactors or malefactors. (38–16)
Attachment and aversion arise, and through these two one exerts oneself; consequently, this person accumulates karma arising from them that leads to an evil or a pleasant rebirth. (38.17)
From that, there is the attainment of the fruition of karma in the form of birth, lifespan, and experience;
one undergoes those fruitions characterized by birth, lifespan, and experience.
Indeed, the creation of the body is solely for the purpose of experiencing the fruits of *prārabdha* karma.
Therefore, it is for the sake of experiencing the fruits of both types of karma. || 38-18 ||
This body of the embodied being has been created as a result of past actions (*prārabdha*).
Diseases arise from sins; indeed, ailments manifest in the body only within the context of *prārabdha* karma. (38-19)
Various other supreme sufferings are experienced by embodied beings;
among those, first is the means for pacifying fever, whether the king, a minister, or another person is overcome by fever. (38-20)
The Mahāsudarśana yantra has been described by those skilled in mantras;
[it is used with] guḍūcī stalks four finger-breadths long, sprinkled with clarified butter.
With this mantra, one should offer a thousand oblations into the blazing fire;
and having drawn a lotus-wheel upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with rice grains, [one should proceed].
Having placed a vessel there and having set down clarified butter filling a *prastha*,
one should mount a lamp upon threads measuring a *pala* in weight.
There, the knower of mantras, having invoked him with this mantra,
[should do so] then upon a pure, adorned sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the western quarter.
Having spread *kalamā* rice there, one should place the *māhendra* maṇḍala;
in its center, one should place a six-spoked wheel, and in the middle of that, the *tāra* (the syllable Om).
Having wrapped a beautiful new pitcher with a web of thread, and having filled it with waters mixed with camphor, sandalwood, and saffron; || 38-26 ||
Outside of that, one should worship him with sandalwood and other offerings, as well as with unbroken grains (akṣata).
[One should offer] the five jewels, a lotus, dūrvā grass, and gold. (38.27)
One should place śyāmāka grain, viṣṇuparṇī, and the goddess inside; having encircled the middle of the jar with a new silk cloth and a garland of nine [flowers]. (38.28)
Having established that auspicious [mantra] in the center of the *tāra* (the syllable Om), joined with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*),
and meditating upon it as the full moon, one should there invoke the Lord.

Having worshipped that [image] according to the rules with incense, lamps, garlands, and other offerings, [one should present] śāli rice combined with curd, honey, clarified butter, and all kinds of side dishes. (38–30)
One should offer to the deity the heart-pleasing and excellent oblation of jaggery with clarified butter;
thereafter, being composed, one should present the bali offering in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Then, O Nārada, one should offer rice-gruel, white flowers, incense, lamps, and so forth to the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) as well as to the Lord of the Field (kṣetreśa).
Then, having seated the patient—who is afflicted with fever—upon a seat facing the east, one should place a mirror before him so that his reflection appears within it. (38–39)
Taking a water-pot, he should consecrate the mirror with the mantra;
immediately, one shall be freed from fever, like the moon released from a cloud. (38–34)
Then, to the learned twice-born, especially to those devoted to Viṣṇu,
[he gave] three niṣkas of gold, a droṇa of clarified butter, and likewise a cow.
O Sage, one should give camphor, sandalwood, and even pure garments to a single person, or rather, to one who knows Brahman. (38–39)
Then he shall immediately become restored to health for as long as he lives; of this there is no doubt.
This is the treatment for diseases according to their nature, with distinctions based on dosage. (38-37)
The Pacification of Royal Consumption: O best of sages, when a king or similar person is overcome by royal consumption (rājayakṣman),
[one should perform the rite] with fuel-sticks of Apāmārga smeared with honey in a fire of Khadira wood.
The one most skilled in mantras should offer a thousand oblations with this mantra;
then, in the western direction, in the fire prepared as before.
Having placed a lamp upon two *palas* of wicks in a vessel filled with one *āḍhaka* of clarified butter, he should thereafter invoke the deity with the mantra. (38–40)
Then, on the western side, which is adorned with rice offerings,
one should prepare a pure, decorated sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) and draw the Maheśvara-maṇḍala.
As before, having inscribed a six-spoked wheel, one should place the syllables of the mantra upon its spokes and the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) upon the hub (*tāraka*). (38–42)
Having placed the consecrated jar there upon the mandala as before,
one should invoke the deity and worship him, who is in the form of the wheel, as previously described.
One should offer the oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with sugar, honey, and clarified butter;
and one should perform the bali offering as before, specifically with milk-rice.
Having covered this [image of] the person to be subdued with a blanket, one should place it facing east upon a seat before the Guru, Kṣetrapāla, Vighneśa, Durgā, and the Guardians of the Quarters.
One should sprinkle him while he is seated with water from the ritual jar according to the mantra; furthermore, one should bathe him daily, having first entered his reflection in a mirror. (38–46)
Two niṣkas of gold, two niṣkas of silver, a woolen blanket, a garment worn [by oneself], and a droṇa measure of sesame seeds. || 38–47 ||
A water-pot, a bronze vessel, an umbrella, and likewise sandals,
[should be given] to a single learned Brāhmaṇa who is indeed a believer.
One should give all these things preceded by every form of hospitality;
having thus honored the practitioner with wealth, one should remain self-restrained. (38–49)
Immediately thereafter, one is liberated from that great disease; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, O great sage, when one is afflicted by the disease of prameha, there is the pacification of the prameha disease.
The mantra-practitioner should offer a thousand oblations with this mantra using wood from the *bailva* tree;
he should present an offering of rice mixed with black gram (*māṣa*) and perform the *bali* rite with this same mantra.
One should perform the consecration oneself and carry out the other rites as before;
one should give a *droṇa* of black gram and five *niṣkas* of silver. (38–52)
O Great Sage, by giving one bull, one shall immediately become free from disease; likewise,
there is the pacification of abdominal diseases,
as well as great maladies of the stomach such as gulma, colic, and others that have persisted for a long time.
Since mortals have been overcome, I shall declare the counter-measure; listen.
Having worshipped the jar as before, attended by Sudarśana... (38–54)

Having kindled the fire in the center of the sacrificial pit in the eastern part of that [area], one should offer two thousand oblations of *arka* wood fuel sticks smeared with clarified butter. (38–55)
Likewise, the knower of mantras should offer sesame seeds with this mantra;
then, having touched the water in the pitcher, he should recite the mantra a thousand times.

Then, O Nārada, the practitioner of mantras should offer the bali-oblation to the guardians of the directions in due order, as well as to the bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and the lord of the field (kṣetrapāla).
With white cooked rice, white flowers, ground flour, and even white banners,
one should [worship] the deity consecrated within the water-pot.
Then one should worship according to the prescribed rule.
One should present as an offering an abundance of pure cooked rice, prepared with plenty of sugar, honey, and curd, and combined with all kinds of side dishes.
Then, having taken a little water from the jar and consecrated it with this mantra,
the practitioner should have the patient drink it while first reciting the mantra.
Then, the wise man should bathe [the image] facing east using water from a water-pot (kumbha),
and he should gratify seven Brahmins with libations.
Concentrated according to one's ability. || 38-61 ||
By honoring the guru with abundant wealth, garments, ornaments, and heaps of grain, all diseases in his stomach will undoubtedly perish. (38–62)
Thereupon the mortal shall become healthy and rejoice incessantly like a god.
(p. 370) Now hear the remedial procedure for a man overcome by epilepsy (*apasmāra*). 38-63.
On the ground smeared with cow-dung, level and endowed with auspiciousness,
one should spread two loads of sesame seeds there in a square shape.
There, one should install the Sudarśana machine, measuring two cubits,
according to the previously described method, even without all the other forms.
Without the *mantra* dedicated to Sudarśana and Nṛsiṃha,
one should [place] the great *yantra* of Sudarśana in the center according to the previously mentioned method.
Having made a formal resolve, he should place a water-pot wrapped with threads,
combined with the previously mentioned substances, and covered with a woolen blanket.
Having placed the fire in the mandala to the east according to the rules,
one should then perform two thousand oblations of sesame seeds with this mantra.
Then, touching the water-pot, the knower of mantras should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times; with this water consecrated by the mantra, [he should proceed].
One should consecrate him while he is seated facing east and overcome by the planets;
then, at that very moment, he shall become happy, freed from the influence of the planets.
Indeed, all other planets are unable even to gaze upon him;
therefore, he should worship his preceptor with wealth, grain, and garments. (38–71)
Whatever substance is in the yantra, that one should offer to it.
Afterwards, one should satisfy eight Brahmins with sesame seeds and gold. (38.72)
And one should also present a silver buffalo to the practitioner;
then that mortal shall become healthy and rejoice on earth like a god. (38.73)
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Prescribed Method for the Removal of Diseases such as Fever," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
From the beginning, verse number 2449:
The thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Great Empowerment which is the Means for Accomplishing All Fruits."
Meditated upon even once, it swiftly destroys the flood of tens of millions of sins;
we meditate upon that divine splendor of the Lord Sudarśana.
The question is: "By what practice is the accomplishment of all goals attained?
Nārada said:
"O Blessed One, O Omniscient One, tell me that by which, through a single action alone—"
By what means are all diseases destroyed, and all enemies as well? || 39-1 ||
By what means would there be the accomplishment of all goals? By what would the world come under one's control? Tell me, by what action is stainless sovereignty attained? (39-2)
The commencement of the subsequent discourse: Ahirbudhnya said—
“O great sage, listen with attention to this secret.”
For indeed, by means of that single application, all purposes are accomplished. (39.3)
The ritual procedure known as the Great Consecration (mahābhiṣeka),
intended for kings, ministers, and all officials who desire to ascend from their current station to the supreme station. (39-4)
Likewise, for others who desire whatever worldly things there may be, the rite called the Great Consecration (mahābhiṣeka) is the activity that accomplishes all aims. 39–5.
As an ancillary part of that [rite], there is an injunction regarding specific locations and so forth:
"In a pavilion in the garden of a temple of Vāsudeva, or in a temple, on a level and purified surface endowed with the eight auspicious signs. (39–6)
Having scattered there nine measures of *kalamā* rice and having placed the circle of Mahendra on the outside with jasmine flowers; || 39-7 ||
In the center, one should place the Sudarśana yantra along the very path by which it was released, and in its middle, one should install something most beautiful with fragrant flowers.
In the center of that, the practitioner should place the unsurpassed yantra-image;
in front of it, with the root mantra, he should place a water-pot adorned with threads.
One should invoke [the deity] into water scented with perfumes, endowed with the nine gems,
and adorned with the powder of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron.
It was surrounded by unbroken grains, wrapped in pure linen cloth, strewn with fragrant flowers, and provided with incense and lamps. || 39-11 ||
Likewise, when the work within the mouth [of the fire-pit] has been performed, one should install well-adorned full jars in the eight directions around the well-decorated Kumbha-kunda.

One should place [the deities] in the east and other directions with mantras such as *ācakrāya*, which serve as the enclosure of fire and the thorns; then, one should worship each of them individually with mantras. (39.13)
The procedure for the fire-pits (agnikuṇḍa) is in the directions starting with the east and in the center;
one should place the fire-pits on the eastern sides of all the water-jars (kumbha).
One should construct a well-adorned fire-pit in the middle, according to the characteristics of the temple. (39–14)
Description of the characteristics of the fire-pits starting from the east:
In the eastern direction it is quadrangular, while in the south-eastern direction it is triangular;
in the southern direction it resembles a half-moon, and in the south-western direction it is shaped like a womb (yoni). (39–15)
In the western direction (vāruṇī) it is like a lotus; in the north-western direction (vāyavyā) it is eight-cornered;
in the northern quarter it is circular; and in the north-eastern direction (aiśānī) it is six-cornered.
Regarding the oblations for the directions, one should select Vaiṣṇava priests;
one should employ eight Vaiṣṇava officiating priests for the oblations to the directions.
In the center, however, the practitioner, as a mantra-master, should offer oblations into the blazing fire.
Regarding the procedure for the house and the number of substances,
one should offer oblations with clarified butter (*ājya*) one thousand and eight times for each. This is the rule for the mantra in the fire sacrifice (*homa*).
In all cases, one should perform the oblation with the root mantra, preceded by meditative visualization.
The Procedure for the Consecration of the Vases:

At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice (homa), having worshipped the deity, the practitioner should touch all the vases and recite the mantra, enclosing the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) within it. (39.19)
Then, one should duly place [the disciple] one thousand and eight times before the great yantra upon a seat, in every respect.
First, there is the consecration with the waters from the jars starting from the east;
then, one should bathe him together with the sounds of kettledrums and the blasts of conchs and trumpets, using the waters from the jars beginning with the eastern one.
Then follows the consecration with the water from the full jar;
subsequently, having taken the well-adorned full jar in the middle, the mantra-practitioner himself should recite the mantra at the end after sprinkling [the disciple] with that water. (39–22)
Through the consecration as described, there is the attainment of all desires;
then, by that consecration, with all impurities washed away, he shines like the sun released from being shrouded by frost. (39.23)
Indeed, all desires choose that sinless one of their own accord;
therefore, without this king, you should perform the consecration of another.
When this great consecration has been thus fully performed by the Great-Souled One, whatever is desired by anyone will be in that person's hand; of this there is no doubt. (39-25)
One who desires long life obtains long life, and one who seeks health obtains that;
likewise, one who seeks wealth attains wealth, and one who desires cattle obtains cattle. (39.26)
One without a son obtains a son; one devoid of virtues becomes virtuous;
one desiring a daughter obtains a daughter; and one seeking victory attains victory. (39.27)
One devoid of status attains his own station, and one seeking the meaning of words attains the supreme state;
one desiring food obtains abundant food, and one seeking fame enjoys renown. (39.28)
What is the use of saying much more here? Whatever resides in the mind, that very thing one attains immediately; no deliberation is required in this matter. (39.29)
First is the procedure for the worship of the practitioner;
then, a man who has thus received consecration and whose desires are fulfilled [should worship] with gold, many jewels, garments, garlands, and ointments. (39–40)
One should properly honor the practitioner and give him a cow together with its calf,
as well as whatever remaining materials and the implements for the consecration.
And he should likewise give a vessel filled with milk-rice (pāyasa) to the officiating priests and the Brahmins; as for the method of satisfying them,
he should gratify all the officiating priests by giving one niṣka to each.
Being composed, he should satisfy other Brahmins according to his ability. (39–32)

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Great Consecration, which is the Means for Attaining All Fruits," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrī Pañcarātra*.
Chapter Forty, titled "The Description of the Nature and Power of the Astras," from the beginning: Verse 2481.
When meditated upon even once, it swiftly destroys a multitude of sins numbering many millions.
We meditate upon that divine splendor of the god Sudarśana.
Having first repeated what was said, Nārada asked about the configuration, power, and essential nature of the weapons:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, worshipped by the best of the immortals of the universe..."
Whatever was previously asked by me has been explained by him in accordance with reality.
"You have correctly and in full detail explained to me, who asked, the forms of all the divine weapons, which consist of the nature of mantras. (40.2)
O scorcher of enemies, if your heart is inclined toward me with favor, you should tell me what the shapes and what the powers of these weapons are.
In order to explain what follows that, Ahirbudhnya proclaims their supreme secrecy:
"This is the supreme secret, unspeakable, and exceedingly difficult to attain."
Weapons do not manifest in their own essential form within the range of direct perception; indeed, no weapons appear in their own essential form to anyone.

Indeed, those [weapons] are commissioned by the gods and asuras in the form of mantras for the sake of the gods' mission toward Indra; at one time they come within their range during the slaying of Vṛtra by Vāsava in his own form. (40–5)
"These [mantras] manifested themselves, thinking, 'This is the work of the gods.

When a task cannot be accomplished through the form of a mantra, they reveal their own true nature; and when a task cannot be accomplished by means of the forms of mantras, they manifest from their own essential being. (40–6)
And they manifest most terrifying weapons, O Sage;
by the mere sight of them, the enemy soldiers are destroyed. (40.7)
The Blessed One maintains them in their own essential form;
the Blessed One, being the very nature of the wheel, sustains them according to their own nature.
This is the promise to explain their essential nature and their powers.
Likewise, I shall describe their essential natures and their powers to you.
1—O Sage, first hear the true nature of the Nārāyaṇa weapon:
it has a thousand streams, is exceedingly fierce, and possesses a splendor equal to a thousand suns. (40.9)
The *taijasa* [astra] has a broad tip and resembles a deluding flower;
the *pāśupata* [astra] is like the moon on the first day of the lunar fortnight, with its center illuminated by eight corners.
This Pāśupata weapon is considered to have a hundred streams and is radiant with lightning;
the Brāhma weapon is endowed with a thousand spokes and has a form resembling a mass of lightning. (3–40.11)
The Brahma weapon is described as resembling a bundle of grass, graspable by the fist at its tip;
the Brahmaśiras weapon is terrifying, formidable with fangs, with bared lips and tawny eyes.
This [mantra] with its tip of hair grasped as tawny is considered the Brahmaśiras;
it is known as the Viṣṇucakra weapon, the thousand-spoked Sudarśana.
6— The wise know the yawning weapon (*jṛmbhaṇāstra*) to have eight faces and limbs, and its staff to be of such a nature.
7— The weapon of the noose of time (*kālapāśāstra*).
The noose of terrible form is indeed known as the "noose of Time" (kālapāśa). || 40-14 ||
8—The Āgneya weapon:
a six-pointed weapon with blazing flames, the supreme Āgneya weapon.
9—The Hayaśiras weapon.
The weapon known as Hayaśiras is considered to be horse-headed and filled with flames.
10. The *prasvāpana* (sleep-inducing) weapon: it causes sleep and resembles a cluster of *kuvalaya* lotus buds. 11. The *tāmasa* (darkness-inducing) weapon.
The weapon of darkness (tāmasāstra) is described as resembling water mixed with drops of water.
12—The Time-Weapon:
the terrifying Time-Weapon, a staff crowded with sixty bells.
13—The Staff-Wheel Weapon.
The pair of wheels at the beginning and end, along with the staff, is known as the "staff-wheel" (daṇḍacakra).
14. The Kālacakra weapon: the Kālacakra is four-cornered, with the zodiac signs situated along its perimeter.
15. The Dharmacakra weapon.
The wheel of dharma should be well-rounded and marked with the ten weapons of sacrifice.
16. The Śaiva weapon is the Śaiva [weapon]; it is proclaimed to be like a staff with a hundred-faced fire.
17. The trident weapon (śūlāstra).
The trident (śūla), however, is said to have three prongs, with sharp edges and a fine handle. || 40.19 ||
18. The axe-weapon (*paraśvastra*), axes, and the fierce weapon (*raudrāstra*) with its sharp edge, which is terrifying;
(p. 381) 19. The trident-weapon (*triśūlāstra*).
The trident, its tip marked with three spikes, should be like a staff. || 40-20 ||
20— The wise say that the form of the terrible Nārāca weapon is the Ghorāstra.
21— The Aghorāstra.
With a black face, tawny eyes, and a mass of flaming hair bound upward.
This is declared to be the Aghora weapon, and by name it is the Asidhāraka. The Sammohana weapon is named Sammohana; it is like a lotus joined with its stalk.
23. The Aiṣīka weapon:
the wise say that the Aiṣīka weapon has the appearance of a reed-shaft.
24. The Aindrachakra weapon.
It has four corners marked with vajras, shines like a dancer, and possesses immeasurable luster.
That weapon known as the Aindra-cakra is terrifying to the enemies of others;
the Śuṣkāśani weapon always has all its limbs ablaze and is fearsome with the form of a buffalo.
This weapon, resembling glowing embers, is called the Dry Thunderbolt (Śuṣkāśani). (p.
382) 26. A weapon of that same kind, but white in color, is known as the Wet Thunderbolt (Ārdrāśani). 40-25.
27. The Painākāstra:
The supreme Paināka weapon, resembling the bow of Takṣaka.
28. The Kaṅkālāstra.
The weapon known as Kaṅkāla shall be terrifying, having the form of a Piśāca.
29— They say the skull-mālā is the supreme *kāpālāstra* weapon; 30—
the *saurāstra* weapon.
The saura-astra is fully described as the continuous succession of the solar disc.
31— The Varuṇapāśa weapon, known as the Varuṇapāśa, which has a cool appearance yet is extremely terrible;
32— the Saṃtāpana weapon.
They know this [instrument], which consists of a staff richly provided with clusters of spikes, as Saṃtāpana (the Tormentor). || 40.28 ||
33. The Vāruṇa weapon is shaped like a net and is provided with thirty-two openings. 34. The Dharmapāśa weapon.
The bond consisting of all reality is known as the "noose of Dharma."
35–36. The Weapon of the Two Śaktis:
One Śakti is already well known; now another Śakti is described.
It has two heads and a single stalk, and is adorned with ten bells. 40–30.
37. The Vāyavya weapon;
the Vāyavya weapon is recited as being like a spotted antelope with horns.
38. The Mausala weapon.
The Mausala weapon is said to be like a blazing bolt of lightning.
39. The Gāndharva weapon:
the Gāndharva weapon is taught as having a form resembling the handle of a lute (vīṇā).
40. The Darpaṇa weapon.
The weapon called Darpaṇa is said to resemble the full moon.
41. The Drying Weapon: the drying, the formidable, the horn-weapon that withers the enemy.
42. The Piśāca Weapon.
The supreme Paiśāca weapon is declared to be Ulkāmukha.
43. The *Tejaḥprabhāstra* is known as the *Tejaḥprabha*; it resembles a spear and is capable of rending the enemy. 44. The *Aindrāstra*.
The Aindra weapon is known to be the form of the thunderbolt and the abode of splendors.
45— The *vilāpanāstra* (the weapon of dissolution),
the weapon named *vilāpana*, is declared to be the bearer of the rain-clouds (*dhārādhara*).
46— The *vaidyādharāstra* (the weapon of the Vidyādharas).
They call that the Vaidyādhara weapon, while the Puṣpamālā is indeed the Mohinī.
47. The Kaṅkāla weapon is the weapon known as Kaṅkāla, resounding with the great bell. 48. The Modakya weapon.
There is a supreme creeper named Modakī, abounding in flowers.
49. The Śikharāstra:
that which is called the Śikhara is declared to be the khaṭvāṅga weapon.
50. The Krauñcāstra.
The great Krauñca-missile is here said to be a bird in the form of a curlew.
51. The sword-jewel weapon, called the sword-jewel, is a divine weapon, a sword of great luster.
52. The pacification weapon.
The weapon known as Praśamana is said to resemble a banner.
53— The weapon beloved by Kandarpa,
and the most beautiful weapon beloved by Kandarpa, which is sugarcane;
54— the weapon of Madana.
And the weapon Madana, resembling a chowrie, which brings fear to enemies.
55. Those skilled in weapons know that weapon to be the Saumanāstra, which has the appearance of a palanquin.
56. The Satyāstra.
A rosary of large pearls is indeed the true weapon that accomplishes all goals.
57. The *saṃvartaka* weapon is the weapon named *saṃvartaka*; it is proclaimed as the great conch (*mahāśaṅkha*).
58. The *māyādharā* weapon.
They call this weapon Māyādharāhvaya, and it is indeed Śākhi.
59. They declare the Soma-missile (*somāstra*) to be an arrow possessing the luster of a crescent moon.
60. [Next is] the Tvaṣṭṛ-missile (*tvāṣṭrāstra*).
And the Tvaṣṭra weapon, together with its staff, is said to be equal to a Caitya. || 40-42 ||
61. The weapon of cold, named Śīteṣu; the river Kumbhāsyā, flowing from her, is the most excellent of streams.
62. The weapon of the female organ (bhaga).
One should know that the triangle, like a staff, is the weapon of the Bhaga, possessing immeasurable luster.
63—The weapon of the fetter is known as the *sadāmana*; the wheel is called the *nirara*. 64—The weapon of truth (*satyavadastra*).
They know that great element, which possesses truth, to be this one with its mouth wide open.
65. The Vāraṇa weapon, known as Vāraṇa, which has the mouth of a serpent and is the supreme goad;
66. The Dhṛṣṭa weapon.
The headless trunk (kabandha) is described as having a bold belly and a wide-open mouth.
67—The weapon of Bhṛśāśvatanaya is known as the two-edged saw, named Bhṛśāśvatanaya. (p. 387) 68—The weapon of Satyakīrti.
But Satyakīrti is called Makara, with his mouth wide open. || 40-46 ||
69— The wise know that delusion is the weapon of delusion, and the upraised hood of a serpent is the weapon. 70— The weapon of impetuosity.
A weapon of impetuous force, resembling lightning, the destroyer of all other weapons.
71— The Sarvanābhā weapon and the weapon called Sarvanābhā are said here to be the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
72— The Parāṅmukha weapon.
They know the weapon called Parāṅmukha as the head of Pañcānana.
73. The Jṛmbhaka weapon:
that which is named Jṛmbhaka is described as having red eyes and three pentads.
74. The Pratihāra weapon.
The spear, Kunta, which was supremely radiant, was indeed the weapon known as Pratihāra.
75. The weapon with its face turned downward is the being known as Ṛkṣāsya, designated by the name Avāṅmukha.
(p. 388) 76. The wealth-weapon.
The weapon called Dhana is equal to a crown and possesses immeasurable luster.
77. The Grain Weapon; this is the supreme Grain Weapon, the binding of the rice-cluster.
78. The Great Elemental Weapon.
They declare the Great Being to have bull-like eyes and to be marked by a bull's face.
79. The weapon of assuming any form at will (kāmarūpāstra), the great weapon of assuming any form at will (kāmarūpāstra), which resembles the sun; 80. The weapon of the firm navel (dṛḍhanābhāstra).
The weapon named Dṛḍhanābha shall appear, and the serpent shall be endowed with many hoods.
81. The *kāmarucya* weapon; the weapon named *kāmaruci* is described as a *svastika*.
82. The *sunābha* weapon.
The sharp razor-edged weapon with a beautiful hub is declared to be the unsurpassed missile.
83. The Makarāstra:
the divine weapon named Makara, which resembles the handle of a lamp.
(p. 389) 84. The Daśākṣāstra.
One should know that this ten-finger span is the unobstructed reach of the sword.
85. Regarding the Vetālāstra:
it is called the Vetāla because it possesses a camel-like face and is endowed with movement.
86. The Daśavaktrāstra.
But when she who has ten faces is situated in one place, it is called "Ten-Faced" (Daśavaktra).
87— The weapon called Rucira shall be the most terrible plow-weapon (hala).
88— The Daśakarṇa weapon.
A ten-year-old girl with a face like a crow's is proclaimed to have ten ears.
89. The Yogaṃdhara missile is known as the Yogaṃdhara, which has a mouth wide open like that of a night-prowling creature (divābhīta). 90. The Vāruṇa missile.
This Vāruṇa [weapon] slays enemies and serves as a warder-off of the missiles of others.
91. They indeed call it the "sleepless weapon," the "weapon that does not slumber," which awakens the world-protector.
92. The axe-weapon (*kuṭhārāstra*).
The weapon called Bhettṛ is declared to be a battle-axe that splits the enemy.
93—The Śatodara weapon; the Śatodara weapon is a being endowed with a hundred bellies. 94—The Saumanasa weapon.
The weapon named Saumanasa is a cluster of hibiscus flowers.
95— The weapon of Padmanābha, the great being Padmanābha, whose navel is adorned with a lotus.
96— The weapon of Mahānābha.
But Baka, who had a hideous neck, [discharged] the weapon known as Mahānābha.
97. The Science of Astronomy: That which is called *jyautiṣa* is designated as the supreme celestial vehicle (*vimāna*).
98. The Projectile Weapon (*kṣepaṇāstra*).
Stepping forward is declared to be the hurling [of the weapon]; it is the great stepping forward with the supreme weapon.

99. The weapon of the three groups (trairāśika) is the three-grouped one (trairāśi), which has the face of a monkey, possesses wings, and has feet like those of a man. 100. The weapon of the garland with flames (sārcirmālya).
Wearing a garland of flames, he was a great being with one foot and many hands.
p. 391) 101—One should know this Vimalāstra (Stainless Weapon) as a palanquin (*ḍolikā*) shaped like crystal.
102—The Dhṛtikāstra (Weapon of Fortitude).
Those who know the ancient lore describe this extremely terrible *dhṛtikāstra* as being joined with the faces of a boar, a lion, a human, a dog, and an elephant. (40.63)
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Weapon and its Power," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrī Pāñcarātra*.
From the beginning, verse number 2544:
Chapter Forty-one, titled "The Description of the Slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha," intended to explain the nature of the sword, its retention, and its purpose.
Meditated upon even once, it swiftly destroys a multitude of tens of millions of sins;
we meditate upon that divine splendor of the Lord Sudarśana.
The Blessed One asked Nārada about the nature of the weapons, their retention, the specific times for their use, and their purposes: Nārada said:
"O Blessed One, these weapons have been described according to their essential nature; it was previously stated that the Lord assumed them in their respective forms. (41-1)
O Lord, Sovereign of the Universe, at what time, in what place, and for what purpose was that performed?
If you have grace toward me, resolve this question. (41.2)
By way of declaring the supreme secrecy of the matter asked about, Ahirbudhnya makes his promise to answer it:
"I shall declare to you the supreme, great, and most wonderful secret."
O Nārada, [this was told] to him who asked with devotion regarding the Supreme Self.
At the conclusion of the dissolution,
at the end of the previous kalpa, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person,
desiring to create the world and eager for the delight of his divine play, set his mind upon creation. (41.4)
Hari first brought forth by himself the two— Pradhāna and Puruṣa— and then produced the creation of the world, from Prakṛti, Puruṣa, Mahat, and so on,
ending with the Viśeṣas. (41.5)
The creation of the four-faced Brahmā preceded by the production of the cosmic egg:
having produced the egg by all of them together, they created Brahmā within it;
for the purpose of the creation of progeny, the instruction of the Vedas was given to the four-faced one.
"Create progeny," [saying this] Janārdana gave the Vedas to him.
The commencement of the four-faced one’s creation of beings; thereafter, he began to create various kinds of progeny.
In that context, the birth of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, who were arrogant because of their strength.
In the meantime, immediately after the creation by Brahmā, two Daityas appeared.
From his two thighs were born the two powerful Dānavas Madhu and Kaiṭabha,
intoxicated with pride, possessed of massive bodies, and arrogant in their strength.
The abduction of the Vedas from the Four-faced One by Madhu and Kaiṭabha:
Having seen Brahmā of immeasurable luster about to commence creation, those two then entered him through their illusory power and seized the Vedas from him. (41.9)
Due to the theft of the Vedas, the four-faced one became incapable of creation; consequently, the Lord of Creatures was unable to create all beings.
This was the manner of the thought of the despondent four-faced one.
Then Prajāpati became filled with supreme despondency. (41.10)
"The Lord Hari commanded me, 'Create progeny.
However, it is not possible to create various kinds of beings without the Vedas. (41.11)
"Today these Vedas have been taken from me by the two Dānavas through their illusory power (māyā).
What other task remains?"—thus he fell into deep reflection. (41.12)
Having thus resolved upon his purpose, the four-faced Creator, the lotus-born Brahmā, determined in his mind what he must do and proceeded to the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk.
There, with four faces, he praised the Lord; he lauded the lotus-eyed, infallible Lord of Gods:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Vāsudeva, whose nature is pure knowledge. (41.14)
Salutations to You, the great-souled one, whose root is boundless bliss, who possesses vast abundance,
and whose form is inconceivable power, sustaining all the worlds.
Salutations to you, whose sovereignty and heroism are boundless, the treasury of splendors;
salutations to you, the inner controller of the universe, whose sole form is pure being.
Salutations again and again to You, whose every ornament is a support for the faultless,
and who bear the conch, discus, mace, sword, and Śārṅga bow as Your weapons.
Salutations again and again to the illustrious Puṣkarākṣa, the Supreme Person, who is served by the divine sages headed by Viṣvaksena. (41.18)
Salutations again and again to the one whose abode is the sky consisting of divine bliss, who always sports with the worlds through the protection [of them] from creation and calamities. 41-19.
Salutations to you, the possessor of great majesty, who possesses every form,
and who manifests a manifold array of emanations out of affection for those who take refuge in you.
Salutations to you who have undertaken the initiation for the destruction of all those who harbor hatred;
salutations to you whose remembrance destroys the dense mass of suffering scorched by the three-fold afflictions.

"Salutations to Viṣṇu, whose nature is inconceivable, the witness of all actions; salutations to the Blessed Four-faced One. Having heard this hymn of praise regarding the granting of a vision by the Blessed One, the Lord Puruṣottama [spoke]. (41.22)
The gracious, lotus-eyed one appeared before him.
Seeing that most wonderful being, he was supremely delighted; having bowed down, he related his own account with four mouths. (41-23)
Endowed with humility, the one of immeasurable soul related his own history;
having heard from the Blessed One this account of the transgression of the two Dānavas, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, the subduer of enemies [related it].
Smiling gently, the Blessed One called to mind Madhu and Kaiṭabha; by his mere thought, those two then arrived at the door of Madhu and Kaiṭabha. (41.25)
Then, seeing Madhu and Kaiṭabha arrived there, arrogant in their strength,
Madhusūdana spoke to them with a voice as deep as the rumbling of clouds.
"The Vedas were brought by you two from the mouth of Brahmā as given by me;
it has been heard that this was through *māyā*, yet it is certainly not fitting to act in this manner here. (41.27)
"Let all the Vedas be given to that Parameṣṭhin.
When the Lord had spoken thus, the two great Asuras, blinded by intoxication, replied to him in this manner, while disregarding the words of the Blessed One. (41–28)
They replied to him: "We will by no means give these away;
we ourselves shall soon create all various kinds of progeny. (41.29)
"O Blessed One, what need is there here for the Supreme Lord [Brahmā] without the Vedas?
Having heard those words of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, the Blessed One, his eyes bloodshot with anger, gave the command to Viṣvaksena to slay them. (41.30)
The Lord of the World resolved to slay those two evil-minded ones:
"Having slain these two wicked and unrestrained men, who are today arrogant with pride... (41.31)
"Take these Vedas and deliver them to this Brahmin," the Lord commanded Śeṣāśana, who stood with palms joined in reverence.
Then, having agreed to that, he brought together all the Vaiṣṇava armies for the equipment of battle; he set forth from there to fight, and those two Dānavas were likewise prepared. (41.33)
Then those two, by means of their illusory power (māyā), created a vast army;
a tumultuous battle ensued between the two armies, and a fierce conflict took place between both sides. || 41-34 ||
Then that battle occurred, such as had never been seen or heard before.
Viṣvaksena, having long since recognized the invincibility of the two wicked Dānavas in combat, reported their unconquerable nature in the presence of the Blessed One.
Viṣvaksena, however, unimpededly reported to the Lord that the Blessed One was setting out for battle, preceded by the manifestation of the true forms of all his weapons.
Then, extremely enraged, Janārdana went forth.
Seeing those two engaged in combat, Hari himself, in the form of a discus,
stood there with sixty-two hands, wielding a collection of divine weapons.
A description of the Lord’s form, which assumes the nature of all weapons:
Having seen him exceedingly enraged, resembling a thousand suns, and surrounded by blazing weapons held in the tips of his hands— (41.38)
It was endowed with tawny hair standing upright, exceedingly terrifying,
its body pervading the limits of the cosmic egg, and resembling a hibiscus flower in color.
(398) It was endowed with three eyes whose fierce movements were rolling like those of a tawny cat;
it was graced by a terrifying face framed by curved eyebrows knit together. || 41.40 ||
With his bitten lips and blazing fangs from which sparks of fire issued forth,
he resembled the great ocean, a cage of sixty-two arms.
Wearing red garments, he is formidable and adorned with the *ālīḍha* stance;
he is further embellished with ornaments such as necklaces, armlets, earrings, and bracelets. (41–42)
It was endowed with the resonant sound of tinkling networks of small bells;
it was of wondrous form, incomparable, and possessed such great splendor.
Upon seeing that form, the armies of the Daityas were utterly destroyed;
those soldiers of the Daityas, who were like the ocean swelling at the end of a kalpa,
perished completely upon that sight, leaving only those two Dānavas remaining.
Seeing those two approaching in great agitation with their weapons raised,
the one of great splendor dispatched his terrifying discus for their slaughter.
With his supreme discus, he severed the heads of Madhu and Kaiṭabha at that very moment;
having recovered the Vedas from them, he presented them to the God.
After bestowing the Vedas upon Brahmā, Lord Hari vanished; having given them to Brahmā, the Divine Hari likewise disappeared.
Then, as before, the creation of beings was carried out by Brahmā.
Having recovered the Vedas, the Creator once again brought forth his subjects as before.
Such was the withdrawal of the form of the Blessed One, the wielder of the discus, whose very form is the discus.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine of the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*, intended to explain the nature of the bearing of weapons and its purpose.
From the beginning, verse 2591:
The forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Śrutakīrti, King of Kāśī."
Meditated upon even once, it swiftly destroys millions of floods of sins;
we meditate upon that divine splendor of the Lord Sudarśana.
Questions regarding the origin, deities, purposes, powers, and objects of meditation for the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra):
Nārada said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, honored by all beings!"
Whatever is to be heard by us has been heard by us in its entirety.
Now, however, I ask this: tell me what dwells in my mind—whence is the origin of his bodily mantras, and who is their deity? (42.2)
"For what purpose? What is the nature of the power? What is the object of meditation? Tell me this according to reality.
[This is] the commencement of the answer by way of explaining the secrecy of the matter asked about—Ahibudhnya says:
Listen with attention to this most excellent secret.

This six-syllable [mantra], extracted by me from the Atharva Veda refined by great mantras as the answer to the question of its origin, has been drawn forth like the Kaustubha gem from the ocean. (42–4)
(401) Likewise, O Sage, all these mantras were extracted from that [source].
The Lord Sudarśana himself gave the answer to the deities' question regarding the mantras of the limbs as well. (52–5)
The answer to the questions regarding the purpose and the power [of the mantra] is as follows:
the supreme act for one established in the great *sudarśana* mantra is the protection of the limbs.
This should be performed by means of the six-syllable [mantra], for thus these [limbs] possess equal power. (6)
This is the answer to the question regarding the object of meditation:
the eight-armed Lord is to be meditated upon by the very same path previously described. Everything has been fully explained; what else do you wish to hear? (42–7)
The question regarding the occasion for employing the weapons that cause cessation:
Nārada said—
O Blessed One, most noble one, eternally satisfied, ocean of compassion!
O ocean of eternal knowledge, action, sovereignty, and universal wisdom!
O All-pervading Lord, whatever was to be specifically stated regarding the Sudarśana great yantra, mantras, powers, ritual actions, and so forth, has been spoken by you.
O one of great luster, the origin of the weapons known as the Pravartakas has been described previously, as well as their essential nature, their powers, and their application.
"But regarding those [mantras] that cause cessation, O Guru, when and in what subject matter is their application? You ought to dispel this great doubt of mine. (42.11)
p. 402) The promise to speak thereafter:
Ahirbudhnya says—“Listen with attention; [I shall explain] the occasion for the ritual application.”
As I am correctly describing the weapons that cause [the enemy] to turn back.
O treasury of asceticism, know that when he is subjected to a great assault by celestial weapons and malevolent spells employed by others, that is the occasion for the application of his own power.
Regarding the question on the means of knowledge for overcoming and subduing others,
Nārada says:
"By what signs is the overcoming and subduing of others recognized?"
And likewise for kings, ministers, and other men as well. || 42-14 ||
Ahirbudhnya describes the signs that serve as the means for knowing that [knowledge]:
"The malevolent power of kings is characterized by these marks."
A transformation occurring at an improper time is terrible and pervades all spheres of experience.
Horsemen, elephant-riders, and ministers perish quite unexpectedly;
the king himself is afflicted, his body overwhelmed by a severe illness. (42.16)
Terrible-looking thunderbolts fall within his realm;
the earth yields little grain, and herds of cattle perish. (42.17)
In his realm, droughts occurred again and again;
moreover, the queens of that king were seized by severe illnesses. (42.18)
Serpents emerge from anthills at the palace gate and in the pavilion;
moreover, great meteors fall with a most terrifying sound.
The ministers, moreover, oppose one another out of envy;
and at night, Indra’s terrible bow shines forth from the cloudless sky. 42-20.
A great fear of fire arises here and there within the city;
jackals enter the inner sanctuaries and remain unchecked. (42.21)
At both twilights, terrifying and discordant cries resound in the blazing quarter;
the enemies of the king, arrogant in their strength, are besieging the city. (42.22)
Abiding in a state of torpor, he does not know for himself what ought to be done and what ought not to be done;
even in his dreams, he sees himself with a shaven head and clad in blue garments. (42.23)
One should recognize an act of sorcery directed against a rival by such signs as [the appearance of] one traveling toward the southern direction yoked to a donkey. (42.24)
If a *kṛtyā* born of hostile sorcery should enter a king, upon seeing it, he will undoubtedly perish immediately. (42.25)
Enveloped in garlands of flames, she destroys in an instant the sons, the ministers, the queen, and likewise the city— indeed, everything.
For the purpose of averting the hostile magic of others, there is the propitiation of Sudarśana, who wields the weapon that turns back [enemies].
Thus, when the king was afflicted by the hostile magic of another, [he propitiated] the Lord of great splendor together with the weapon that turns back [enemies]. (42.27) p. 404)
Then, one should satisfy with devotion the Lord who has the nature of the wheel,
using silver, gold, stone, or copper.
Having fashioned an image of Sudarśana, one should worship it as the bringer of cessation;
or, having painted it on a cloth, one should meditate upon him who is honored by the three worlds. (42.29)
In this way, through emanation from meditative absorption, or by means of worship, prostration, consecration, or hymn of praise, the king should fully gratify the deity. (42.30)
O Sage, in this way others, whether ministers or men, should likewise act;
through the propitiated Sudarśana, there occurs the burning away of hostile magic.
Thereupon, the Lord, the omnipresent one who is without beginning or end, was pleased.

But by means of his grace toward those who have taken refuge [in him], he reduces to ashes through mere remembrance even the malevolent spells performed by others that were directed at them, in an instant.

The Lord warded off the divine weapons with his own counter-weapons; he brought about the destruction of both the sorcery employed by the enemy and its practitioner. Indeed, he neutralized that most terrifying sorcery sent by the foe as it approached him.
Having himself gone forth in the form of the discus, that Lord of the universe,
the wielder of the weapon, then reduces even the one who employed it to ashes.
The example of the historical account of the King of Kāśī:
likewise, a king named Kāśīrāja, residing in Vārāṇasī, having worshipped Mahādeva Viśveśvara with a concentrated mind... (42.35)
Deluded, he indeed produced a *kṛtyā* with Kṛṣṇa as his target. That *kṛtyā* thus created was hideous and terrifying to behold. (42.36)
Having reached Dvārakā, he then went into the presence of Kṛṣṇa;
seeing her approaching, her face wreathed in garlands of flames.
The Blessed One dispatched the unsurpassed Sudarśana;
seeing it rushing toward him, blazing like a thousand suns, she [fled]. (42.38)
Afflicted by fear, she fled back the way she had come toward her employer;
he, having slain her as well as that King of Kāśī, likewise [entered] the city.
The wheel of great splendor returned once more to the side of Viṣṇu.
Listen now to me regarding this ancient history and account of past events, namely the illustration of the narrative concerning Śrutakīrti. 42-40.
King Śrutakīrti ruled the earth with its seven continents according to the Dharma;
he was renowned as Śrutakīrti, the lord of Saurāṣṭra, a subduer of enemies dwelling in the city of Bhadraśālā. (42–41)
Endowed with elephants, horses, and chariots, powerful like Vāsava,
devoted to the great Sudarśana mantra, and supremely righteous.
Bearing supreme devotion toward Sudarśana and intent upon its worship,
he enjoyed the sovereignty of the earth consisting of seven continents by its grace.

p. 406) Then Śrutakīrti set his mind upon conquering another world; desiring to win that other realm, he first performed worship to the Sudarśana discus and proceeded toward the Gandharva city named Svastika.
Endowed with the fourfold army, he worshipped Sudarśana.
The one of great strength ascended the wonderful chariot that moves at will;
then, endowed with power, he first set out through the atmosphere.
Description of the Excellent City of Svastika: Therein was a vast city of the Gandharvas called Svastika, possessed of supreme splendor, which was protected in this manner by Vīṇāvinodana. (42–46)
His enemy's troops were being warded off by weapons that moved of their own accord,
and he was surrounded by a fire that required no external fuel.
It was a supreme golden hall, adorned with jeweled gate-towers,
surrounded by mansions of precious stones, and filled with the sounds of singing.
It was graced with celestial chariots made of light, adorned with divine groves,
and frequented by lakes of golden lotuses, rivers, and ponds.
It was frequented by celestial women and served by apsarases;
it was always joined by gandharvas, kinnaras, siddhas, and cāraṇas.
Desirous of battle, Śrutakīrti, arrogant in his strength, besieged that city in such a manner;
then, with a vast army, he sought to fight Vīṇāvinodana.
Having heard of the dispatch of the army by the king of the Gandharvas, and hearing also of the siege by humans,
the king of the Gandharvas laughed and dispatched an army of Siddhas and Gandharvas. (42.52)
There, that tumultuous battle took place; he fought with that powerful king using sharpened arrows.
That great battle commenced, tumultuous and hair-raising. (42–53)
Then, with ease, the king caused the army of the Gandharvas to flee; Śrutakīrti pursued that Gandharva host,
which was overwhelmed by fear, back to its own city.
Hearing that the Gandharva king had set out himself for battle in his anger, Vīṇāvinodana, becoming exceedingly enraged,
mounted a great chariot and went forth accompanied by his soldiers.
The battle between the Gandharva king Śrutakīrti and [his opponent] continued for eight days;
then their combat became like that of Vṛtra and Vāsava.
Their soldiers struck one another with various kinds of arrows. (42–56)
There, the sky was completely covered by the showers of arrows from both sides;
neither victory nor defeat could be discerned in that battle between the two of them.
Thus, for eight days, there remained only this single, terrifying form [of conflict].
(p. 408) The king cut through the bow and other weapons of the Gandharva king and routed his army; thereafter, the king severed the Gandharva king’s bow. (42–58)
With straight-jointed arrows, he sent his banners, parasols,
and horses to the various quarters, driving his entire army away.
Perceiving that the king was invincible by weapons, the Gandharva king also fell into despondency;
seeing his own army defeated by men, he too became dejected.
Thinking, "The king of the Gandharvas is employing Gāndharva weapons against human forces;
I shall slay him with divine weapons," the one of great splendor discharged a Gāndharva weapon at that human army.
By that [means], the human army was bewildered;
by that very [means], the entire host of Śrutakīrti was deluded through the power of the Gāndharva weapon, and remained fixed right there in the battle.
By the power of Sudarśana, that divine weapon did not reach the king.
Then Śrutakīrti, being unable to counteract it, reported his own situation to his priest;
for Śrutakīrti lacked proficiency in those divine weapons. (42–63)
Unable to retaliate, the king approached his own domestic priest and informed that priest of what had occurred. (42–64)
After the family priest had first instructed him on seeking refuge in the Sudarśana [discus],
he, the knower of dharma and expert in the supreme weapons, spoke, imparting the mantras for all the missiles.
O Śrutakīrti, do not fear here; go to him alone for refuge. (42.65)
To the God who removes the suffering of those who bow before him, who bears the form of the Sudarśana discus, the source of all divine weapons without exception, the Supreme Lord; 42–66.
O Lord of the Earth, meditate upon the deity in the center of this great wheel, which is thus constituted, joined with sixty-four spokes, and provided with two rims.
Having thus meditated upon the supreme one, possessing sixty-two arms, extremely fierce, and bearing the weapon of destruction,
and having recited this mantra, look upon the army.
Thus he instructed him in all the weapon-mantras (astramantras).
Having received all the mantras that initiate and withdraw [the weapons], Śrutakīrti, whose strength had been restored by them, returned once more for battle. 42–69.
Returning once more to the battlefield, that king, victorious in assembly,
meditated upon the God who liberates one from the delusion of his own soldiers; reciting the mantra, he surveyed his army.
Then, having regained consciousness, he engaged once more in the great battle;
victory in the fight belonged to Śrutakīrti, and the subjugation of the world of the Gandharvas ensued.
Once again, combat broke out between both armies.
Having conquered Vīṇāvinodana in battle with divine weapons,
the powerful universal monarch brought that world under his own control.
Then,
honored by the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and even the Kinnaras and Cāraṇas,
he returned to his own city and reached his capital of Bhadraśālā once more with the splendor of victory. (42.73)
Having arrived, he ruled the earth just as the Lord of the Gods rules heaven;

then, his mind filled with wonder, he recalled the manner of his consultation with the family priest regarding the power of the Sudarśana [discus], and being struck with amazement once more by that power of the Sudarśana, [he spoke]. (42–74)
Approaching the family priest, who was like a blazing fire,
the lotus-eyed king consulted with him in this manner.
The statement that one's own prosperity has its cause in the grace of the Blessed One: "By the grace of the God, this earth of mine, girt by the ocean, has today come under my control."
And likewise, I believe that even in another world,
the Lord is indeed inclined toward showing me his grace.
Through the grace of the Blessed One, he declares the absence of doubt regarding his own attainment of liberation:
"This one, bearing the form of Cakra, will grant me, who am terrified of saṃsāra, final emancipation."
Thus, I have no doubt in this matter;
beyond this, we worship the Supreme Deity.
(p. 411) Regarding the king, the priest’s instruction on the installation of Sudarśana and so forth:
when the king had spoken thus, the high-minded priest addressed him with palms joined in reverence.
Having fashioned a preeminent celestial chariot, multi-colored and peaked, equipped with wheels and complete with its magical power (sādhya), || 42-78 ||
Having installed here, in the center of the excellent wheel,
[the deity] with sixty-two arms, possessing the *nivartaka* weapon,
having the form as described, and adorned with many ornaments—
Worship Sudarśana for the sake of all accomplishments. || 42-79 ||
Having been told by the king, "Let it be carried out exactly so," he accepted his words, which were endowed with ultimate truth, upon his head.
In that very city, the king, skilled in what ought to be done, caused [the work] to be performed.
For that purpose, the king provided means of livelihood for the twice-born;
he established one hundred and twenty twice-born men all around the temple of the gods.
Then, having established [shrines] and having given them many riches and many lands, he [bestowed these] upon them.
Having established the God as one possessed of sovereign power,
the king rejoiced, his desires fully attained;
thereafter, through the grace of the Blessed One, the king obtained the supreme goal of human existence.
Having worshipped the Lord there in Mahālaya day after day, one attains all desires;
thereafter, in no time at all, one becomes liberated from attachment.
And by his grace, he attained the supreme state. || 42-82 ||
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Kāśīrāja Śrutakīrti," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the illustrious *Pāñcarātra*.
From the beginning, verse number 2673:
The forty-third chapter, titled "The Contemplation of the Means for the Slaying of Jalandhara.
Even a single meditation [upon Him] swiftly destroys a multitude of tens of millions of sins.
We meditate upon that divine splendor of the god Sudarśana.
Nārada, having asked about the "how" of the entire wheel of the world, said:
"I ask you this again; tell me, O Lord of all."
All this, consisting of the wheel of the world, was previously proclaimed by you.
Therefore, tell me clearly when it was shown by the Lord;
you alone are the knower, and there is no one else besides you in the three worlds. (43.2)
In order to relate the narrative that follows these two chapters, an introductory story is told; first,
there is the determination of the gods and others as the initiators of the path of dharma,
[beginning with] Ahirbudhnya:
All the gods, the sages, Manu and his sons, as well as all the kings and the members of all castes who promote the path of dharma. (43-3)
The obstruction of Dharma by Dānavas and others (p.
414): "In the same way, all Dānavas, Bhūtas, Vetālas, and Rākṣasas, as well as cruel men, beasts, and bandits of terrifying form [are obstructors]. (43-4)
In the same way, O Sage, other people have entered an asuric womb;
all of these constantly and excessively bring about the destruction of dharma.

Thinking of a means for the destruction of sinners, Ahirbudhnya went to the peak of Mount Meru; thus, overcome by supreme anxiety as to by what means those evildoers might perish, he arrived at the summit of Meru. (43–6)
While I was established in that concentration and seated there, a vision of a particular splendor appeared to me in an instant;
a great light, difficult to behold and supremely radiant, became manifest.

Out of fear, preceded by the recitation of an Atharvan mantra, I beheld him once more; then, from that vision, I uttered the Atharvan mantra. While uttering that great mantra, I beheld that Great Light once again.
The question, preceded by the direct realization of the Sudarśana Puruṣa within that radiance:
"In that blazing splendor, [I beheld] the Puruṣa, dark-brown, with vital energy drawn upward, three-eyed, resembling a thousand suns. (43.9)
The supreme Sudarśana, situated in the center of a thousand-spoked wheel,
is garlanded with flames, difficult to behold, and undisturbed.
Having seen him, [Nārada], who was free from fear, asked, "Who are you? From where? To whom do you belong?
Thereupon, the Blessed One, being pleased, revealed his own true nature; then the Blessed One, that treasury of splendors, spoke with joy. (43.11)
"O Lord, from this day forward I shall be known by the name Sudarśana;
because I am difficult to behold yet possess great light, I am your Sudarśana. (43.12)
The narration of the reason for his arrival from Vaikuṇṭha, namely his desire to show grace to Ahirbudhnya:
"Residing in the abode of Vaikuṇṭha, I have come here to see you—a wonder never before seen by those possessed of the contemplation of the three states. (43.13)
Ever hidden and secret, it is honored by all the worlds;
having churned with the churning-stick of the intellect, it has been extracted from the ocean of the Vedas.
O Supreme Lord, since you have yielded this [teaching] to me like nectar from the ocean of milk, I have thereby attained your very essence as mantra; what more may I do for you?
I see no difference at all between you and Dāmodara;
therefore, O Śaṅkara, I shall behave toward you in exactly the same way as I do here.
Then, when Ahibudhnya had ceased speaking after thus addressing his own intended request to the Blessed One— [he who was] resplendent like a thousand suns—
I, filled with wonder, spoke to him of incomparable splendor.
In this world, there are many evildoers who obstruct the path of dharma; desiring their restraint, I destroy them by various means. (43.18)
