(416) While I was thus intent on reflection and established in yoga, the King of Mantras appeared; it is my conviction that the task was thereby accomplished. (43.19)
A prayer for the destruction of the Daityas and others:
"Therefore, O Lord, when the virtuous are being oppressed by them, you must come with effort at the mere thought of us; accomplish that which is to be accomplished. (43.20)
When the Blessed One said "So be it," he departed for Kailāsa, saying "So be it"; I too followed him to Kailāsa.
In the meantime, Indra held a consultation regarding the slaying of Jalandhara.
Then he was oppressed by the Dānava named Jalandhara.
Vāsava consulted together with all the hosts of Maruts regarding the invincibility of that evil-minded Dānava by means of weapons and missiles.
Having observed him, he urged, "By what means shall I destroy that sinner?
Thereupon, Vāyu, having expressed his own intention, rose up and spoke to Purandara. (43.23)
"Truly, this great asura cannot be conquered by missiles or weapons;
he is arrogant, endowed with strength and heroism, and has been granted a boon by the Creator. (43.24)
He desired to consume the entire world, like a risen comet,
while the glorious, immeasurable, and immensely radiant Lord of all worlds looked on.
Against that Śaṅkara, the God of gods, the Great God, the creator of all beings, a great calamity has been wrought by that cruel enemy of the gods.
"Śaṃkara is currently engaged in that [battle] in a state of supreme fury;
therefore, let us go there for the sake of slaying that evil-doer. (43.27)
We entreat that god through the mouth of Bṛhaspati himself, for that Blessed One alone knows what ought to be said in this matter. (43.28)
Having accepted the words of Vāyu, Śakra urged Bṛhaspati to go to Śaṃkara; when that Wind had ceased, Vāsava said, "So be it," to Bṛhaspati, who was seated there like a blazing fire. (43.29)
The Lord Pākaśāsana, possessed of great splendor, approached [him];
therefore, you must go to the wielder of the Pināka bow for the sake of slaying Jalandhara.
Highly incensed at that, he will undoubtedly slay him;
for in all the affairs of the gods, you alone are our ultimate refuge.
"Therefore, let the Lord who bears the crescent moon on his crest be approached on Mount Kailāsa.
When the lord of the gods, Puruhūta Indra, had spoken these words to Bṛhaspati at the request of Indra regarding the journey to Kailāsa— || 43-32 ||
"So be it," having promised that, Vākpati, who is honored by Śakra,
departed for the peak of Kailāsa with a joyful heart.
Therein is the vision of Śaṅkara:
seated there in a most beautiful assembly hall together with the gods, my mind was filled with wonder at a dance performed by an Apsaras. (43.34)
Then the Blessed One, resembling the rising sun, beheld me from afar;
having prostrated and stood up, that Lord of Speech praised me.
For the sake of slaying Jalandhara, Bṛhaspati offered praise to Śaṅkara:
"Be gracious, O Lord of the gods; be gracious, O Lord of the world!
Be gracious, O Lord who brings about the protection and the end of all the gods! (43.36)
Be gracious, O Blessed One, O God; be gracious, O You who are worshipped by the gods!
Be gracious, O Supreme Lord, ocean of universal consciousness! 43-37.
Salutations to you whose abode is the sky; salutations to you who are adorned by serpents.
Salutations to the supreme auspicious one; salutations to the destroyer of Tripura.
You are the Ordainer, you are the Vaṣaṭ-call, you are the oblation, and you are the consumer of the oblation;
you are existence and non-existence, you are the syllable Om, and you are likewise Indra and Yama.
You are the noose-handed one, you are Soma, you are Nirṛti, and likewise Marut;
you are Āditya, you are Vasu, you are the universe, O you whose face is turned in every direction.
You are the unmanifest and you are the Great One; you are indeed the ego-sense as well.
You are the extremely subtle elements, and likewise, you are both knowledge and ignorance.
What is the use of saying more in this regard? This entire world, with its moving and non-moving beings, is you alone, O Lord of the masters of all creatures, the cause of all causes.
To you, whose body is complete with the earth, water, wind, ether, fire, the thousand-rayed sun, the moon, and the sacrificer,
and who are constantly sought after by the minds of the supreme sages; [salutations].
Salutations to you, O universal form, who destroys the fear of worldly existence.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Contemplation of the Means for the Slaying of Jalandhara," in the Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā, a secret doctrine within the Śrī Pāñcarātra Tantra.
Chapter Forty-four, titled "The Manifestation of the Nature of Sudarśana," beginning from verse 2716:
Meditated upon even once, it swiftly destroys a multitude of sins numbering many millions.
We meditate upon that divine splendor of the god Sudarśana.
Śaṅkara, pleased by the praise, asked the reason for my arrival; thus,
having addressed the one praising me with "O Ahirbudhnya," I spoke as follows.
"O Lord of Speech, tell me, what is the purpose of your coming? || 44-1 ||
Thus addressed, Bṛhaspati related to Śaṅkara the entire reason for his arrival:
"O Śambhu, O God, ocean of compassion, please listen to this with respect. (44-2)
O Lord of all, your mind is full of grace toward all the worlds;
therefore, for the sake of the task of the gods, I have come to you for refuge.
A powerful Dānava named Jalandhara, of wicked conduct, who had received a boon from Brahmā, was constantly harassing the gods. (44.4)
All the gods, as well as the Lord of the Gods, were powerless to slay him;
therefore, all those hosts of Maruts gathered together and deliberated.
Arrogant due to a great boon, that invincible great asura cannot be destroyed at the forefront of battle by anyone except Mahādeva. (44.6)
Having deliberated thus, Śakra, together with the host of Maruts,
spoke to me regarding the means for slaying the great Asuras and the Blessed Three-eyed One.
I do not see anyone else; go for refuge to Śiva.
For the sake of the gods' mission, you must entreat the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Thus addressed by Puruhūta, I have come here into your presence;
so that all these gods may be happy and free from affliction.
"O Lord of Pārvatī, let it be done swiftly in that very manner.
O Sage, when I was thus addressed by Śaṅkara regarding his vow for the slaying of Jalandhara, I became lost in thought.
Having observed this, I spoke to the Lord of Speech:
"I shall slay the cruel Jalandhara, the perpetrator of evil deeds."
To demonstrate that the grace of the Sudarśana is the cause of his own power to subdue the Daityas, [he said]:
"O best among those who know mantras, while I was established in meditative absorption, I beheld one bearing the form of the Sudarśana—the mantra from which all mantras arise. (44.12)
He is the eternal accomplisher of all aims, the terrifier of all the wicked,
skilled in protecting everywhere, and the bestower of the fruits of the fourfold goals of life.
Devoted to protecting his own knowledge and warding off the knowledge of others, the six-syllabled mantra of Atharvan is beyond the range of hearing for those with six ears. (44.14)
Then, as I uttered the mantra, that Sudarśana wheel became an invisible mass of light, difficult for me to behold.
"He has been seen by me, and thus he spoke: 'I am pleased by the sight of you, O Lord; I am an eternal servant residing in the supreme heaven. (44.16)
"Remembered through mantra, I shall come and perform your task with a portion of myself.
Having spoken thus, that god, assuming the form of Sudarśana, departed.
"By that very means, I shall remove that evil-souled one; do not delay.
Thus addressed, Bṛhaspati, being exceedingly pleased, also hurried toward Śaṅkara in order to receive the *Saudarśana* lore. (44–18)
Having bowed down again, he spoke once more: "O Blessed One, if you have favor toward me, grant me this *saudarśanī* lore."
Śaṅkara gave that instruction to him;
thereafter, I bestowed that knowledge upon that great-souled one.
Having acquired the knowledge, Bṛhaspati performed its preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) on the slopes of the Himavat.
Having obtained her, he went to the Himalaya mountain, supremely delighted.
In that place, the Blessed One recited this unsurpassed mantra;
thereafter, Sudarśana appeared directly before Bṛhaspati, assuming a form of supreme wonder and manifesting his presence.

(423) That Blessed One was a universal monarch (cakravartin), gentle in form and beautiful to behold. Seeing him—radiant in body, serene, and glowing with the luster of saffron—Bṛhaspati, filled with wonder, questioned him regarding the cause of his having only two arms. (44.22)
The supreme deity, who bestows grace upon all beings, has two arms;
he holds the conch and the discus and is adorned with divine garlands.
Clad in yellow silk garments and adorned with two eyes,
he is the support of all powers and weapons, the scorcher of his enemies.
Seeing him, he was overcome with wonder and, having prostrated, asked:
"O Blessed One, what is this? You are renowned in the world as the Eight-Armed One. (44.25)
Appearing before me in human form and appearance,
Sudarśana addressed me, saying, "Let my reply be heard," and spoke as follows.
Among the infinite arrays of the Sudarśana, four hold preeminence;
there are thousands of such arrays fashioned by me according to my will.
Of these, O Lord of Speech, four are my primary arrays. (44.27)
Know their enumeration as follows: first me with two arms, then me with eight arms, then me with sixteen hands, and after that me with sixty-two arms. (44.28)
The purpose of the other manifestations is for the sake of favoring devotees;
there are many other manifestations according to the desires of those who worship.
(p. 424) The fourfold manifestation is inherent, eternal, and characterized by purity (*sāttvika*).
This form is innate, eternal, and supremely characterized by sattva.

My supreme [state] is devoid of decay, destruction, and so forth. The conclusion—that these various [mantras] are for the sake of favoring other devotees—is established as being for the purpose of favoring those whose minds are fixed on Me. (44.30)
The demonstration of the existence of another form of his own that is most wonderful:
"Another form consisting of the entire universe, unseen by gods or dānavas, beyond deliberation, boundless, and not within the range of sight by its very nature. (44.31)
"Just as the Lord Hṛṣīkeśa is, so am I," said Bṛhaspati; thus he spoke to that god who bore the form of Sudarśana, making a request to behold his true nature. (44.32)
Having prostrated before him, Vākpati, the best among speakers, said to him:
"That form of yours which consists of the universe, which is beyond the range of sight and without limit—"
"I behold [the world] through the vision of yoga; show that to me now.
Then the Blessed One, the Soul of the Universe, revealed his own exalted form, which consists of the wheel of the universe. (44–34)
O Nārada, he revealed himself to his guru, who was established in yoga;
with a mind filled with wonder, the guru gazed upon the god standing before him.
The description of that form (p.
425): [He is] one whose exceedingly terrifying body occupies the belly of the universe, possessing an unprecedented form that transcends the reach of the senses.
Possessing a multitude of thousands of wondrous wheels clinging to the peaks of its rising, formidable rays.
Shining with a series of throbbing staffs held at his feet, he stands established in his own ground,
like the mass of rays from the sun blazing at the end of an eon.
Adorned with a lofty crown radiant with the luster of gems.
With tawny eyes whirling like the eddies of a great ocean, frequented by hosts of gods,
and with the world caught between his pure fangs—
Devouring the world, with a face made terrifying by a frown.
Him whose chest was marked by a necklace resembling the expanse of Viṣṇu’s foot, strewn with the moon and clusters of stars,
and [adorned] with a garland of blazing light rising and expanding—
A great web of missiles, bearing every kind of weapon.
p. 426) Consisting of brilliance, like the sparks of light from the sun, moon, and fire at the end of an eon,
[he] fills the entire space within his own body—
And the surface of the earth and the sky were indistinguishable. || 44-40 ||
From seeing a form never seen before, Bṛhaspati experienced delusion,
as the entire world was filled with the tinkling sounds of anklets and other ornaments.
Beholding that supreme object of knowledge never seen before, the Primordial God was bewildered;
having regained his composure, he offered praise to Sudarśana.
Then, having regained consciousness with great difficulty,
the high-souled Dhiṣaṇa offered praise to the god.
Oṃ,
homage! Homage to you, O Blessed One, invincible Sudarśana, whose essential nature consists of wisdom.
To you, whose every power is eternally manifest in its entirety, who sustain all that is stationary and moving; || 44-42 ||
To you, whose heroic power is irresistible, who possess abundant majesty, who are an ocean of all auspicious qualities,
and whose form consists of pure radiance—
Salutations again and again to the one who bears the form of a wheel.
Homage to Jayā, who possesses incomparable valor, who is well-prepared to protect those who have sought refuge,
who has a thousand wheels, and who has a thousand names.
Homage to the one who bears a body with a thousand spokes.
To you, the sole cause of the creation, preservation, and destruction of the world;
to you, the excellent navigator for crossing the ocean of worldly existence;
[to you] who are the adversary of the hosts of Maruts and the Daityas and Dānavas—
Salutation to the one who subdues, whose subtle splendor is profound. || 44-45 ||
O Lord, since Your lotus-feet have been desired from the very beginning by the mind of Madhuripu, just as it was intended;
In this world, he accomplishes his desires accordingly. || 44–46 ||
O Lord, whose pair of lotus feet serves as a boat for the fathomless ocean of the flowing mass of great sins of all dependents whose memories have been destroyed;
O Maker of Day, who has made your own body a mere drop within the ocean of your radiance!
Salutations to Him whose supreme abode is praised by Śiva, the Lord of Umā, and by the Moon. || 44-47 ||

Salutations eternally to You, whose self is the wheel of the dissolution of the world and time, who are worshiped by the gods headed by the four-faced Brahmā, and who have attained the essence of the eternal service of Govinda.
May it be for the sake of the Self, which is filled with the mass of the bliss of equanimity.
His mind was gladdened by hearing of the multitude of great heroic deeds— beginning with his many births— which were constantly remembered by all the foremost of the gods;
and [he was honored] by the mass of rays from the crest-jewels of all the lords of the gods and asuras.
Salutations to you, whose pair of lotus feet are joined together. || 44-49 ||
Salutations to You, who are devoid of time conditioned by units such as *kalās*, *muhūrtas*, and *nāḍikās*, and whose self-form is free from decay, increase, birth, and destruction.
I bow to you, the most excellent one, who transcends the sphere of speech and mind,
who is untouched by any quality to be abandoned, who is compassionate toward those who take refuge in you,
and who is worthy of worship by all, attainable only by those whose merit is undiminished.
A divine body composed of knowledge and consisting of the supreme elements.
O Lord, this prayer for the manifestation of Your form does not truly distance You from me in this world—
neither among mortals, nor among the gods, nor among others.
Even the Vedas do not know that which is beyond them; O Lord, be gracious toward this form of yours, which is terrifying and never seen before.
Having become eight-armed Sudarśana, he spoke of the extreme secrecy of his own true nature;
thus addressed by that Guru, the Blessed Lord, assuming the form of the Discus, manifested before him as the eight-armed Master. (44–53)
With a serene countenance, the illustrious one then addressed his preceptor:
"This very form, unseen by gods and dānavas, has now been revealed."
Truly, no one other than the god Janārdana knows me.

[This is] the determination of the nature of Sudarśana as the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) of the Blessed One: "I am the power of action of the god who wields the Śārṅga bow; this is a secret. (44–55)
"Therefore, O sage, all that work—including the entire creation of the world—is performed by me alone. Having said this, he vanished. (44–56)
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the True Nature of Sudarśana," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
From the beginning, verse number 2772:
The forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Legend of Kuśadhvaja.
Even a single moment of meditation swiftly destroys a multitude of sins numbering many millions.
We meditate upon that divine splendor of the god Sudarśana.
A question concerning the inner science (*adhyātmavidyā*) and other subjects:
Nārada said—
"O Blessed One, O Supreme Lord, this has been declared by you previously."
The knowledge of the inner science and the knowledge of the outer [world] are, by their very nature, higher knowledge. || 45-1 ||
"O Lord, what is accomplished by them, or what is brought to cessation by them?
You alone know this; explain it to me in detail. (45.2)
Ahibudhnya’s description of the effects of ignorance:
"I shall tell you this supreme secret; listen as I speak."
Through ignorance, the supreme nature of the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) [is obscured]. 45.3.
The knowledge of the reality of those two is indeed covered and obstructed.
Through the attainment of the yoga of the supreme self, there arises the knowledge that defines the purpose of spiritual knowledge. (45.4)

Just as that which is produced is turned back, so too is beginningless saṃsāra, which consists of bondage. The description of the effect of supreme knowledge is characterized by non-return [to rebirth] through the realization of one's own true nature. (45-5)
O sinless sage, supreme liberation, which yields the fruit of eternal bliss, is accomplished by this [practice]; for it has been established since beginningless time through previous efforts. (45–6)

Future actions are cast off along with their latent impressions (vāsanā). However, that which is *prārabdha-karman*—which is to be destroyed solely through experience—is not destroyed without such experience. (55–7)
All this has been told to you by me in brief.
[This concludes] the inquiry regarding the existence or non-existence of specific karmas that destroy *prārabdha* karma.
Nārada said:
O Blessed One, by what action is prārabdha-karma destroyed? (45-8)
"Or does it not perish through some particular action?
With the desire to explain that, Ahirbudhnya [gave] the illustration of the legend of Kuśadhvaja."
Listen to this ancient history that occurred in the Tretā Yuga.
Among the Janakas there was a lord of the earth named Kuśadhvaja,
a knower of Brahman, supremely generous, and devoted to the protection of his subjects.

(432) While Kuśadhvaja was ruling over the entire circle of the earth, that lord of the world was greatly afflicted by Great Delusion (*mahāmoha*). Once, however, Great Delusion appeared, causing torment to his limbs. (45.11)
Although the lord of the earth was severely tormented by him for another kalpa,
that slayer of enemies did not personally take him into account, thinking, "He shall go [of his own accord]."
Even though he remained indifferent, an intense affliction assailed him again and again;
moreover, the lord of the people was repeatedly tormented by it. As he was thus utterly distressed, his manner of reflection was as follows:
Then he thought thus: "This powerful one has appeared quite unexpectedly."
It oppresses me, who am constantly devoted to the inner self, like one who is helpless; for what reason has this arisen, and why does it not subside of its own accord? (45.14)
Thinking, "I shall approach Yājñavalkya, the preceptor of my own lineage," the king, intent on this reflection, went to the preceptor’s hermitage, which was holy,
filled with the chanting of the Vedas, and perfumed by the smoke of sacrificial offerings.
Having entered the interior, he saw the treasure of asceticism seated in the fire-sanctuary,
surrounded by knowers of Brahman like another Vivasvat.
Filled with humility, he beheld Yājñavalkya, his family preceptor;
having bowed down to that great-souled one, Kuśadhvaja reported his own circumstances and spoke these words. (45.17)
From you alone have I obtained both the higher and the lower knowledge;
by the fire of that supreme knowledge alone has all my karma been consumed. (45.18)
It is heard in the scriptures that an action commenced without regard for its prior or subsequent consequences is called *prārabdha*;
indeed, the attainment of the kingdom was the fruit of that very *prārabdha* karma. (45.19)
As I remained thus, a great delusion, unbearable and destructive to my memory, arose, tormenting my very body. (45.20)
"By whom has this misery come, or by what means will it be pacified? Tell me.
Being thus addressed, the Blessed One replied to Kuśadhvaja with these words of Yājñavalkya.
The purpose of the creation of the body is for the experience of results:
the formation of bodies for embodied beings is for the enjoyment of pleasure and pain;
the same applies to the body of one who knows Brahman.
Understand that the bodies of even those who know Brahman are exactly like that.
Therefore, you too must experience the fruit of your own actions with this body;
for those very actions that are performed by means of the body, they belong to you as well.
Their fruits are enjoyed [by others] and never by them alone;
therefore, know that this fruit of great delusion is indeed a sinful fruit which has been obtained, O Lord of the Earth. (45.24)

p. 434) The promise to describe the evil that serves as its cause: Listen, for I shall explain in truth that by which delusion arises—namely, insanity (*unmāda*), great insanity (*mahonmāda*), derangement of the mind (*cittākṣepa*), and fainting (*mūrchanā*). (45.25)
The destroyer of perception, the agitator, the babbler, and the breaker of mindfulness—these eight defects, which harm living beings, arise from great sins. (45.26)

The king’s investigation into the causes for the arising of defects such as insanity; the punishment of the slayer of a Brahmin; the perception of truth in what is false; the neglect of the image of his own worshipful deity; and the execution of the monarch. (45.27)

Through the seizure of land granted to Brahmins, through causing distress to Brahmins, through the violation of established boundaries, and also through sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached; 45-28.
O King, these faults arise in kings due to those causes.
[The narration of Kuśadhvaja’s attainment of great delusion: "O Great King, you previously slew a highly righteous monarch without a battle. (45.29)
"O King, through this very sin to be experienced in this body, this wretched and terrifying swoon has come upon you. (45.30)
By the greatness of the Sudarśana, the eight defects are certainly destroyed;
by the power of the Sudarśana, these eight kinds of defects perish—of this there is no doubt—and by that, he too is destroyed. (45.31)
(p. 435) Instruction on the effort required to accomplish the Sudarśana temple: Therefore, my dear, apply yourself to its construction while reflecting;
first, the construction of the pavilion and so forth.
First, [one should construct] a lofty pavilion, endowed with all auspicious things.
It was crowded with many pillars, adorned with lofty archways,
enriched with canopies of white silk, and decorated with networks of tiny bells.
It was crowded with many banners, adorned with flags, strewn with strings of pearls, and decorated with many garlands. || 45.34 ||
With pillars wrapped in linen cloth and adorned with lamps, it measures thirty-six paces in width and fifty-four paces [in length]. (45.35)
It was as long as it was wide, beautiful, endowed with the eight auspicious symbols, perfumed on all sides with incense of sandalwood and agallochum, and entirely propitious.
The procedure for constructing the pavilion on the bank of the Sarasvatī:
"In this very manner, O Kalyāṇa, quickly have a pavilion constructed on the pure bank of the Sarasvatī outside the city; do not fear, and do not hesitate. (45.37)
In that regard, the promise of one's own arrival is: "I shall come to that very place and perform the rite for pacification;
I shall carry out the king's instruction exactly as taught."
When the wise teacher had spoken thus, the king departed.
Then, being exceedingly pleased, he summoned his servants and had a pavilion constructed there according to the prescribed characteristics. (45.39)
The sage was capable of neutralizing that fault through his own power by going to Yājñavalkya’s pavilion;
nevertheless, reflecting with the thought, "This is the duty of a king," he [did not do so]. (45–46)
He went to the pavilion there on an auspicious day during the bright fortnight;
having summoned the artisans, he had a royal throne prepared in the western part of the pavilion. (45–46)
In the western direction of this [area], on the third well-adorned [portion],
in the middle of the two eastern sections, he had sacrificial fire-pits (homakuṇḍa) constructed; indeed,
he caused the sacrificial fire-pits to be made in the middle of those two eastern sections.
Upon the tops of the platforms and grounds of the altar, which were endowed with the characteristics of celestial palaces,
he respectfully prepared sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in the shape of wheels.
Having constructed a pair of such fire-pits (kuṇḍas) in the center, he likewise caused eight fire-pits to be made in the same manner in the eight directions outside of them.
One by one for each pit, and placing two jars in the center of each,
he scattered *kalamā* rice, measuring a *bhāra* in weight, around all the pits,
having strewn it on every side at their eastern edges. (45–45)
There were eight silver jars and two golden ones in the center; they were filled with fragrant water and endowed with the nine gems. (45–46)
Then the sage Yājñavalkya himself, together with the wise Śatānanda, performed the worship of the pitcher (kumbha),
having wrapped it with linen threads and honored it with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata).
Having adorned the jars and respectfully invoked the deity therein, he worshipped with mantras, incense, lamps, and flowers. (45–48)
Having installed the great yantra, including its consecration, drawings, and so forth, the Guru [places] two jars in the center;
the great yantra is devoid of a deity and is endowed with all mantras. (45–49)
Having painted upon a cloth the aforementioned [deity] together with all the divine weapons, one should scatter these over the royal throne, and then place that [throne] covered with an upper cloth.
Then he caused the king of immeasurable splendor to mount [the chariot],
and he prepared for him a canopy equipped with mechanical paintings.
And having fashioned with gold a mechanical device adorned with a network of jewels and possessing the characteristics as previously described, he placed it upon a mirror.
In the same manner, having well-prepared a birch leaf with yellow orpiment,
one should inscribe the yantra with a golden needle, excluding the divine weapons (divyāstras).
He placed this well-consecrated amulet upon the king’s head and also caused him to apply a sectarian mark (*tilaka*) with the ashes of Sudarśana. (45.54)

Then, having summoned eight officiating priests who were established in the mantras, self-restrained, and devoted to Viṣṇu, he appointed those brahmins to the sacrificial pits of the various directions.
Then, having drawn a curtain all around the pavilion,
[the rites were performed] in the consecrated sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) which were adorned with golden ornaments.
Having first performed the prescribed rites together with the officiating priests, the Guru,
accompanied by Śatānanda, offered oblations into the blazing fires.
Accompanied by dancing and instrumental music, and joined with the chanting of the Vedas, he,
being composed in mind, first performed the rite of oblation (homa) while proclaiming an auspicious day.
When the primary rite was joined, Śatānanda was the preceptor,
and all those officiating priests were likewise engaged in the oblations for the quarters.
Having respectfully resolved upon a million oblations with purified clarified butter, he performed ten thousand daily;
thus it was carried out for ten days.
Bathed daily by the Guru with water from ritual jars consecrated by mantras, he was freed from the planetary influence, purified in soul, free from fever, and became joyful in mind.
When ten days had passed, the king honored his preceptor with jewels and much gold, as well as a pavilion together with all its furnishings.
Having presented everything to his guru, he, being composed in mind, gratified all the officiating priests with abundant wealth, grain, and honors.
The wise one ruled this earth like the Lord of the Gods in heaven;
this same rule is prescribed for all other beings as well. (45–64)

In the Dvāpara age, this rite for kings is prescribed with fifty million *niyuta* oblations; and in the Kali age, it is performed with ten million (*koṭi*) oblations. Thus, even for those who know Brahman, the karma that has already begun must be experienced.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Kuśadhvaja," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrī Pañcarātra*.
From the beginning, verse 2837:
The forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Quantity of Materials and Other Details for the Sudarśana Oblation."
Meditated upon even once, it swiftly destroys the flood of tens of millions of births;
we meditate upon that divine splendor of the Lord Sudarśana.
Regarding the sequence of duties to be performed upon the king’s arrival at the sacrificial pavilion (homamaṇḍapa),
Nārada says:
"Whether it be due to divine causes, or human causes, or even by spirits and the like..."
Out of pride or because of a more powerful opponent, or due to other obstacles, the lord of the earth [fails]. || 46-1 ||
If he should not reach the sacrificial pavilion from the very beginning, then how can the great planetary influences of the Lord of the Earth be averted? (46.2)
Ahirbudhnya said:
Listen, O King; if the king himself does not act, let the skillful domestic priest act.
For he alone is the king’s everything in the accomplishment of matters pertaining to the unseen world.

The characteristics of a domestic priest (purohita) are: he should be righteous, endowed with Vedic learning, of good conduct, truthful in speech, pure, of noble birth, free from egoism, patient, mindful, and self-controlled. (46.4)
One who knows the divisions of place and time, who possesses insight into the treatises, who is untiring, invincible, vigilant, generous, and skilled in policy. (46.5)

The officiating priest should be one who knows the means and the goal, who performs sacrifices regularly, who is free from greed, who understands the divine, who speaks kindly, who is learned in the Vedas, endowed with goodness, and a capable master. (46.6)
Devoted to Viṣṇu, ascetic, knowledgeable in what ought to be done, diligent in action, and sinless;
desiring the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful for kings, he was esteemed by all. (46–47)
The priest alone performs all the duties of the king;
such a person is a rare find among kings, for he is like a preceptor to them.
Indeed, such a one is capable of warding off the flood of sins that afflict kings. (46–8)
Therefore, he alone indeed deserves the method of protection for kings;
he who has such a guru shall become a sovereign emperor among monarchs. (46.9)
He shall be long-lived, without rivals, free from disease, and a slayer of enemy heroes; moreover, no calamities such as drought shall arise in his realm. (46.10)
Regarding the declaration of misfortune for the king in the absence of such a priest:
"If another person, other than him, should become the king's preceptor or priest, the opposite will happen to that lord of the earth; of this there is no doubt. (46.11)
Regarding the question of the dimensions and other characteristics of the *kumbha* and other vessels,
Nārada says:
"The measurement of the *kumbhas*, as well as the defining characteristics of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles..."
Tell me everything: what kind of officiating priests (ṛtvij) does he have, and what is his entire manner?
The supreme measure is that of Ahirbudhnya:
[vessels] well-filled with pure perfumed waters weighing one bhāra.
One should have jars made of gold and silver; this is the most excellent [method]. || 46-13 ||
Jars carrying half a bhāra each constitute the medium measurement; this is recorded as the medium procedure. The inferior measurement is...
In the lower category, one should fill it with half of that; this is the settled rule.
The construction of the *sruk* and other implements should be performed according to the rules;
likewise, O best of sages, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles must be prepared according to the rules. [Now follows] the number of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Then he should choose eight Vaiṣṇava officiating priests who are endowed with sattva.
The ritual procedure for the limb-mantras and so forth is performed with the limb-mantras, the Gāyatrī, and the Vahni-prākāraka;
likewise, the two principal sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) are prepared according to the Guru-kalpa by one who is composed in mind.
All those intent on protection should perform the oblation with the root mantra using *śamī* wood, *dūrvā* grass, sesame seeds, and likewise mango leaves. (46.17)
The Guru should offer oblations in sequence with *caru*, milk-rice, and cakes on *palāśa* leaves;
he should then perform the fire-sacrifice in the two central pits with pure clarified butter. (46.18)
Alternatively, one should offer oblations in all the fire-pits with pure clarified butter; for here, in the ritual procedure for remediation, it must be performed by the Guru alone.
Regarding the king's beds, seats, vehicles, and so forth, even during his private activities,
one should perform the canopy and other rites according to the previously mentioned procedure.

At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice (homa), the consecration (abhiṣeka) of the king takes place; at the moment the sacrifice ends, his preceptor, having summoned the king there as before to a seat consecrated with mantras, [proceeds with the rite]. (46-21)
Having performed the consecration and other purificatory rites, the preceptor should proceed;
thereafter, with a tranquil mind, he should gratify the preceptor and others, whereby he is immediately released from the bonds of the planets. (46.22)
Having prostrated, one should give to the guru according to his merit one's own insignia,
as well as highly precious ornaments made of pearls and gems.
Then, having given jeweled pedestals, gold, various kinds of gems, and vast tracts of land, he should satisfy the officiating priests.
Each and every officiating priest shall be honored by all with a hundred pieces of gold,
and each one individually with ten cows and various kinds of garments.
To the performer of the principal oblation, however, one should especially give a gift;
specifically, to the preceptor who performs the principal oblation, one should give much wealth, a single complete horse together with its vehicle. (46.26)

Then, with a joyful mind, the king should provide the gratification of the Brahmins by means of a pavilion equipped with ornaments and all necessary furnishings, and thereby bring about their satisfaction. (46.27)
When this ritual has been performed by the king himself as described,
he should give wealth to the instructor alone, who is knowledgeable in the mantras.
Everything was performed by the family priest; this is the eternal law (dharma).
It has been explained in detail specifically in the context of the king's example. (46.29)

This same procedure is prescribed for all others as well. Then, desiring the prosperity of the king, the preceptor, the most skilled in mantras, should, with a concentrated mind, perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with a verse dedicated to Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Quantities of Materials and Other Details for the Sudarśana Homa," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
From the beginning, verse number 2867:
The forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Ritual for Great Peace.
Meditated upon even once, it swiftly removes a multitude of sins numbering many tens of millions.
We meditate upon that divine splendor of the god Sudarśana.
Nārada asked regarding the single means that accomplishes all fruits pertaining to this world and the next:
"O Blessed One, O Lord who possesses the five mantra-limbs, O Destroyer of the bonds of the individual soul!"
O you whose celestial abode is the sky, who have directly realized every particularity by yourself! 47-1
By means of this mantra, one constantly attains benefits both in this world and the next;
likewise, the defects of both are destroyed—of this there is no doubt. (47-2)
Thus it was said by him; therefore I ask: by which single action alone may both types of accomplishment and the destruction of both types of undesirable results come to pass? (47.3)
O Śaṅkara, if such a rite exists, tell it to me;
for no one other than you is capable of explaining such a planetary ritual. (47.4)
The commencement of the subsequent discourse by Ahirbudhnya:
"I shall now relate this supreme [teaching], which brings about all peace."
Regarding the specific ritual to be described, the authority belongs to kings;
it is to be performed by illustrious great monarchs, even if they belong to different castes.
(446) Its nature as the means for accomplishing the desired fruit, preceded by the cessation of all suffering,

consists in the destruction of all three types of suffering— namely, the internal and so forth— and the complete destruction of all mental afflictions (*ādhi*), which is its auspicious characteristic. (47–6)
O Sage, it destroys all enemies, is peaceful, is the cause of great victory, slays demons, bestows nourishment, and brings everything under control.
This meritorious rite, which bestows the supreme lifespan, was performed by former kings;
through its performance, Ambarīṣa and others obtained the results as described:
Ambarīṣa, Śuka, Alarka, Māndhātṛ, and Purūravas. (47–48)
Rājoparicara, Dhundhu, Śibi, and Śrutakīrtana—these kings attained universal sovereignty in ancient times by performing this [rite]. (47.9)

Free from affliction, without rivals, and possessing far-reaching, stainless fame—therein lies the conclusion of the authority of kings; therefore, those who rule the earth on this ground desire human bliss. (47–10)
They should respectfully perform this rite characterized by great pacification (mahāśānti) in a specific location,
either outside the city on the bank of a great river or in a temple. (47–11)
O Sage, in a spacious, auspicious, and secluded place provided with a body of water,
one should prepare a pavilion that exceeds the previously described characteristics.
One should make the length and width such that it is provided with a royal throne;
one should construct this supreme structure with these characteristics all around. (47.13)
The sequence for the construction of the pavilion:
It is crowded with many pillars, adorned with jewels and gold, provided with lofty archways, and beautified by hundreds of lamps. (47.14)
It was provided with a network of small bells, adorned with banners,
equipped with a canopy and stairs, and furnished with every kind of ornament.
It was perfumed with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, incense, and garlands;
it was provided with lofty *sāla* trees and surrounded by a sacrificial hall.
Having thus made this pleasing arrangement, one should fashion the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) there;
one should fashion them in the four directions on the eastern side of this pavilion.
For the purpose of the application of the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha), one should have the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) made square;
then one should worship Keśava and the others in the directions beginning with the east.
One should arrange the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) for the four [deities] beginning with Keśava in the intermediate corners,
and for the remaining forms in those gaps, in due order.

A triangle, a hexagon, a half-moon, a womb-shape (yoni), and a lotus-shape in sequence; a circle, a lotus-like [shape], an octagon, a thunderbolt-shape (vajra), and one with the luster of a bow. 47–20.
One should have these pits constructed so that they resemble a trident or a winnowing basket;
having installed the Lord in the center, assuming the form of the Yantra. (47.21)
One should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) endowed with the characteristics of a celestial mansion (vimāna) in front of that [main altar].
The arrangement of the weapon-pits (astrakuṇḍa) should be made all around the fire-hall (homaśālā) in successive order.
One should diligently fashion one hundred and forty [images],
and then have them adorned with the appropriate insignia of their weapons.

The selection of the officiating priests (ṛtvijvaraṇa) takes place within the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) inside the pavilion; one should select sixteen virtuous Vaiṣṇavas as priests in due order with the verses of the Puruṣasūkta.
Then, in the missile-pits (*astrakuṇḍa*), one should select other officiating priests; finally, by their own names, one should choose those who have mastered the Vedas,
even for the Brahma-missile and the others in the external missile-pit hall.
One should choose all the officiating priests (ṛtvij) who are skilled in rites for pacification;
[one should honor them] in sequence with fifty verses beginning with "brahmajajñānam" (RV 2.3.10). 47-26.
And with their own names, one should duly choose three hundred learned men, such as those who have composed the Brahmāstra and other works, using the Brahma-sūktas in the proper sequence.
Then, in that very place, he was addressed as "Bhavān Mitra" with five verses, and further with thirteen Ṛgvedic verses beginning with "mātrābhiḥ. (47.28)

And with the five verses beginning with "asya vāmam," the six verses beginning with "ato devā," and also the ten verses beginning with "cakṣuḥ," [one should worship] by means of the Viṣṇu-sūkta. (47–29)
One should choose six [priests] with the verse "prati va enā" using their respective names;
furthermore, one should have the implements for the oblation made of gold or silver. (47.30)
One should place water-filled jars in the eastern parts of the sacrificial pits;
these jars may be made of gold, silver, or even copper. (47.31)
One should prepare jars, each weighing one *kalama* or one *bhāra*, as before;
for the purpose of the fire-oblation (*homa*), one should follow the procedure for selecting additional officiating priests (*ṛtvij*),
and the sacrificer should choose the remaining priests for the sacrificial rites.

The best of mantra-knowers should perform [the rite] with his own respective mantras. Regarding the procedure for the fire-oblation (homa) performed by the preceptor in the central pit: the instructor, in the middle pit, accompanied by the sound of the Sāman chants... [47-33]
Accompanied by the sound of lutes and other instruments and joined with the chanting of auspicious days,
one should commence the rite of pacification (śāntikarma) with a *koṭihoma* for each according to the prescribed number of oblations. || 47-34 ||
The procedure for the worship of the respective deities in their respective jars:
having summoned those respective deities, one should worship them individually in the jars with their own respective mantras, as well as with incense, lamps, and so forth. (47.35)
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, the consecration of the king is performed with the water from the ritual jars:
"When the rite of the fire sacrifice has been completed, one should then place the king upon the yantra-throne and consecrate him with the waters from those respective jars. (47-36)
Regarding the procedure for the fire-oblation (homa) in the weapon-pits:
those twice-born ones who have been assigned to specific weapon-mantras should, with tranquil minds, offer oblations in their respective pits using those very mantras. (47.37)
There is an option regarding the number of oblations according to the distinction of superior, middling, and inferior:
a *koṭi-homa* (ten million oblations) for each [type] is the primary; half of that is the middling;
the inferior should be known as one hundred thousand (*niyuta*), up until this is completed. || 47-38 ||
In that much time, the task must be accomplished by those who are vigilant and untiring.
[Now follows] the rule for the materials used in the fire-oblation (*homa*) from the group of weapons belonging to Nārāyaṇa:
the *Nārāyaṇīya*, the *Brāhma*, the *Vimala*, and the *Krauñca*. (47–39)
And the Dharmapāśa, Lakṣākṣa, Saṃvarta, Satyamuttama, Dundunābha, Śīteṣu, Viṣṇucakra, and Mānava. || 47-40 ||
One should offer oblations of clarified butter to this group of missiles, beginning with the *aindra-jyautiṣa*. (p.
451) Regarding the procedure for the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) in the group beginning with Kālacakra:
Kālacakra, Dharmacakra, Vajrāstra, and that called Gadā. (47–41)
The Brahma-head, the arrow of Eṣika, the trident, the two thunderbolts,
the noose of Time (Kālapāśa), the Pināka bow, and the noose of Varuṇa.
The Āgneya, the beloved [Vaiṣṇava], and likewise the supreme Pāśupata—
this group of mantras should be offered with the sacrificial oblation (caru) according to the prescribed rule.
In the section on the Kaṅkāla and other groups, there is the procedure for curd:
the Kaṅkāla, the Musala, and also the Vāyavya, then the Kaṅkaṇī,
the Asiratna, the Kāpāla, and likewise the Śakti and the Vaidyādhara.
The Prasvāpana, Praśamana, Darpaṇa, Śoṣaṇa, Saṃtāpana, Gāndharva, Paiśāca, and Vilāpana [mantras]. (47–45)
These weapons are to be offered with curd by supreme believers.
Regarding the group beginning with *madana*, the rule for milk is as follows:
*madana* is indeed *tāmasa* and is highly beloved by Kandarpa. (47–48)
The Saumana, the Musala, the terrible Saṃvarta, the Māyādhara, the Soma-missile, the Vāruṇa, and the Tvāṣṭra as well. || 47-47 ||
Those intent on the meditation of those weapons should offer oblations of milk with the *prasvāpana*, the *bhaga*, and the *raudra* weapons, which are discharged while turned away from the enemy.
(p. 452) In the section beginning with Rabhasa, the procedure for the milk-rice offering (*pāyasa*) is as follows:
Rabhasa, Satyakīrti, Pratihāratara, Avāṅmukha, Viṣama, Dṛḍhanābha, and Sunābhaka. (47–49)
To the ten-eyed one, the hundred-faced, the hundred-headed, the hundred-bellied,
the lotus-navelled, the great-navelled, and also to the slayers of despair.
This group [of deities] should be offered oblations with milk-rice (pāyasa) by those of pure mind.
Regarding the group beginning with Yogandhara, the procedure for sesame seeds is as follows:
Yogandhara, Vinidra, Naidra, and likewise Saumanasa. (47–51)
Dhṛtimālī, Pramathana, Vidhūta, Vṛttimān, Mahārcirmālī, Makara, Rucira, and Karavīraka. (47–52)
And for their sake, an oblation with sesame seeds should be performed according to the prescribed rule.
Regarding the group beginning with wealth: the ritual of honey, wealth and grain, the form of desire, delusion, and likewise the delight of desire. (47–53)
Varaṇa and Āvaraṇa were both supreme weapons;
and Jṛmbhaka and Sarvanābha were the great [missiles] belonging to the son of Bhṛśāśva.
One should thoroughly satisfy the *saṃdāna* and the *paraśu* with honey;
for other weapons, the procedure involves rice grains (*śālitaṇḍula*).
One should also offer oblations with rice grains for other [weapons] not mentioned here. (47–55)
p. 453) The procedure for the propitiation of Sudarśana by means of specific mantras at the conclusion of the fire sacrifice:

Having offered oblations with their respective mantras as prescribed, [one should worship] the all-pervading Lord Viṣṇu, who is the source of all weapons, who has the form of Sudarśana, and who consists of all yantras. (57–56)
One should commence the rite of pacification (*śāntikarma*) with *ṛc* verses that have been applied as mantras.

Regarding the specific ritual procedure for the mantra-consecration in the libation (*tarpaṇa*), one should respectfully perform each of the primary collections of weapons (*astrajāta*) belonging to Nārāyaṇa individually. (47–57)
One should respectfully perform the rite of peace (*śānti*) with this hymn, "paro mātrā" (RV 10.128).

Regarding the specific ritual procedures for the mantras within the *Kālacakra* and other cycles, one should [worship] Jātavedas individually as situated within each of the *Kālacakra* and other groups. (47–58)
And for the sake of pacifying the group headed by Kaṅkāla, one should satisfy them by offering oblations into the blazing fire with the hymn beginning "divaspari. (47–59)
Regarding the specific ritual procedure for the group of mantras beginning with *madana*:
one who is composed should perform the pacification (*śānti*) of the group of weapons beginning with *madana* using the hymn "ato devā" and likewise the hymn "viṣṇornukaṃ". (47–60)

Regarding the specific ritual procedures for the *rabhasa* and other such groups, [it is taught that] one should pacify each of the various types of weapons beginning with *rabhasa* using the five mantras starting with "mitra" (RV 10.87.1–5); this is the Vedic injunction. (47–61)
p. 554) Regarding the specific ritual procedure for the mantra of Yogaṃdhara and others:

"The pacification of the weapon (astra) of Yogaṃdhara and the rest should be performed by those who are composed. And with this hymn, 'May each of the gods protect us' (ato devā avantu), [the rite should be performed] one by one. (47–62)
Regarding the specific ritual procedure for the category of wealth and so forth:
the wise one should pacify the collection of mantras situated within the category of wealth, grain, and the like, by means of the supreme hymn beginning with "juṣasva na" (RV 10.102). || 47–63 ||
Regarding other weapons, there is a specific procedure for the mantras;
one should satisfy the other weapons not mentioned here with the Viṣṇu-sūkta, using these purifying hymns employed in conjunction with the great yantras. (47–64)
One should worship the deity, who consists entirely of yantras, with hymns of praise and fire oblations.
At the conclusion of the libation (tarpaṇa), there is the rite of feeding a thousand Brāhmaṇas;
then, having worshipped the gods, one should subsequently honor the Brāhmaṇas. (47–65)
One should feed a thousand pure persons with boiled rice and milk-rice;
then follows the ritual of consecration for the king with waters empowered by the Astra-mantra.
Then, the king, seated upon his throne with a tranquil mind— || 47–66 ||
The preceptor should perform the consecration with all the auspicious waters for the weapons-mantras brought by the officiating priests,
which have been empowered by the root-mantra of that [deity].
p. 455) Regarding the ritual for sprinkling a sick king: O Sage, if a king should be afflicted by disease, one must perform the sprinkling;
there is a necessity for consecration with water from a jar situated within the pavilion.

One should certainly perform the consecration with the water from the jar situated within the pavilion; thus becoming free from disease and free from mental anguish, one becomes victorious in an instant. (47–68)
As it has been said, the proclamation of the fruits of the Great Peace (mahāśānti) consists of health, long life, victory, prosperity, mastery, faith, and immortality.
The accomplishment of all aims and sovereignty over the earth shall undoubtedly belong to the king. (47-69)
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Great Peace," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
From the beginning, verse 2936:
The forty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Power of the Throne and Other Items Constructed with the Auspicious Sudarśana Mahāyantra."
Meditated upon even once, it swiftly destroys the multitude of tens of millions of sins;
we meditate upon that divine splendor of the Lord Sudarśana.
Regarding the question of means other than recitation (*japa*) and so forth for accomplishing the desired goal,
Nārada says: "O Blessed One, everything— recitation, burnt offerings (*homa*), worship (*arcana*), and so on— has been told."
Consecration is great peace; it is the ritual procedure for the performance of great pacification. || 48-1 ||

Since the wielder of the Śārṅga bow possesses the form of a wheel by virtue of accomplishing all purposes, is there any means for achieving desired goals that exists apart from these [weapons], or not? (48.2)
Regarding the statement that the seat and other factors are means (*upāya*), Ahirbudhnya says:
"Even without these, other kings attained their desired goals."
With the seat, the ring, the mirror, and the banner. || 48-3 ||
And Vitāna, whose wealth was extensive; Devasaṃnibha; Muktāpīḍa; Viśāla; Sunanda; and Citraśekhara. || 48-4 ||
And the kings beginning with Kīrtimālin, protecting the entire earth, attained their desired success through the *āsana* and other [methods] of Muktāpīḍa and the rest;
indeed, in former times, Muktāpīḍa conquered the earth by means of the *āsana* alone. (48-5)
Even King Viśāla conquered Death by means of a ring, and the monarch Sunanda [conquered] the world of the Nāgas by means of a mirror alone. (48–6)
With his banner, Citraśekhara won a battle against the asuras;
with his canopy, King Kīrtimālin attained the third heaven.
Nārada asked regarding the inquiry into how mere postures (āsana) and so forth become means for achieving the desired goal:
"How did mere postures and the like attain the status of being means?"
O Lord, tell me this great wonder concerning that which is to be accomplished.
In order to describe the power of the seat, Ahirbudhnya relates the story of Muktāpīḍa:
"The highly resplendent King Muktāpīḍa was the son of Suśravas."
Upon his father's death, he enjoyed the earth, which has the ocean for its garment.
Due to King Hārāpīḍa’s attachment to sensual pleasures, there was a decline of righteousness in his kingdom; with his mind attached to the women of his own inner apartments,
that lotus-eyed king failed to consider the seven constituent elements of sovereignty.
The subjects in that kingdom, practicing a deviation from dharma under his rule, caused the realm to be agitated and seized by powerful bandits. (48.11)
All the subjects reported the agitation to the king, but he, distracted by wine and sexual dalliance, did not even perceive it. (48.12)
The manner of consultation among the ministers together with the family priest:
Then the ministers held counsel together with the family priest;
for the king, being addicted to sensual pleasures, had seen his kingdom overrun by bandits.
Having reflected thus, they all approached their immensely radiant preceptor and said: "By your grace we shall be victorious; there is no other recourse for us. (48.14)

Thus addressed by them, the priest replied to them, "So be it. Having said this, he prepared a seat fashioned from a mechanical device and adorned with jewels, according to the means instructed by Vasiṣṭha. (48–15)
Following the path described by Vasiṣṭha, he performed a most wonderful feat for him;
he placed the king, who was devoted to women, upon that [chariot].
The priest’s instruction regarding specific rites for the king:
"He should have the Vedic branches recited in order in the four directions.
Here, in accordance with the two preceding verses, the subsequent sentences [should be understood as follows].
Although the use of the *liṭ* (perfect tense) alone would be appropriate— since it is logical that the preceptor should be intent on performing the ritual duties,
making the use of the *liṅ* (optative) and other such suffixes in phrases like "he should cause [the student] to recite" (*vācayet*) untenable— nevertheless,
this applies to the verses beginning with "The Vedic branches" (*vedaśākhāḥ*) and ending with the forty-eighth verse.
There is no inconsistency [in this], as it is devoted to the instruction imparted by the priest (purodhāḥ). Therefore,
it should be noted that the natural consistency of the passage in the forty-ninth verse— “he was thus instructed by him”— is also maintained.
(459) [He should provide] songs, instrumental music, and dances accompanied by blessings and auspicious rites. 48.17.
The wise practitioner should contemplate the water in the *kalaśa* as inexhaustible nectar (*amṛta*).
From the midst of that, there arises a golden eight-petaled lotus.
He has four arms and three eyes, holds a lotus in his hand, and is golden-hued;
he is covered with all ornaments and resplendent with pearl necklaces.
Adorned with a crown, necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and other ornaments,
wearing yellow garments, he was gentle, with a gracious countenance and auspicious.
Adorned with a waist-thread, resplendent with two earrings,
bearing the Śrīvatsa on his chest, the Lord of Śrī, the bestower of prosperity, and the abode of Śrī.
[He beheld] Hari, who is ever graced by splendor, whose eyes resemble perfectly formed copper-colored lotuses,
whose navel is a lotus, whose limbs are noble, and who pacifies the suffering of his devotees.
One should contemplate Lakṣmī seated on his right lap;
the Lord is both the essence of the mantra and the deity whose form is the mantra. (48.23)
Then, as he enters, one should visualize him in the form of the mantra;
contemplating the mantra in this way, one should recite it while touching the water-pot.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight thousand times and consecrated one's own body,
one shall become an immediate bringer of peace for the nine groups of planets.
A wise man who desires long life and prosperity should first of all honor all the officiating priests and then have that person consecrated with it. (48.26)
One should satisfy the Brahmins by giving them excellent sacrificial fees;
in this way, one brings about benefit for oneself as well as for others. (48.27)
In this case, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given, consisting of gold weighing exactly one hundred [units].
One should not shake the hair, nor shave it, nor touch the bathing garment. (48.28)
Then the wise man should not stand in the bathing water, but should adorn himself;
he should look upon auspicious objects, a bull, and auspicious women. (48.29)
One should wear white garments on the birth-star of oneself;
likewise, one should perform [the rite] seven times on Fridays for one who is performing it.
The desires conceived by him will certainly be fulfilled; it is not otherwise.
One who desires prosperity should perform the water-carrying rite which destroys sin. (48.31)
Standing with palms joined in reverence, one should again consecrate water one hundred and eight times in the morning and sprinkle it upon the head; this destroys all sins.
One who desires clothing should offer oblations with flowers such as the kumuda;
by offering flowers of whatever color, one shall obtain clothing of that same color. (48.33)
One who desires rain should, in a pure place smeared with cow dung,
prepare a mandala there using red-colored substances.
One should cause a new water-pot to be placed in front of the maṇḍala;
it should be properly wound with thread and filled with fragrant water. (48.35)
Then, with a concentrated mind, he should invoke the Sun into the bright pitcher;
there, the best of practitioners should worship Viṣṇu as before. (48-36)
There, the wise one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) one hundred and eight times;
meditating with one-pointed mind on the Lion, he should recite the mantra a thousand times.
One should perform this for seven days or even twelve;
then the Blessed One, being pleased, releases a great rain.
By means of this very oblation of cane, rain will certainly come about in every way. One who desires rain should always recite [the mantra] while fasting and wearing wet clothes. (48.39)
Within seven days, a great rain shall arise by the divine command, either through the proper offering of ashes or again with salt. (48–49)
One should again ward off the rain; a wise person should perform a rite of pacification (śānti).
He who, having bathed in the morning, should daily recite this mantra a thousand times, [attains success]. (48–49)
Prosperity, health, and splendor always increase for that person who, having conquered the senses and subsisting on a diet of milk, recites [this] on all days. (48–42)
And by performing worship according to his capacity ten million times every day,
he shall attain incomparable perfection, endowed with the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest.

He who, having fasted for a day and night, then drinks the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while constantly reciting [the mantra] eight thousand times, effects the destruction of all sins. (48–44)
Having drunk the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should indeed recite [the mantra] for five days;
one is immediately liberated from all sins, such as the killing of a Brahmin. (48–45)
One should sow all seeds after consecrating them one thousand times;
a great abundance of crops will arise, there is no doubt about this. || 48-49 ||
One should bathe the supreme deity with ghee and milk-rice;
then the Blessed One, being pleased, grants whatever is desired by the mind. (48–47)
The wise man should eat food consecrated with seven mantras every day; while performing the work of another, he should always remain seated and say, "Do it."
Through the practice of what was thus instructed, the king attained a realm free from thorns; having been taught in this manner, he practiced for exactly one month,
whereby all his enemies were destroyed by diseases and their forces.
By means of that [ring], the earth, including the oceans, became free of thorns and subject to his will.
To describe the power of the ring, the narrative of Viśāla begins:
there was a king named Viśāla who dwelt in the city called Viśālā. (48–50)
The righteous-souled one protected the earth, including its oceans and cities;
he was one whose virtues were celebrated for their vastness,
a speaker of truth, impartial toward all, a friend to his kin, a believer in destiny, and a lover of dharma.

Dwelling in his twentieth year as a student of the Brahmins, he was a wise devotee of the Brāhmaṇas, a delighter of his subjects, and firmly established in the rites for the gods and the ancestors. (48–52)

Upon hearing a voice from the sky indicating the death of her own son, the mother lamented: "O Sage, as he was living thus, separated from his father since childhood, his mother heard an incorporeal voice in the sky. (48–53)
"On the coming fourth day, you will meet your death.
Having heard these words, "O son," and so forth, she lamented, deeply distressed. (48–54)
After the king had first consoled his mother,
he went to the hermitage of the priest Pulaha; having heard that his mother was distressed, he spoke with great composure.
When she was thus questioned persistently, "For what reason do you weep? she, being a virtuous woman, [spoke].
He related the events exactly as they had occurred; having heard this, the high-minded one said to her, "Do not fear," and departed for the hermitage of Pulaha.
Having seen the sage engaged in ascetic penance, she prostrated before him and reported her own circumstances to Pulaha; meanwhile,
her mother likewise heard an incorporeal voice from the sky.
The sage thus instructed him in the means for its remedy;
having been addressed in this manner by him, the sage said to the priest: "A ring fashioned from the great *saudarśana* yantra... [48-58]
"Maintain this; by this alone, death will undoubtedly perish. (p.
464) Having been thus instructed by the king regarding the performance of the prescribed practice, the noble one summoned the ring and put it on. (48–59)
Then the king met with the servants of Yama when that well-fastened ring had been seized by Viśāla.
Thereafter, at the appointed time, the servants of fearsome appearance were dispatched.
They came unimpeded to his presence to seize his life;
yet, due to the power of the ring, the servants fled from afar, and because of the power of the ring, they were unable to approach his side. (48–61)
While they, with their arms raised in fury, had not yet hurled their nooses at him,
[he was struck] by various weapons emerging from the great rims of his wheel.
Being severely tormented, they fled back exactly as they had come;
because the King had conquered Death and the others, Yama and his attendants were filled with amazement, and the gods, along with Kāla himself, were likewise struck with wonder.
"By the power of the Sudarśana, he has crossed over death.
Thus ends the narrative of Sunanda for the purpose of describing the power of the mirror;
likewise, O great sage, hear also of the prowess of the mirror.
In ancient times, there was a king named Sunīti in the city called Śṛṅgāra;
at the end of the Tretā Yuga, he protected the earth.

Having worshipped Śatakratu for a long time, he obtained his son named Sumati; having been led to the world of the Nāgas by a Nāga maiden, he raised him, who grew day by day, under the name Sumati. (48–66)
Then, in the course of time, the illustrious Janaka reached youth;
after no small period, he became accomplished in learning and skilled in the use of weapons.
Once, he went to the outer grove to hunt;
there he saw a woman of lovely limbs, endowed with beauty and youth.
Seeing her, whom he had never seen before, he fainted, afflicted by love;
taking Sumati with him, she departed for her own abode.
Having deluded him with her illusory power (māyā), she entered the world of the nāgas.
There, having married Anaṅgamañjarī, the daughter of Vāsuki, she resided for a long time in that very place, in the beautiful city of Bhogavatī, the capital of the nāga kings. || 48–70 ||
Having entered, Ramā gave Sumati to Anaṅgamañjarī;
seeing him, she was exceedingly pleased and chose Sumati as her husband.
Having beheld that world, that city, and that enchanting Naga maiden Anaṅgamañjarī, he was filled with wonder.
Having taken her as his wife according to the Gāndharva rite, he took his pleasure with her,
having forgotten all his possessions, his city, his father, and his kin.

(p. 466) While the king was grieving due to his separation from his son, he heard through his spies that his son had not yet returned. Overcome by the utmost urgency, he spoke thus to his ministers: || 48-74 ||
"My only dear son, obtained with great difficulty, must be admitted today;
I shall eat together with him, for I will not eat today," he urged. (48–75)
Having heard these words of his, spies and other swift messengers dispatched by the ministers went forth in all directions. (48–76)
In the intermediate directions, the cardinal directions, the corners, on mountains, in waters, and in rivers;
in villages, in cities, in shrines, and among the trees—they wandered. (48–77)
Having searched everywhere— in cities, forests, and sacred fords—
all of them failed to see Sumati, and they reported this very fact to the king.
Having heard that news regarding his son not being found, the king undertook a vow of fasting;
having heard it and lamented greatly, tormented by grief, the lord of the earth lay down within, overcome by profound sorrow, refusing to eat. (48–79)
The priest’s report on the king’s conduct, following his journey to Kaṇva’s hermitage:
"While this great king was thus overwhelmed by grief, the family priest, having approached his own guru Kaṇva, who dwells on the banks of the Tamasā river... (48–80).
He reported such conduct of the prince;
(p. 467) the sage Kaṇva revealed the account of the royal prince, and having heard it, that sage was again filled with compassion. 48–81.
Having perceived the account of the prince through his yogic power,
the sage arose from that state and related the entire event to him.
There was a most magnificent city named Bhogavatī in Pātāla, belonging to Vāsuki, the king of the Nāgas, who possesses immeasurable splendor.
In that city, he had a daughter named Anaṅgamañjarī,
who was endowed with beauty and grace, and in time she reached the bloom of youth.
"Whomever she desires as her husband, to him I shall give her"—
perceiving this resolve of Vāsuki, the celestial beings moved about here and there.
They were unable to find a bridegroom worthy of her;
thus, they wandered through the world of the Nāgas as well as upon the earth, seeking a suitable husband.
There, having seen that charming prince Sumati, the sons of the great king, who resembled the god of love, said to her: [48.87]
"Only one equal to you on this earth, and like Indra in splendor, could he be brought under control; yet even by means of conciliation and the other [stratagems], he cannot be subdued. (48–88)
Having heard that, she said to them, "Bring him here at once," and out of eagerness for union with him, she fell into deep anxiety.
Then, having consulted together, those friends said to Ramā, who was skilled in illusion:
"Having deluded him with illusion, bring Manorama here. (48.90)
Having spoken thus, she brought him there by means of her illusory power (māyā) as she had been told; then Sumati, having married her, now enjoys himself there.
Regarding the recovery of the prince, instruction is given that only a mirror fashioned from the Sudarśana machine is the means for the act of retrieval without the power of the Sudarśana.
There is no other means for him; therefore, I bring it by that [means].
Having fashioned the great Sudarśana machine out of gold, bring him here by that means along the previously described path; do not delay.
Having spoken thus, he again performed an extremely severe penance;
through the performance of the practices as instructed, the king’s success in going to the world of the Nāgas was achieved.
The domestic priest, having gone forth, reported everything to the king. (48–94)
And the king, exceedingly delighted, having restrained his pride and stationed it at the front of the chariot, then proceeded to the entrance of the cave.
By the power of his pride, Sunanda was able to approach;
and from seeing the most wonderful world of the Nāgas—as if entering another world of heaven—the king experienced an exceeding sense of wonder. (48–96)
He attained supreme wonder upon beholding that prosperity:
the bringing back by the king of the prince and his wife to his own city;
and in that [city], the beautiful Bhogavatī, the city of the Naga kings. (48–97)
Then, having entered from the inner apartments, Sumati, who was exceedingly affectionate toward his son, brought his son there so that he might see his father together with his wife. (48.98)
He set forth accompanied by the women, like Madana himself;
he [proceeded] with those Nāga maidens in that excellent chariot.
Having escorted him to his own city, the king, the slayer of enemy heroes, set out;
meanwhile, Vāsuki became enraged and prepared for battle.
Then the lord of the earth [brought] his daughter’s husband from his own inner apartments.
Having heard that someone was departing after mounting a chariot, Vāsuki set forth,
exceedingly enraged and surrounded by his army of hooded serpents.
Seeing that tiger among kings, he cried out, "Wait! Wait!
Where are you going, taking the bride and her groom away from here? (48.102)

Then Sunanda, having heard that the king had achieved victory through the power of the mirror fashioned from the Sudarśana-yantra, turned back his excellent chariot and chose the mirror, saying, "Slay the enemy army this very day! (48.103)
Then, as soon as the divine weapons Prasvāpana and Āgneya had been discharged,
the Prasvāpana entered the army of the Nāgas, and by means of it, they were put to sleep.
He launched the fiery weapon (*āgneya-astra*) with great vigor to burn that city;
however, seeing that the king had offered him worship after being defeated and seeking refuge, Vāsuki, the king of the *nāgas*, approached him for protection. (48–105)
"O Lord, we did not know all this; may it be forgiven by you.
Considering that this is a great peril for women, please attain tranquility. (48.106)
"Accept these highly precious jewels, O one of great splendor, as well as this maiden and another thousand nāga women. (48.107)
"Having taken up and withdrawn the divine weapons, you ought to depart.
Then, saying "So be it," Sunanda withdrew the weapons and remained composed as the king, along with his retinue, entered his own city. (48-108)
Then, having taken his son, great jewels, and excellent women, and having bid farewell to him, the successful king departed for his own city.

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Power of the Seat and Other Items Constructed with the Great Sudarśana Yantra," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the illustrious *Pāñcarātra*. 48.
From the beginning, verse 3045:
The forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Radiance of the Banner Constructed with the Great Sudarśana Machine."
Meditated upon even once, it swiftly destroys the flood of millions of births;
we meditate upon that divine splendor of the Lord Sudarśana.
Ahirbudhnya’s declaration of intent regarding the description of the splendor of the banner fashioned from the great Sudarśana machine:
"Of the banner, however, which is fashioned from the great Sudarśana machine..."
O Nārada, listen properly and according to the truth regarding his power.
Description of the excellent city of Bhadravāṭī, presided over by Citraśekhara:
On the lovely bank of the Sarasvatī lies the city renowned as Bhadravāṭī, filled with thousands of palaces made of gold. (49.2)
The city, rich in various desires and endowed with golden walls, was like the third heaven in its prosperity; it was difficult to find on earth. (49-3)
The son of King Uparicara, known by the name Citraśekhara, of great prowess, dwells upon that mountain, protecting it for many years. (49.4)
(p. 472) His father, Uparicara, once slew a demon named Śaṅkukarṇa in a duel;
he [Uparicara] had formerly received from Indra a divine [bow], which had been passed down through his lineage.
Having mounted his chariot, the powerful one travels through the sky for the sake of the gods' mission.
A Dānava known as Śaṅkukarṇa, who had terrifying eyes, desiring to seize his chariot, seized its pole on the road. (49-6)
And he said: "Fight with me, or [destroy] my chariot; or slay me. When he had spoken thus, the other agreed, saying "So be it," and took up his bow. (49.7)
Then, after that great battle had proceeded for one day,
the Asura was slain in a duel after he had cast aside his multitude of weapons.
O Queen, after the sage had passed away in time, having conquered that Asura named Amarṣaṇa— the son of Śaṅkukarṇa— who had tormented Citraśekhara;
then the son of Śaṅkukarṇa, who was exceedingly wrathful, [conquered] his son.
Known as Amarṣaṇa, that master of illusion constantly oppressed the city and the army of the king, desiring to destroy them.
Once, filled with indignation and rage, Amārṣaṇa approached Bhadravāṭī to fight Citraśekhara along with his army—the son who had slain his father. (49.11)
"Having slain him, I shall seize this entire, most excellent chariot";
having said this, he, arrogant in his strength, besieged the beautiful city.
(473) Having equipped a great army, the king marched out from the city for a fierce battle with Citraśekhara;
there, a battle took place between the king and that evil-minded one. 49-13.
With mutual retreats and advances, and with hair-to-hair grappling that was terrifying,
the elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry were thrown into confusion as their chariots were shattered.
It was filled with the flow of rivers of flowing blood, strewn with severed umbrellas and banners,
with dancing headless trunks, and covered with heads whose lips were bitten off.
Even though he fought for three days, there was no victory; thus the battle continued for three days, causing the hair to stand on end. Citraśekhara did not obtain victory in that conflict.
Both armies withdrew from the battle; thus, out of exhaustion, both forces desisted.
Having rested their mounts, they both returned to their respective cities. (49.17)
Thus, despite fighting for seventeen times, victory was not achieved; Citraśekhara fought with him for these seventeen times, yet the lord of the earth did not attain victory anywhere. (49–18)
The King’s Mode of Reflection while Distressed:
Then, having considered the great Asura Durjaya to be intolerant and invincible, he became absorbed in thought as to by what means he might be conquered. (49.19)
"Without the grace of Mahādeva, there can be no victory for me;
therefore, I shall resolve to please that God through ascetic penance. (49.20)
Having resolved upon going to Kailāsa and having mentally renounced the kingdom to his ministers, the virtuous king ascended his chariot that travels at will and departed for the sake of asceticism.

The lord of the earth traveled through the sky toward the beautiful peak of Kailāsa; as he proceeded through the heavens, his chariot’s progress was obstructed by Mount Mandara, and thus his chariot came to rest upon that mountain.
O Nārada, even as his excellent horses were being urged forward, the chariot remained stationary;
wondering at the cause of this, he traveled on until he beheld Kubera, filled with amazement, thinking, "Why has my chariot suddenly come to a standstill? (49.23)
The lord of the earth descended from his chariot at its beautiful peak;
having alighted from that chariot, he wandered upon the mountain summit.
There, on the shore of the lake, he saw a youth endowed with divine marks,
remaining unperturbed as he performed his evening twilight devotions.
Resembling the rising sun and blazing with his own radiance,
the mighty-armed one bowed down to him and, with palms joined in reverence, addressed him in conversation. (49.26)
"Who are you? Are you the Ancient Puruṣa, or perhaps the Lotus-born Brahmā; are you Umā’s Lord Śiva, or one of the other world-protectors? (49.27)
Thus addressed by him, the Blessed One spoke with a profound voice:
"Tell me, what is your name, and what is the reason for your coming? (49.28)
"How did you reach this region all alone?"— to this question as well,
Kubera, the son of King Uparicara, then related his entire account to the king.
He [described] himself as the lord of the earth named Citraśekhara,
the activities of the great Asura, and his own oppression by him.
For the sake of conquering that [obstacle] and for the purpose of pleasing Īśa, he performed austerities;
consequently, his chariot arrived there and was obstructed.
At the word of Kubera, he gained knowledge of Lakṣmī’s dwelling on that mountain; thus addressed by him, he replied: "Know me to be the Lord of the Guhyakas.
