Right here dwells Mahālakṣmī, the cause of all causes. (49.32)
I have come here for the sake of serving her, for she is the supreme goal of all states of existence;
by her command alone, the moon and sun move through the sky.
By its power, the movement of your chariot was indeed obstructed. (p.
476) Having said, "Having seen her, accomplish your desired goal," [Kubera] vanished after first giving the instruction on propitiating Lakṣmī. 49-34.
For the purpose of assisting the king, there was the arrival of a person sent by Kubera;
desiring to help him, another approached at his command.
Having bowed to the lord of the earth, he said: "By his command, I am a Guhyaka. (49.35)
Desiring to assist you, I have arrived here and shall remain for this very night;
at dawn, I will do whatever is required, and not otherwise.

At his word, they spent that night in that very place; having passed the night there in mutual affection, they heard the sound of the Gandharvas' singing and instrumental music in the assembly hall of the Goddess.
Listening to those stories, they both spent that time on the bank of the lake.
At dawn, desiring to know the location of the abode of Lakṣmī, the king questioned the Guhyaka after performing the first twilight prayer at the hour of daybreak.
He said to the Guhyaka: "Where on this mountain does that goddess reside? By what path shall we go to her abode, and when shall we behold her? (49.39)
The Guhyaka’s reply: The Guhyaka answered this: "That supreme palace is a *krośa* away, from where the great sound of songs and drums is heard. (49.40)
After attending upon her for some time, Dhanada will depart in an instant; once he has gone, you shall enter and pay homage to this eternal goddess. (49–51)
Then he set out for Lakṣmī’s abode together with the Guhyaka; having waited for him for only a watch (yāma),
the king also halted his own chariot there and followed after him.
At the entrance of the cave was the abode of a Guhyaka; from there, a temple was seen on the side of the great cave.
He remained at that cave's entrance, guarding the mountain cavern.
Having passed through four inner courtyards made of jewels,
he then entered the divine assembly pavilion made of gems located within the king's palace.
Description of the Pavilion:
A pavilion was seen, enriched with a thousand pillars of precious gems and adorned with couches made of more than a hundred great jewels. (49–45)
It was adorned with jewel-lamps of auspiciousness and possessed lofty archways;
it was crowded with many celestial beings and embellished with jeweled pedestals.
Its interior was powerfully perfumed by the fragrances of *mandāra* flowers, the secretions of musk deer, and the scents arising from *kastūrikā*. (49.47)
It possessed a merit exceeding the radiance of the sun, was adorned with strings of pearls,
enriched with garlands of golden lotuses, and beautified by banners and flags.
It was perfumed on all sides with incense produced from black aloe-wood,
and adorned with a paste made from camphor mixed with Kālīyaka powder.
The interior resounded with the tinkling of ornaments from the Śaktis moving here and there, and with the jingling sounds of their anklets.
In the center of the pavilion, upon a couch situated on a lotus seat, he beheld Mahālakṣmī;
seated there upon a refined lotus throne on a jeweled couch, she was Mahālakṣmī, the embodiment of great bliss, supported by all the Śaktis. (49–51)
Adorned with all ornaments and beautified by every kind of decoration,
her limbs were like the nectar of loveliness, and her face resembled the orb of the moon.
Beholding her clad in divine silken garments and adorned with celestial sandalwood paste and garlands, he bowed down and became motionless with wonder. (49-53)
The king, purified by drinking the water from her feet, offered praise to her; then Rati, taking that water from her feet, made him drink it.
Thereupon, being well-pleased, he praised that goddess of auspicious eyes. (49–54)
(p. 479) Therein, the manifestation of Lakṣmī’s sovereignty over both types of prosperity is described:
"O Mahālakṣmī, O auspicious one, you who dwell in the supreme void (paravyoman), the infinite one called Suṣumnā, who are cherished by the wise..."
O Victorious One, O you who delight the wise, O Refuge, O you of auspicious fame, please bestow your grace upon me, who have sought your protection. || 49-55 ||
Obeisance to you, O Gaurī, Gāyatrī, Gārgī, Dhruvā, Kāmadhenu, and you who are worshipped by the Lord of the Gods;
O Sunīti, as cool as the full moon, O Kumārī!
Bestow your grace upon me, who have come to you for refuge.
I delight in Rāmarāma, who is constantly praised by perfected beings, gandharvas, lords of yakṣas, and vidyādharas,
and who is extolled while being served by all the immortals.
Grant your favor to me, who have come to you with devotion. || 49-57 ||
The justification for the sincerity of human effort lies solely in Lakṣmī herself—
she who is pure, capable of warding off floods of misfortune, and attainable through radiant good fortune.
Salutations to you, O beloved of Hari, who are known as the radiance of the reality that is the object signified by the Praṇava. || 49-58 ||
O perfected one, O you whose form is mantra, O most excellent one, O secret one, O satisfied one, O eternal knowledge of the *udgītha*,
O manifest one, O you who are cultivated by the wise, O you who are known as creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*).
O auspicious lady, grant prosperity to me who have sought refuge in you.
In the universal support, the true path, the inner science;
in that which is becoming, moist, and liberated, the inner creeper;
in the overseer of the universe, the ground for the abode of auspiciousness.
O auspicious lady, grant what is auspicious to me who have taken refuge in you.

Because she is the ultimate source of auspicious qualities, Lakṣmī serves as the ornament of the crest of the Vedas; her service is unfailing, and she illuminates the head of the sacred tradition through the abundance of her own excellent virtues.
O lady of great power, whose gaze is beyond causal investigation,
please take me as your object of vision.
The state of being a manifestation of Mahālakṣmī belongs to Umā, Śacī, and others,
despite the various distinctions among the powers (śakti) such as Umā, Śacī, Kīrti, Sarasvatī, Dhī, Svāhā, and so forth.
O you whose very nature is the ornament of the entire world, take me as the object of your vision. || 49-62 ||
(481) Having heard this praise, Lakṣmī, pleased by the eulogy, spoke to the king who was desiring a boon:
"I grant you today whatever you have requested; tell me what it is, O Lord of the Earth. (49–63)
The king’s narration of his own history; the presentation of the Sudarśana-yantra and its banner by Lakṣmī;
and the king’s account of his lineage and how he was oppressed by great asuras.
He told her everything, and she said, "Do not be afraid."
Although I am the very foundation of the powers of the universe,
by the majesty of Sudarśana, I provide protection to those who take refuge in me.
With these words, he then presented him with a banner, saying, "By this, slay your enemy.
Through the power of the banner bestowed by Lakṣmī, the king attained a kingdom free from thorns, preceded by victory over his foes.
Having obtained that banner, which had been brought under control, the king went to his own city.
By means of that [weapon], he conquered the vast army of the Asuras;
having slain him as well, Citraśekhara ruled his kingdom in happiness.

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Glorification of the Banner Constructed with the Great Sudarśana Yantra," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine of the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
Chapter Fifty: The Description of the Narrative of Kīrtimālā (Total Verses from the Beginning: 3112).
Even a single meditation [upon Him] swiftly destroys a multitude of sins numbering ten million.
We meditate upon that divine splendor of the god Sudarśana.
Ahirbudhnya provides an indication of the meaning to be explained hereafter:
"But listen to this, O celestial sage Kīrtimālin, from Vitāna."
By that very same method, the powerful one formerly conquered the triple heaven.
In ancient times, there was a king of noble conduct known as Bhadraśṛṅga, a most righteous ruler of the earth, who resided in the city named Viśālā. (50.2)
As he ruled the earth consisting of seven continents like his own city, being equal to Śakra himself, ten thousand autumns passed by.
The description of the virtues of his son, Kīrtimālin:
His son was Kīrtimālin, long-lived, yet arrogant with pride;
he was a hero with eyes like lotus petals, as handsome as Kandarpa himself. (50.4)
Powerful, without rival, and proficient in all scriptures; knowledgeable in discipline, most magnanimous, majestic, and true to his promise. (50.5)
Never retreating in battles, profound and proud of his wealth,
with a roar as deep as a thundercloud, he was desirous of victory and a scorcher of his enemies.
Like a rutting elephant, he wandered freely over this earth.
Following his father's death, he likewise protected the kingdom in accordance with dharma.
While he was conducting himself in this manner, his father met his end. (50–7)
When his father had passed away, the illustrious prince ruled the earth as if he were his father;
he learned of all the events occurring in the world through certain spies.
He knew his own conduct within his seven cities and even within his own limbs;
once, at midnight, as he was moving secretly outside the city,
the king— alone and armed with a bow— overheard the private conversation of men.
Having gone out at midnight to hear [him], he wandered everywhere through the city—
in the marketplaces, on the streets, at the crossroads, and in the houses.
At all the gates, on the ramparts, in the lakes, and in the forests; in the pavilions, at the shrines, and in the temples of the gods.
While wandering through armories, sacred fords, forests, and garden grounds, he saw a brahmin seated at the foot of a śamī tree outside the city.
The fearless king beheld him, who was like a blazing fire, his body adorned yet tranquil, having manifested the Sudarśana [discus] in person. (50.13)
Having bowed down with humility before him— who had attained all desires, was established in yoga, and was stainless—
the lord of the earth asked this:
Desirous of knowing his history, the king questioned him: "Who are you, and for what purpose have you now taken refuge at the foot of this tree?
From where have you come? O sinless one, tell everything to me who asks. (50.15)

Established in yoga and not understanding the king's question, he remained silent; though addressed in this manner, he who was fixed in yoga did not perceive what was said, and even when spoken to again and again, he did not address the king. (50–16)

When the king, enraged, attempted to seize the brahmin by force, he became paralyzed through the power of the brahmin; at that moment, by his influence, the king’s movements were rendered motionless. (50.17)
Filled with wonder, the king sought to appease the brahmin with hymns of praise;
perceiving himself to be paralyzed by astonishment, he fell into a state of supreme amazement.
Then, bowing down, he further gratified him with those very praises.
(485) The disclosure of his own history by the pleased brahmin: Satisfied, he rose from his yoga and spoke these words to the king:
"There is an unsurpassed abode of Viṣṇu known as Sālagrāma. (50.19)
The Lord of the Universe, in the form of the Discus, is eternally present there;
and everything there, whether stationary or moving, is marked with the discus.
Merely by entering there, living beings are freed from defilement;
those who cast off their bodies there attain supreme nirvāṇa.
In that region was born a Brāhmaṇa esteemed by the learned,
who had accomplished all his spiritual goals through the power of Sudarśana.
"O Lord of the World, today I was going to the Pauṣkara Tīrtha;
by the force of the path at night, I have arrived at this prosperous city of yours. (50.23)
Having observed that the gates were closed, he took refuge here at the foot of a śamī tree.
Then the king, who had learned the news, spoke thus regarding the bringing of the blameless brahmin back to his own city; having honored him, the king [acted accordingly]. (50.24)
He caused him to enter the beautiful city; there, too, he entered the temple of Hari.
Having stayed there for that night with every mark of hospitality, [he departed]. (50.25)
On the following day, the twice-born man set out toward Puṣkara to offer beneficial advice at the king's request; meanwhile,
the king, having performed his morning rites, addressed him.
"The sight of the virtuous is meritorious and the means for accomplishing all desired goals; this I have heard. Therefore, O Blessed One, I ask: what is beneficial for me? (50.27)
"Grant me such grace that I may find happiness here and, moreover, be without rival in the next world; for your mind is moist with compassion. (50.28)
He gave the instruction on the great mantra of the Sudarśana with its ancillaries to the king;
then, being pleased, the twice-born sage [taught] the six-syllabled great mantra of the Sudarśana, which accomplishes all things, to the king who had approached him in devotion. (50.29)

Then, having first shown him honor, he taught that king the mantra along with its auxiliary limbs (aṅga), as well as meditation, the means of accomplishment (sādhana), and the mystical diagram (yantra).
Likewise, O great sage, he taught all the weapon-mantras that cause both engagement and withdrawal, as well as fifty equipped vehicles.
Having given everything to him, he prepared to depart. The king, being exceedingly pleased, presented a collection of wealth as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for his preceptor. || 50-32 ||
O Sage, [he gave] a thousand cows and ten million pieces of gold;

here, the sentence should be construed by supplying the word *abhilakṣya* (aiming at). And regarding the word *upasannāya*, that wise one [taught] to him who had approached, whose mind was perfectly tranquil, and who was endowed with self-restraint.

This is an indicator of other necessary qualities of a disciple taught in such scriptural passages as these. And so, by signs such as humility and gentle speech, that twice-born man [perceived] that the king was endowed with qualities such as a tranquil mind.
The syntactical connection is that, having observed him to be fit for the instruction of the knowledge of Brahman, he taught him the great Sudarśana mantra along with its ancillaries. (p.
487) "And seven other golden vessels filled with jewels. (50.33)
Likewise, the most virtuous king gave to his preceptor many garments of great value and eight villages.

Without first accepting that [gift], the Brāhmaṇa did not desire to go to the region favored by his teacher; for he said: "O King, what is to be done with these sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*)? Everything would be accomplished once the resolve is made. (50.35)
When told, "Employ this as you wish," the king replied:
"This must certainly be accepted; if it is not, then I am no seeker of perfection. (50.36)
"O sir, let it be abandoned as you wish; for that which was given by me has indeed been given.
Thus addressed, the brahmin spoke to the king of immeasurable splendor.
"Let that collection of wealth intended for my sake be given to the Brahmins";
having said this, the brahmin departed, and the king followed after him.
Having been turned back by his preceptor, he gave wealth to the Brahmins;
when he had departed, the great king, having lawfully entrusted that wealth of the kingdom to him, governed the realm righteously. (50.39)
He governed this earth just as Maghavan governs the triple heaven,
having divided day and night so that they do not conflict with dharma and liberation.
The lord of the earth pursued wealth and pleasure at their proper times,
and he did not transgress in the slightest regarding the duties of kingship or any other matters.
And thus, following the path of Manu, that lord of the earth delighted his subjects solely through righteous protection. (50.42)
Once, out of a desire to ascertain whether his own kingdom and those of others were submissive or unsubmissive, the king summoned all his ministers to the assembly hall and questioned them.
The protector of the earth asked: "And who are those who are submissive, or otherwise? (50.43)
"Regarding the provinces, the rulers of the earth, or my own subjects—tell me everything, for you possess the eyes of spies. (50.44)
This was the reply of the ministers; thus commanded, all those ministers said:
"O King, O scorcher of foes, while you yourself are ruling this earth..."
The opposing forces dissolve away just as darkness vanishes when the sun shines;
by means of this virtuous practice, the entire circle of the earth—including its mountains, oceans, and cities—is brought under control. (50.46)
O King of the World, just as all the kings of the gods are barred at the gates of heaven, what need is there to speak of your own subjects? (50.47)
The demonstration that gods and others lack the power to bring [you] under their control:
Neither the gods, nor the gandharvas, nor the asuras, nor the pannagas serve you, the Supreme Lord, in the manner that we do. (50.48)
"The King is the authority," they said, and having thus informed him, they ceased [their deliberation].

(p. 489) Again, the king questioned his ministers regarding the means for victory over the gods and others; and Kīrtimālī, having heard that, [acted] with the desire to conquer the gods and the rest. (50.49)
Then he yawned and spoke this to all the ministers:
"How shall we conquer these who are so powerful and endowed with such heroism? (50.50)
Diverse warriors, arrogant and endowed with the power of illusion, who were favorable, distinguished, and had resorted to the other world. || 50-51 ||
"Speak without delay so that they may become submissive.
Having been addressed with these words by the ministers, the counselors deliberated and spoke thus to the great king.

"We shall set out this very day and conquer them in battle. Having first ascertained the abundance of strength on our own side, they incited the effort for military expedition, saying: "Our entire army is equipped with the fourfold forces. (50–53)
Elephants resembling Mount Meru and Mandara, who are exceedingly difficult to conquer—even a single one of them is sufficient for the crushing of the enemy host. (50–54)
There were ten million such Nāgas,
and five crores of rutting horses, O scorcher of foes.
And there were three full crores of chariots belonging to those heroes who had displayed their prowess, who were honored for their deeds, and who never retreated. 50–56.
(490) There are fourteen akṣauhiṇīs of fourfold infantry; O Lord of the Earth, our sharp weapons in battle are beyond counting. (50–57)
On one side all this [power] combined, and on the other side you alone, the powerful one; we consider that you are superior in valor. (50–58)
Furthermore, you have obtained divine weapons from the Brahmin;
who indeed could stand before you when you are thus surrounded by them? (50–59)
Like the elemental beings of Śambhu, who desires to burn the world at the time of universal dissolution,
wherever your desire to conquer arises, do not delay there.
"Employ us, O mighty-armed one; know that victory rests in your hand.
At these words of the minister, the first [plan] being an expedition against the world of the Nāgas, the exceedingly powerful Kīrtimālī was filled with supreme joy.
Having summoned all the ministers, he said: "These various armies have been gathered by me;
let them go today to the world of the Nāgas and fight with the serpents this very day."
"And I myself shall depart this very day, together with my roots, army, and mounts.
Having spoken thus, that lord of the earth set out, surrounded by them.
By the power of the Garuḍa weapon, victory was attained there by the king;
there, a hair-raising battle took place with those serpents.
Then, in a short time, by means of the divine weapon of Garuḍa— || 50–64 ||
Having achieved victory there, the high-minded one took tribute consisting of jewels and other wealth from them and set his mind upon the destruction of the Daityas.
Likewise, O great sage, there was a fierce battle with the Daityas that lasted for a long time;
having destroyed their army, he attained supreme victory. (50.66)
Having first achieved victory over the yakṣas, gandharvas, and others, the powerful king returned to his own city;
thereafter, having defeated all the yakṣas, gandharvas, siddhas, and vidyādharas in battle, he made them his servants.
Having conquered these in battle, he returned once more to his own city.
There, while seated in the assembly hall surrounded by kings, and because the gods were no longer visible among his own retinues, he dispatched a message to Indra. (50–68)
Likewise, at his own assembly hall, the universal monarch then beheld the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Dānavas, and lords of the Pannagas.
Then he spoke these words to the Gandharva named Manojava:
"Today, having gone to the third heaven at my command, [inform] Vāsava."
"You should say: 'Quickly release for my sake the elephant Airāvata, the thunderbolt, the wish-fulfilling tree, and likewise the eight Apsarases. (50.71)
At the king’s command, the messenger named Manojava,
having said "So be it," took the command of the universal monarch upon his head like a garland and departed for Amarāvatī.

There, in the pavilion of non-abiding, he beheld Vāsava; having entered that beautiful city, which was the supreme model for all cities, he saw Vāsava surrounded by the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas. (50.73)
[He saw] the Lord of Śacī seated in a pavilion of precious stones, attended by throngs of apsarases,
and being praised by Siddhas headed by Viśvāvasu.
Then he beheld the God, eager for the sight of the dance;
and having seen him, he bowed and offered praise once the performance of the dance had ceased.
Seeing the messenger welcomed by Vāsava, the Lord of the Gods was pleased and gazed upon him, who possessed the speed of thought. The messenger then delivered the king’s message to Indra.
Considering himself to have been purified, he [proceeded] with his glances.
He reported the events exactly as they had occurred without delay to the slayer of Vṛtra:
"O Lord, on the surface of the earth there is one renowned as Kīrtimālin."
The Cakravartin reported this to the Lord of the Gods through a messenger:
"I have conquered all the worlds, including the three heavens and the intermediate spaces. (50.78)
"O Lord of the Three Heavens, I now desire to see you [mounted] upon the unobstructed Airāvata, the king of serpents, for the purpose of ascending."
"O Gopati, release for us here a barber, a thunderbolt, and eight women"—
thus was he commanded by that great king.
"The Lord is the authority in this matter," said Manojava, and then he ceased speaking.
(p. 493) Upon hearing this message, Indra became enraged; then, laughing, Maghavan proceeded to take action against him in his assembly hall frequented by the gods. (50.81)
Having recognized this mockery, he spoke with a profound voice:
"Today I shall send both Vajra and the elephant Airāvata to you."
"Let him come himself, or let him depart after having gathered others," having said this, he dispatched Vajra and the elephant Airāvata.
With the thunderbolt-bearing Airāvata,
they both emerged and entered the great city of Kīrtimālī;
having entered, the elephant Airāvata took up his thunderbolt against the army.
O great sage, he struck her with an invisible form.
While the troops—elephants, horses, warriors, and their own men—were being slaughtered, the terrified citizens reported that incident to the king. (50–85)
All the inhabitants of the countryside, being terrified, reported this to the king:
"O Lord, the serpents born from Sāma have been slain and lie upon the earth. (50.86)
Likewise, O Lord of the Earth, these excellent, heroic, and most splendid warriors are seen to have been slain all of a sudden. (50.87)
Having heard of the destruction of his army, the king, overcome with grief, questioned his domestic priest.
Having heard this, the great king, enveloped by intense sorrow, summoned the domestic priest and spoke these words: (50–88)
Elephants, horses, and warriors are slain without cause;
no disease is seen among them, nor any suffering brought about by time. (50.89)
No malevolent spell performed by another is seen here, even when carefully examined.
O Brahmin, what is this? Let it be considered; my mind seems to be wandering. (50.90)
Having heard what was said—that the priest had declared the anger of the gods to be the very cause of that—the priest also reflected;
having reflected, he said this: "It has come about from the anger of the gods. (50.91)
"Thus I suspect, O scorcher of foes, that you have not fallen under the power of grief.
While the two of them were reflecting thus, Manojava arrived. || 50.92 ||
Bowing with palms joined in reverence, he stood by the side of the great king.
The king’s question to Manojava: "Manojava, what has been brought of the four jewels that were mentioned?"
"What did Vāsava say? Tell me everything now without delay.
Thus addressed by the king, he reported to him in full everything that had been asked with the speed of thought.
Then follows the narration of Indra’s speech, Maghavan’s astonishment,
the dispatching of Vajra and Airāvata by him, and subsequently their words.
Having learned that his own army had been destroyed by Airāvata,
the king, having resolved upon Airāvata’s course of action, dispatched [an arrow] with the elephant-weapon (*vāraṇāstra*) against Airāvata himself.
Having consulted with the family priest regarding a remedy for that, at that very moment—
He discharged the divine weapon named Vāraṇa, which wards off elephants;
when that weapon reached the elephant, it then became motionless.
Upon hearing that, Vāsava dispatched the divine army for the sake of battle;
then the gods, following Airāvata, informed Maghavan of the great-souled one’s [use of] the thunderbolt and that weapon by which Airāvata had been paralyzed.
Hearing that, Maghavan became exceedingly enraged and prepared for battle;
seeing Indra thus equipped with armor, the gods then were agitated.
Dispatched by him, all those soldiers went to that city—
the army of Śatakratu resembling the ocean surging at the time of universal dissolution.
Then, observing the onset of a terrible battle between the divine and human armies, the king quickly emerged from the city with his forces;
thereupon, the combat between the divine and human armies commenced. (50–101)
A description of the battle in progress— unprecedented, wondrous, causing cries of "Alas!", and terrifying,
accompanied by the sounds of divine drums as well as the blasts of conchs and kettledrums. (50.102)
The sky was filled with shouts and the clapping of palms;
elephants fought with elephants, and likewise, foot-soldiers with foot-soldiers.
Chariots [attacked] chariots, and horses [attacked] horses, with one another, using iron arrows, iron clubs, spears, sharp-edged swords, and even mallets. (50.104)
With bows, spears, swords, barbed missiles, lances, and axes—
with such various kinds of weapons, they struck one another.
Some had their heads severed by enemies, some had their chests cut open;
some had their weapons snatched away, while others had their chests pierced. (50.106)
Some elephants were seen with their trunks severed, others with their heads split open by swords;
likewise, horses were seen with their hearts pierced by broad-headed arrows.
Rivers of blood from elephants, chariots, and horses have begun to flow;
the battlefields are seen covered with falling weapons and mangled bodies. (50.108)
In that situation, as the battle thus proceeded, Indra, desiring victory, swiftly urged on all the commanders of the celestial army, saying: "O subduers of Pāka, you who seek victory! || 50.109 ||
The commanders of the divine armies attained victory at that moment;
the gods, dispatched by him, routed the king's forces and immediately achieved triumph, whereupon the king became enraged. (50.110)

1. First, there is the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound *syandanavājinaḥ*, meaning "the horses of the chariots. Then, there is the two-word *dvandva* compound *hastinaś ca syandanavājinaś ca*, meaning "elephants and the horses of the chariots. It is not, however, a three-word *dvandva* consisting of *hastinaś ca syandanāś ca vājinaś ca*, because [in the latter case] the chariots would be inanimate.

Because it is impossible for the word *syandana* to be a constituent of a *dvandva* compound due to its connection with the flow of blood (*raktasaṃsruti*), [the king] discharged a divine weapon (*divyāstra*). (p. 497)
When his own army was destroyed, he then discharged divine weapons;
O great sage, the Āgneya and other weapons were set in motion.
Because they too were repelled by Indra, the king, becoming despondent,
took refuge under a canopy fashioned from the Sudarśana weapon;
thereupon the slayer of Bala, enraged, warded them off with counter-weapons.
Then Kīrtimālin fell into a state of despondency because of that best of brahmins.
Having obtained the celestial chariot, he remembered it and then caused it to be made accordingly:
equipped with the great Sudarśana machine and provided with a canopy.
Having sat down in the shade of that tree,
the lord of the earth dispatched the supreme Vaiṣṇava discus, born of great weapons and employed by the King, to strike back against the army of the gods.
Having filled the entire universe with his splendor, he shone forth in the sky;
by that very splendor, all the gods were repelled in battle.
O Sage, the hosts of gods were utterly unable to act;
even the divine weapons dispatched by Vāsava met their destruction upon that discus of Viṣṇu.
Thereupon, enraged, Maghavan released his own divine weapons. (50–116)
Having emerged, all of them dissolved into Viṣṇu’s discus,
just as moths dissolve into a fire that is the source of all weapons.
Thereupon, he hurled all his weapons again and again;
they dissolved right there, just as rivers merge into the ocean. (50.118)
Finally, even the thunderbolt proved to be of no avail;
thereupon, becoming supremely enraged, he hurled the thunderbolt—which is highly honored by the gods—but it vanished right there in that very same manner. (50.119)
The conversation between Śakra, who was astonished by his own defeat, and the king;
having seen that, Śakra approached the side of the king, while Kīrtimālī stood before the Lord of the Gods as he remained in his celestial chariot. (50.120)
Having risen and bowed down, he praised him with auspicious words;
thereupon, the Lord of Śacī, being pleased, spoke this to the king: || 50-121 ||
Formerly, the weapons released by you were rendered fruitless;
now they are seen to have the opposite effect—tell me the reason for this.
The king’s proclamation of his own invincibility through the power of the canopy fashioned from the Sudarśana machine:
by the efficacy of that which is constrained by the great Sudarśana machine.
O Hari, know that invincibility has been attained by our canopy.
After establishing friendship between the king and Śakra, they each returned to their respective abodes.
Then [Śakra] said: "O Great King, let there be friendship between us two;
whatever belongs to me shall be yours, and whatever belongs to you shall be mine. (50.124)
That god went to the third heaven with his army, weapons, and vehicles;
and he, garlanded with fame, satisfied and victorious, returned to his own city. (50.125)
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Kīrtimālin," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
From the beginning, verse number 3237:
The fifty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Meaning of the Nature of the Seed-Syllables, Tārā and Others."
Meditated upon even once, it swiftly removes the flood of millions of births;
we meditate upon that divine splendor of the Lord Sudarśana.
The inquiry regarding the meaning of the mantras beginning with Tārā;
Nārada said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, destroyer of the eyes of Bhaga!"
For the benefit of practitioners, there is a yantra consisting of various types.
It is said to consist of various mantras and is augmented by various powers;
and here, O Śaṅkara, two kinds of weapons have been demonstrated.
The divine and great consecration ritual has also been proclaimed;
and this various pacification has been taught, which diminishes all torment. (51.3)

The power of the weapons, though correctly proclaimed in various ways through the Ṛg-verses, yields manifold fruits and possesses great potency; in this matter, the mantras themselves are the cause. (51.4)
O Śaṅkara, you have previously spoken those mantras beginning with Tāraka; you ought to explain their purposeful nature.
That great knowledge which is proclaimed as arising from the meaning of all scriptures—that is entirely composed of mind; for you are the eternal omniscient one. (51.6)
The commencement of the subsequent discourse: Ahirbudhnya said—
Listen, O Nārada, to the truth regarding the glory arising from the meaning of the mantras.
By the knowledge of which, a person may eternally attain omniscience. || 51.7 ||
The demonstration of Tāraka’s supreme excellence:
That reality named Tāraka is the essence of all speech; for from it all sounds arise, and into it they again dissolve. (51.8)
Sustained by this [breath], the sounds nourish their own respective state (bhāva).
Even though there is a commonality in the mantra, the object has a threefold nature;
thus, the state within the mantra exists in three ways: gross, subtle, and supreme. (51.9)
The general definition of the gross and the other [levels] is as follows:

that which arises from conjunction is the gross; that which is manifested by words is the subtle; and that which abides in the Imperishable through states such as the immeasurable is known as the supreme. (51.10)
The gross characteristic (sthūlalakṣaṇa),
through conjunctions associated with well-known [terms] according to their respective designations of the expressed objects,
brings about what is called "conjunction" (saṃsarga)— the human goal whose nature is non-differentiation. (51.11)
(502) That state which is realized at every step through the mere observation of its own nature is produced by yoga; that is declared by the wise to be the subtle [state]. (51.12)
The characteristic of the other is that entity which, based on color, consists of entities such as the immeasurable;
this is called "the other" by the wise. Thus is the threefold establishment of objects. (51.13)
The manifestation of the gross meaning within the *tāra* is "o-tam-asmin" (in this, it is *ota*). The meaning is that everything is measured (*mita*); thus, it is called "gross.
Through the syllable *o* and the syllable *m*, there is a conjunction based on the *tāraka*. (51.14)
These two phonemes are expressive of both the unstruck (anāhata) and the struck (mita).
Whatever else exists apart from the Blessed One, all that is considered "struck. || 51-15 ||
The Lord is to be designated as possessing power; the manifestation of that power is His volition, as was previously stated by you. (51.16)
In that context, the object to be conceptualized is prosperity (bhūti), consisting of both pure and impure natures;
its unimpeded contemplation is the conceptualization (saṃkalpa), which is the Sudarśana [discus]. (51.17)
"All this, consisting of the conceivable and the conceiving, is held to be measured by that [Oṃ].
From here until the forty-fifth verse, [the author proceeds] under the guise of demonstrating the two-fold meaning— the gross and subtle forms— of the Praṇava.
The profound and supreme secret meaning hidden within the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad is here elucidated. For this very reason,
[it also clarifies] the entire body of Pāñcarātra scriptures, which are devoted to defining the nature, attributes, and functions of the fourfold emanation (vyūha) beginning with Vāsudeva.

Those proficient in the Vedānta maintain that its authority is established either through its being rooted in the *Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad* as a form of its expansion (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), or independently, by virtue of having been spoken by Vāsudeva, who is renowned as the self-evidently omniscient one at the pinnacle of the Śruti.
Chapter Fifty-one:
That [universe] is woven within the Imperishable Blessed One, like jewels upon a thread. (51.18)
The root *ava-tiṣṭha* has the sense of entering; "going" (*gati*) means pervading or entering.
[The Lord] has entered the measured space within the lotus of the Lord of Gods like a subtle atom. (51.19)
And having seen this, the Lord of Gods entered [the heart] like a thread into a gem;
this gross meaning of the Praṇava has been explained, and now its subtle meaning is being described. (51.20)

The Promise to Investigate Subtle Matters: therein, it is stated that Aniruddha, Pradyumna, and Saṅkarṣaṇa are portions of the undivided power of the Lord. "There are three powerful powers that effect creation, maintenance, and dissolution. (1)
They have become partial manifestations of the one Bhagavat-śakti, Pūrṇā.
In sequence, they possess the state of being signified by the three syllables of the *praṇava*; they are most wonderful, having the form of the triad of syllables beginning with *a*.
Each one of them bears the respective name of the forms Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña.
The power of the syllable *a* is called Viśvā, while that arising from the syllable *u* is Taijasī.
The power of the letter *ma* is called *prājñā*; hear again their form.
Thus, by means of the description of the gross object, [the nature of] the Self, which is the essence of Brahman as expressed by the entire *praṇava*, [is established].

Having demonstrated the meaning of the first section of the Māṇḍūkya, the meaning of the three subsequent sections— from the second onwards— is now clarified here by means of an examination of their subtle significance; this meaning consists of the fourfold manifestation (vyūha) beginning with Aniruddha, which is expounded through the analysis of the individual components of the Praṇava.
Thus it should be known. (p.
504) The manifestation of the form of Nīruddha, who is named Viśva, has nineteen faces; he is named Viśva and is the sustainer of the universe. || 51.23 ||

Having first specified the particular location of Aniruddha himself, there follows a description of his specific objects of enjoyment: "In the waking state, she experiences the universe consisting of manifold creations as gross objects;
it takes the form of substances, actions, and qualities, and is variegated by various universals. (51.24)

The gross [aspect] satiates the universe, the unborn one consisting of universal creation; this is the determination of the specific locus for the objects of enjoyment of Pradyumna. That very same [universe], when called subtle, is commensurate with the internal organ. (51–25)
One propitiates the Taijasa Śakti residing in the letter *U*, which pertains to the dream state.

Furthermore, the central face is shaped like an elephant's face, while on both sides there are nine faces each shaped like human faces; thus, one should understand that there are nineteen faces in total.

This is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of its seven-limbed nature (*saptāṅgatva*), as seen in the Śruti: "He has seven limbs and nineteen mouths. There are four hands, two feet, and one elephantine trunk due to his elephant-head—thus constitutes the seven-limbed nature.

Furthermore, this word [“jāgaritasthāna”] has the purpose of specifying a particular location, as seen in the scriptural text: “He whose station is the waking state” (jāgaritasthānaḥ). That which, being situated therein, perceives the world—that is the waking state. The suffix -kta is used here in the sense of a locus (adhikaraṇe). He whose station is that very thing is “jāgaritasthānaḥ,” meaning “one whose station is the eye.”
That is its meaning.

Herein, the meaning of "āmaya" is as follows: the word "viśva" refers to the gross world. That very gross world which is the object of enjoyment for Aniruddha is now [referred to] by virtue of being produced from latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

By means of the internal organ known as *citta*— which is measured by the internal instrument (*antaḥkaraṇa*), designated by the term "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) as a synonym for "separated" (*pravivikta*) because it is known as distinct and different from external objects,
and which is accompanied by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) produced by the cognition of external objects.

Being correctly measured and known as real, she is the dream-state (*svāpnī*), which, by virtue of sustaining the dream, resides in the region of the throat; she abides in the letter *u*, the second syllable of the *praṇava*, through the relationship of being its denotation; she is the Taijasa state, because she resides within the mind composed of light (*tejomaya*).
By virtue of being connected with the mind, one satisfies the power of Pradyumna, who bears the name Taijasa. (p.

505) [This is] the determination of the specific locus for the particular object of enjoyment belonging to Saṃkarṣaṇa: "The universe itself, having abandoned its subtlety, has attained the state of bliss. (51.26)
It satisfies the supreme power known as Prājña, which pertains to deep sleep;
this three-faced, subtle power of the syllable *U* was previously described as belonging to the state of dreaming. (51.27)

The stainless power called *Makārā*, which partakes in bliss, is the activity of Aniruddha as the presiding deity of the gross body; having presided over the gross city, she manifests as the Viśvā within the body. (51–28)
Pradyumna functions as the presiding principle over the subtle body;
taking up the subtle "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka), he exists as the dream-city.
Saṃkarṣaṇa functions as the presiding principle over bliss.
Having reached the supreme city born of bliss, the wise one proceeds.
The meaning is this: the word *viśva* refers to the subtle world (*sūkṣmajagat*), which is a synonym for "distinct" (*pravivikta*).

That very subtle world, which constitutes the object of enjoyment for Pradyumna, now, having abandoned even its subtlety and attained the nature of bliss (*ānanda-rūpatā*), becomes the state of deep sleep (*sauṣupti*) for the individual soul (*jīva*).
She who abides at the tip of the pericarp of the heart as the sustainer of deep sleep is named *prājña*;

she is called *prājña* because she does not cause [the soul] to know (*pra-jñāpayati*) anything—whether external or dream-like—that exists apart from the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*). Thus, she is named *prājña*.

From the root *jñā* preceded by *pra*, with the sense of the causative (*ṇic*) internalized and the negative particle (*nañ*) as its attendant word (*upapada*), the suffix *ka* is applied according to the grammatical rule *ātaścopasarge*. [The term] *parām* means the final one, that is to say, the position of the letter *m*;
he satiates that power (*śakti*) which is of the nature of Saṃkarṣaṇa. This is that third power.

She is established [as such] by the passage beginning with "ukāra" and ending with "bhojinī. She is called "Ānandabhojinī" (the Enjoyer of Bliss) because she herself enjoys bliss and causes the individual soul (jīva) to enjoy it; through the intended non-difference between the signified and the signifier, she is designated as the letter "ma," this very third power in the form of Saṃkarṣaṇa, who is stainless and untainted.
Because it experiences mere bliss even without the enjoyment of sense objects,

that whose sole nature is the experience of eternal, perfect bliss possesses the state of being the enjoyer of the gross phenomenal world through its form as Aniruddha, and the state of being the enjoyer of the subtle through its form as Pradyumna.

It is indeed of the nature of play; yet, even for the sake of play, such a state of being an enjoyer does not exist for Saṃkarṣaṇa, who is the enjoyer of pure bliss—thus he is "stainless" (*nirañjana*). (p.
506) [This is] the "outward-directed consciousness" (*bahiḥprajñatva*) of Aniruddha.

The state of the grossness of the universe, established on the plane of external means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), is that of Pradyumna; the state of his subtlety, established on the plane of the internal organ, is indeed his state of internal cognition (*antaḥprajñatva*). (51–30)
The nature of Saṃkarṣaṇa as consisting of bliss:
His state is that of the supreme condition of the universe, which consists of eternal bliss;
and this state is the cause of delight for the triad of powers, Aniruddha and the others, through the three states beginning with the gross.
These three stages gratify those three powers.
One should contemplate those powers of the enjoyer as having the forms of Aniruddha and the others.
The fourth power, called Vāsudeva, is that which is expressed by the *nāda*; it is the divine half-measure (*ardhamātrā*), arising from the letter *M*, which is illuminating. (51.32)
Know that unadulterated power to be composed of Vāsudeva.
"Unadulterated" means [free from] Aniruddha, Pradyumna, and Saṃkarṣaṇa, who are the instigators of the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.

The meaning is that [the fourth state] is not permeated by those operations consisting of the engagement in various [objects]; for the Śruti, beginning with "not inwardly cognitive," establishes the difference of the *turya* (fourth) from the triad of *viśva*, *taijasa*, and *prājña*. For this very reason, *viśva* and *taijasa* alone are regarded as bound by cause and effect.
The wise one is bound by the cause, but the two [other states] are not established in the fourth.

Thus, it should be understood that even by this verse, which accords with the meaning of the mantra, the prohibition of both the operation of the regulation of the bondage of cause and effect and the operation of the regulation of the bondage of cause alone is established with respect to the Fourth State (*turya*), thereby clarifying its very difference from Viśva and the other states.
When the fourfold power has dissolved, there arises the state of stillness of the indivisible power of the Lord; she who shines forth when the three and a half mātrās have dissolved. (51.33)
Know that to be the power of the Lord, inexpressible and stainless.
Regarding the method for dissolving the fourfold power:
while clearly uttering "Om," one should gradually cause [the letters] beginning with 'A' to disappear. (51.34)
Four powers have been indicated in the successive stages.
That power, whose nature is stillness (*staimitya*), assumes the form of the fifth decade:
"That which appears as if it were nothing, being neither existent nor non-existent. (51.35)
The divine state of *grasanī* is the fifth stage of all the powers (*śakti*).
It is the cause for the direct realization of such power through the specific practice of the *praṇava*.
O Sage, for one who utters "Om" correctly and gradually attains tranquility, [this occurs]. (51–36)
The great speech, free from appearance, that power unfolds within.
(1) [Note: "Ādīḥ" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those which have 'a' as their beginning"; it is an adjective in the feminine plural ending qualifying the word "śaktīḥ."

2. This is the intended meaning here: just as bubbles in the ocean possess the nature of being an emergence of the ocean's water, and upon the disappearance of their state as bubbles, the ocean's water possesses the quality of having swallowed the bubbles; and after that swallowing, because the water lacks existence in the form of bubbles, it is non-existent in that form, yet existent in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).

And because of existence, there is the absence of non-existence; likewise, the fourfold powers beginning with Aniruddha are also of the nature of the manifestation of the indivisible power of the Lord. Upon the departure of the states such as Aniruddha, the indivisible power becomes the devourer of Aniruddha and the others, and after this devouring—
Because that unbroken power does not exist in a form such as being "unrestrained" (*aniruddha*), it is non-existent [in that respect];
yet because it exists in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), there is no absence of existence.
Of that power, [there is] Lakṣmī, who is an inseparably established attribute (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇa*) of the Lord.
That supreme, eternal power Lakṣmī, who is none other than the nature of form (rūpatva), belongs to Viṣṇu. || 51.37 ||
Gaurī, Sarasvatī, and Dhenu are to be expressed, yet they are beyond the sequence of expressible words.
For the sage who practices the syllable *oṃ*, there arises in his heart a causeless manifestation of his own true nature; as he hears the inner *oṃ* spontaneously, it dawns of its own accord. (51–38)

In the Supreme Brahman, whose nature is existence, in Viṣṇu—who is eternal, stainless, pure, partless, and free from conceptual construction—the being of Lakṣmī is manifest; for existence resides in Brahman, the source of all that comes into being. (51.39)

The fourfold designations of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others mentioned in the Purāṇas have Lakṣmī as their ultimate referent: "She alone, the divine one, who has been described by these four names—namely Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and likewise the Unmanifest—is praised as the fifth. (51.40)

In the Pāśupata doctrine, that very Śakti is declared to be the referent of the four designations beginning with Īśa; she is likewise designated by the names Īśa, Vidyā, and Śiva—thus by these four names. (51–41)

O Sage, that very Śakti is indeed declared in both Sāṃkhya and Yoga by four names— namely as the Manifest (Vyakta), the Unmanifest (Avyakta), the Person (Pum), and likewise as Time (Kāla)— even though these four designations are mentioned in Sāṃkhya and Yoga. (51.42)
(1) That the Supreme Brahman, distinguished by *lakṣmī*, is that which is attained by the liberated:
"Having reached that fifth power, when he finally comes to rest, that is the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Abode, the highest station of Viṣṇu. (51.43)
Clarifying the very meaning already stated by means of another formulation:
"Tasting within the divine power that rises above the half-measure (ardhamātrā), which resembles the sound of a long bell, one becomes the imperishable Self consisting of bliss. (51.44)
Whatever state or form one attains at the end, that is the radiant form of Viṣṇu;
thus has the subtle meaning of the Praṇava been demonstrated to you. (51.45)

Now follows the determination of the "other" (parārtha): listen now from me regarding that object which is called "the other. One should contemplate this Praṇava, which consists of two syllables. (51.46)

Brahman, characterized by the gross sentient and insentient and endowed with the power oriented toward creation and so forth, is that which is signified by the syllable *A*; for that supreme Vaiṣṇavī power is indeed the performer of the five cosmic acts.

This is the intended meaning: that person, through the practice of the *praṇava*, having become liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra and having attained the fifth power in the form of Lakṣmī whose nature has been described, [attains] the vicinity (*parisara*)— that is to say, the proximity— of that Supreme Brahman characterized by Lakṣmī, at the end of which, or near the end of which, [he resides].

He "ceases" from that [activity], meaning he becomes one whose activity directed toward the object to be reached has ceased due to the absence of anything further to be reached; that is the supreme state of Viṣṇu, who is by nature all-pervading—a state devoid of equal or superior, which is called a "state" (pada) because it is reached, gone to, meditated upon, or attained; the meaning is that it is his very essential nature (svarūpa).

That very [reality] is further qualified as "the supreme Brahman" and "the supreme abode. It is that which is distinguished by qualities such as vastness (*bṛhat*), being supreme and not inferior in the form of Hiraṇyagarbha and so forth;
it is that very supreme abode, consisting of unlimited splendor, precisely because of its connection with the aforementioned Lakṣmī.
The state of possessing immeasurable splendor belongs even to the Supreme Brahman; as was stated by the Primordial Poet:

"For that splendor is immeasurable, of which she, the daughter of Janaka, is the embodiment. As for the use of a distinct designation in the phrase "the station of Viṣṇu," it is figurative, like the expression "the body of a stone statue."
Brahman, conditioned by that very [limitation], appears as if possessed of various conceptual forms. (51.47)
The Supreme Lord, the Creator, designates the supreme Viṣṇu;
for Brahman— characterized by subtle consciousness and non-consciousness and endowed with a power not yet intent upon creation—
is that which is signified by the syllable *U*.
With her fivefold functions unmanifested, she shines as if she has become silent.
Stainless, without appearance, and truly immovable, she is the supreme power of Viṣṇu;
though she is eternally expanding, she remains unperceived by subtle states that lack defining characteristics.
It appears as if devoid of activity, like the stillness of the ocean;
by that very [power] is Brahman—beyond conceptual construction and untainted—conditioned. (51–50)
The all-pervading Lord of Space, the radiant Viṣṇu, designates the Supreme;
through the syllable Om, there is the realization of the non-difference between the two Brahmans as described, which constitutes the unification of these two phonemes. (51–51)
That syllable "Om" is Brahman; it is known as the supreme Ajapā.
That very form, called Praṇava, is the dissolution of the universe.
For one who is established in the meditation on the meaning thus explained, there is the perfection of yoga-mastery;
here, the yogin who is attentive shall attain the supreme samādhi.
Herein lies the intention: because it is accomplished through the unification of the two syllables in the form of *a* and *u*.

That *o*-kāra, being of the nature of a diphthong (*saṃdhyakṣara*), is not a separate phoneme. In that regard, both syllables [of the diphthong] sequentially denote Brahman as qualified by gross *cit* (consciousness) and *acit* (non-conscious matter), and Brahman as qualified by subtle *cit* and *acit*. And by means of the *o*-kāra, which is produced through the unification of those two denotative syllables, the unification of the two denoted objects is effected.

Through the process of awakening the instruments [of perception], non-duality (advaita)—in the form of the identity of the two Brahmans characterized by the aforementioned attributes as the substrate—is made known; thus, the non-duality of cause and effect is established.
(p. 511) Thus, these three states of the *praṇava* have been demonstrated. (vv. 51–53)
The promise to describe the meaning of *tārā* and *anutārā*: "Listen to three other methods regarding *tārā* and *anutārā*.
Among them, here is the determination of the gross meaning of *tārā*."
It removes all sins without exception and is praised by gods and asuras alike. || 51-54 ||
Because it is measured by all means of knowledge (*māna*), it is therefore proclaimed as *hrī* (shame/modesty). This was the definition of the gross; now listen to the subtle. (51–55)
Everywhere manifest as "the living being," she does not fall into non-existence; having the nature of constant upward movement, she pervades the entire universe. (51–56)
"The determination of the Supreme Goal has been briefly indicated to you; now listen further to that which is supreme—the Supreme Self, the transcendent God known as Nārāyaṇa. (51–57)
His inseparable power is the Goddess, who possesses his attributes as her own;
through her wondrous power of *māyā*, she eternally performs the five cosmic functions.
Pervasive in the form of Viṣṇu, she follows all states of being;
she is the manifestation of the will that serves as the support for the entirety of the worlds.
Having fashioned the manifold world by resorting to the state of fire, she,
clearly pervading the Lord of Space (Vyomeśa), establishes herself once again.
O Great Sage, this further meaning has been indicated regarding the *Tārikā*: [the explanation of the gross meaning of] the *Anuttarā* is as follows:
(1) it destroys all defects, and (2) it nourishes the world with virtues. (51–61)
O great sage, this [nature] is eternally resorted to by all, and it itself resorts to the supreme state; thus has the gross aspect of Śrī been described in brief.
The investigation of subtle reality:
Let the lotus, the supreme abode—eternal, imperishable, and undecaying—be resorted to;
therein let Śaṅkarī take her stand, crushing the ocean of worldly existence.
Having become a performer of various wonders through the bestowing of those respective enjoyments,
[the stage] called "The Determination for the Sake of Others" has been briefly indicated to you; now listen further to the supreme [instruction].
That which is the supreme Brahman— tranquil, eternally pure, stainless,
possessing the six divine attributes, immovable, and celestial— is called by the name Nārāyaṇa.

His consort, the Goddess Śakti, is inseparable from him; she is the substratum of his attributes and, by virtue of her power to produce the marvels of Māyā, she is eternally the performer of the five cosmic acts.
Pervasive in the form of Viṣṇu, she is the experiencer of all states of being.
[The word] *śr̥* is derived from the root *śr̥* (meaning "to injure") belonging to the *kr̥yādi* class; this form *śr̥ṇāti* is the present indicative (*laṭ*).
By virtue of her being the Puruṣakāra (the active agent), she [destroys] the [karmas] accumulated since beginningless time by those who have taken refuge at the lotus-feet of her own feet.
The purport of the sentence is that "Śrī" is so called because she "shreds," "strikes down," or "destroys" all defects in the form of karma when they are being gathered together.
Alternatively, this form "śrīṇāti" is derived from the root *śrī* (meaning "to cook") belonging to the *kryādi* class, used in the present tense (*laṭ*).

The meaning of "Śrī" is as follows: she pleases (śrīṇāti), cooks (pacati), and softens (mṛdūkaroti) by removing the hardness of mind— that entire multitude of sentient beings intended by the word "jagat"— through her own qualities such as compassion and maternal affection, which are inherent to her nature as a mother.
She who expands through the volition that serves as the support for all worlds without exception. (51.67)
Having established the manifold world by abiding in the state of non-existence,
she, clearly pervasive as the Mistress of Space, becomes firmly established once again.
This meaning has been described for Anutārā just as it was for Tārā;
it is a summary of all that has been said.
O Nārada, listen now to this summary concerning the scope of all expressible meanings.
That god who has been praised by you is the eternal Supreme Self,
the omnipotent one, the abode of all, and is augmented by the six divine attributes.
The power inherent in that [substratum] is one, inseparable from it;
it is the Goddess who follows all beings, like the stillness of the ocean. (51.71)
She is perceived by herself through an exceedingly minute portion;
as the distinction between the object of manifestation and the manifestor, she is the manifestation that is both white and its opposite.
The practitioner, whose resolve is fixed on Viṣṇu and who is named Sudarśana, [attains] prosperity (bhūti);
this [prosperity] proceeds in two ways according to the distinction between word and meaning, with the former [the word] being primary.
That which is the act of signifying by means of sound is determined with respect to its object;
it should be known as having the nature of an action, this body consisting of the Sudarśana. (51.74)

For that which is the state of sound as the object, termed its state of being an objective (karman), is also traditionally held to consist of the nature of action (kriyā) and to be composed of Sudarśana. (51.75)
Therefore, the volition of Viṣṇu, which consists of vibration, is the Sudarśana;
all action residing in the factors of agency is composed of that very [volition], without a doubt. (51.76)
Every word and every denotable object functions in two ways:
either by means of a quality (guṇa) or by means of an action (karman); no other mode exists.
Therefore, words do not at all function with respect to Brahman in terms of its formal nature;
rather, these two—qualities and actions—belong to one who is immersed in Brahman.
And those [mantras] exist within the form of the Sudarśana as its specific attributes;
for whatever collection of mantras there is that penetrates into Brahman, [it is contained therein]. (51.79)
"By the power of the Sudarśana [mantra], let all that be so contemplated.
Thus has this concise summary, in accordance with the scriptures, been correctly declared to you.
Now, with an undistracted mind, learn from me its detailed expansion for each individual mantra.

Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Nature and Meaning of the Seed-Syllables Beginning with Tāra," in the Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā, a secret doctrine within the Śrī Pāñcarātra Tantra.
From the beginning, verse 3317:
The fifty-second chapter, titled "An Exposition on the Meaning of the Mantras of Viṣṇu and Others.
Even meditated upon but once, it swiftly removes a multitude of sins numbering many millions.
We meditate upon that divine splendor of the god Sudarśana.
Having first restated what has preceded, Ahirbudhnya makes a promise to explain the meaning of the mantras of Viṣṇu and others:
"The essential nature of the Tāra, the Anutāra, and the Anuttāra has been shown to you."
Among the gross, subtle, and supreme [states], [the distinction] arises from the causes of the qualities (guṇa) and actions (karman). || 52-1 ||
Now, listen to the meaning of the mantras beginning with Viṣṇu.

Regarding the demonstration of the word-meaning in the determination of the gross meaning of the word *namaḥ*: the activity of a discerning person is by its very nature one consisting of prostration. (52-2)
Salutation is proclaimed by directing it toward that which is supreme;
for there is a twofold division of sentient beings based on the distinction between the superior and the inferior.
Indeed, the class of sentient beings in the world is described as being of only two kinds. (52-3)
He is greater, and even greater than that; indeed, there is nothing superior to these two.

The word *jyāyas* (greater) has its primary meaning in reference to that which is distinguished by an infinite and unsurpassed excellence, wherein pre-eminence abides both in terms of time and qualities. (52–4)

The word "jyāyān" (superior) applies to him in its primary sense; therefore, others are considered non-superior, and for this reason, the other group consisting of sentient beings is regarded by the wise as inferior. (52.5)
And the conjunction of these two, when they are not equal, is desired for the relationship of the subordinate and the principal;
all those that are not greater are considered subordinate, while the one that is greater is regarded as the supreme principal. (52–6)

Having first established the relationship between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para), there is the determination of the nature of the worshiper and the object of worship; through this relationship of worshiper and object of worship, they are unified with Him.
The Supreme is declared to be the object of worship and the ultimate beneficiary (śeṣī), while the souls are said to be the worshippers and the subordinate (śeṣa). (52–7)
The relationship of subordinate and principal between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) is unconditional.
This state of being the worshiper and the worshipped is not preceded by any motive;
it is the very nature of the low and the high, consisting of the relationship between the worshiper and the worshipped. (52.8)
The knowledge of superiority and inferiority that is free from limiting conditions is the cause of bowing.
That state by which a conscious being, devoid of limiting adjuncts, bows to one who is superior—that, or its expression, is called "bowing. (52.9)
"The Blessed One is always supreme to me, and I am always inferior"—this disposition is called *namas*, for it is indeed the cause of *namas*. (52.10)
Alternatively, with the intention of expressing the causative sense (*ṇij-artha*) inherent within it, there is another etymological derivation for the word *namaḥ*:
"Or rather, [the devotee] causes the Lord to bow, that is, certainly makes Him inclined toward humility;
for when one perceives the lowliness of another, that other person indeed becomes humble. (52-11)
Therefore, "namas" is designated as that which itself inclines [the self] toward [the object].

Or rather, it is the completeness of the *namas* accompanied by the three instruments (of body, speech, and mind), when one has uttered "namas" with speech while [inclining] with both mind and body. (52.12)
That is designated as complete; anything other than that is called deficient.
This constitutes the completion of the ritual means (karaṇa); now hear this completion of the ancillary parts (aṅga).
An exposition on the surrender of the self consisting of humility and its opposite:
"This eternal perfection of mine is that I become humble; directed toward the Supreme Person, my perfection is not otherwise. (52.14)
Thus, this limb [of yoga] is declared to be the most excellent; the desire for fruits is its opposite.
The determination of miserliness and its opposite arises from the ascent of beginningless latent impressions, from a lack of mastery, and from innate nature. (52–15)
And because it is enveloped by impurity, there is indeed an obstruction of vision and action;
that is wretchedness (*kārpaṇya*), and its awakening is this second limb. (52-16)

1. Here, by the word *dṛk* (vision), the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) is intended, and by the word *kriyā* (action), the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*). This also implies the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*). Their "striking" (*vihati*) means their obstruction or blunting; that itself is wretchedness (*kārpaṇya*). Knowledge of that is the second limb.

This is the intended meaning: the consciousness possesses two types of agency—namely, being a knower (*jñātṛtva*), an agent (*kartṛtva*), and an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*)—which are both natural and adventitious. Among these, the state of being a knower refers to the knowledge of the Supreme Person along with His attributes; the state of being an agent refers to the performance of service toward His lotus feet, which are the ultimate reality.

Furthermore, the status of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*), as taught by such scriptural passages as "He enjoys all desires together," is inherent because it is inseparable from one's essential nature (*svarūpa*). And that [status], though [potentially] complete, has been entirely blunted until liberation by the three aforementioned causes, consisting of the ascent of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and so forth. As for those [attributes] of the conscious [self]...

The states of being a knower, an agent, and an enjoyer, which have as their objects various worldly entities, are adventitious (*aupādhika*) because they are caused by knowledge that possesses independence conditioned by karma; they function in varying degrees throughout successive births until liberation, in accordance with those very conditions. This is it.
It is said that the realization of one's own sovereignty is opposed to the aforementioned state of wretchedness. (p.
518) Furthermore, the realization of one's own sovereignty is declared to be its opposite.
This is the exposition of great confidence and its opposite.
Being supreme, this god is compassionate toward all beings.
"His mind is always solely intent on bestowing grace"—this is the third [attribute].
"He is indifferent [to the fruits of action], yet he bestows results according to karma"—such is the conviction. (52.18)
This third [cause], consisting of faith, indeed always destroys [the obstacles].
(1) The determination of the protector, the choice [of him], and that which is opposed to them:
even one who is thus [chosen] is not capable of being a refuge if he is powerless. || 52-19 ||
Thus, by means of this cognition, the determination of the protective power (goptṛśakti) of this deity is declared as the fourth limb; furthermore, its pervasion (vyāhati) is [the fifth].
"Indifferent because of the absence of qualities"—this arises from the cause of equanimity.
The avoidance of hostility and the discernment of its opposite consist in the cessation of one's own ownership [of objects], which is the relinquishing of hostility. (52–21)
The fifth limb is declared to be the avoidance of obstructing the command;
indeed, service contrary to the scriptures is said to be its obstruction. (52.22)
The determination of the resolve for conformity and its opposite:
"All beings, moving and unmoving, are the body of the Blessed One"—this is a qualifying attribute containing a reason, meaning "He is of such a nature. "The Supreme Person" is the substantive.

This is understood from the context. The construction is as follows: if the Supreme Person were thus incapable by Himself, He would not be able to be the protector of sentient beings; therefore, being capable, He is indeed able [to protect them].
Therefore, my firm resolve is this: "I must act in accordance with that. (52.23)
The sixth limb is declared to be the refutation of its contradictions;
the conclusion of the stated meaning, complete with limbs and sub-limbs, is proclaimed as your salutation. (52.24)
This meaning of the word *namaḥ* is gross; now listen to its subtle meaning.
In the determination of the subtle meaning of the word *namaḥ*, the syllable *ma* denotes the notions of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*) and "mine" (*mamakāra*).
When there is a sense of "mine" toward oneself and one's own possessions for one who possesses volition. || 52-25 ||
The two syllables "ma-ma" signify that which belongs to the "I" (mamyasya).
The word "namaḥ" functions to turn back the notions of "I-ness" and "mine-ness," which are rooted in false knowledge dependent upon beginningless latent impressions (vāsanā). (52–26)
The notion of independence and ownership directed toward the objects of "self" and "mine" is here prevented by the correct understanding that "this is not mine. (52.27)
This is an elaboration of the very meaning already stated;
the meaning of "I am not mine, I am not independent" is now expressed:
"My body and other such things do not belong to me; they are the remainder belonging to the Supreme Self. (52-28)
Thus, by means of this understanding, those various personal fancies are turned back.
This demonstrates the logical justification for how the knowledge of the meaning of the word "namas" functions as a remover of the notions of "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) and "mine-ness" (mamātā).
By those cognitions, which are conceptualized and born from beginningless latent impressions (vāsanā). || 52-29 ||

The meaning is that the sixth limb, which consists of the resolve for favorability (*ānukūlya-saṃkalpa*), is opposed by the rejection and disparagement— through hatred and so forth— of those beings, both moving and unmoving, who constitute the very body of the Blessed One, as well as by the harming of them.
That mind which is firmly colored by the notion of independence and ownership [is purified] by the awakening to the universal identity with Viṣṇu arising from that very [realization]. (52.30)
By this word "not," the non-mantra is excluded from itself;
thus has its subtle nature been indicated to you. Now, listen further to the supreme [explanation]. (52.31)

The letter *na* is designated as the path for defining the supreme object of the word *namaḥ*; the letter *ma* is defined as the primary [element], while the *visarga* is the Supreme Lord. In this regard, the following meaning is defined: || 52–32 ||
The Supreme Lord is beginningless, possessed of power, and the Highest Person; this path known as "contemplation" (namana) is the primary means for attaining Him. (52-33)

Thus, the threefold meaning of the word "namaḥ" has been declared to you in this manner. Now, listen to the explanation of the gross meaning of the Viṣṇu-mantra, concerning Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, and the others.

The fourth case-ending (caturthī) used in reference to Viṣṇu and others indicates the "recipient" (saṃpradāna), which is the self-surrender that is clearly manifested through a state of humility. (52.35)
For this self has become base because it is attained through the need for protection;
in response to the inquiry "for what purpose?", it is stated: "for Viṣṇu. (52-36)
The meaning obtained through the connection of action and its factors is said to be gross; (p.
521) [this concludes] the determination of the specific qualities that manifest the supremacy in Viṣṇu within the investigation of the subtle meaning of the Viṣṇu-mantra.
That which is subtle, produced by the perception of the nominal stem (prātipadika), is designated as such. || 52-37 ||
The desire for pervasion, radiance, and entry is based on the respective elements;
these manifest the supremacy of the divine Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self. (52.38)
The definition of the quality of pervasion (*vyāpti*):

That which pervades everything by way of space, time, and also by its own form, is declared by the wise to be "supreme" (*para*), based on the etymological derivation from the verbal root *viṣ*. (52.39)
The Description of the Quality of Radiance (Kānti):
Radiance is the excellence of qualities; the qualities are knowledge, power, and so forth. That [being] in whom these are pre-eminently intensified is said to be "radiant" (kānta). (52.40)
All sentient beings are unattractive, whereas that Supreme Person is attractive;
this quality is called "attractiveness" (kānti), as it is derived from the verbal root *vaś* (to subdue). (52.41)
The description of the quality of entry:
Since all things, both conscious and unconscious, enter it of their own accord;
and since that which is itself minute enters the Great One, and likewise enters into the minute. (52.42)
That is declared by the wise to be the supreme [self], because it is determined from the verbal root *vis* (to enter);
it is that which is always desired by all sentient beings as their very own self through the quality of desire. (52.43)
1. "viṣl" in the sense of pervading;
2. "vaśa" in the sense of desire;
3. "viśa" in the sense of entering.
(522) That [meaning] is declared by the wise to be the supreme, because it is derived from the verbal root *iṣ* (to seek).
Regarding the word *Viṣṇu*, the meaning of each individual syllable is as follows:
"For therein the entire world of entities is born and indeed merges. (52.44)
And Viṣṇu always bestows the fourfold aim of human existence upon the virtuous; for he is derived from the three verbal roots *vi*, *saci*, and *snuta*. (52.45)

Thus, this subtle meaning of the word "Viṣṇu" has been declared to you in brief. Now, listen to the reality of His supreme nature—the ultimate goal which is attainable through the Imperishable (Akṣara). || 52-46 ||
Having rendered all goals like nectar and serving as fuel for the three lights, it bestows fearlessness; this is proclaimed as the supreme goal. (52.47)

Thus, O Sage, the threefold goal within the Vaiṣṇava mantra has been declared. Now learn from me, O Sage, this triad of forms belonging to the Nārāyaṇa-mantra, which defines its subtle meaning. (52–48)
The gross meaning obtainable from the action and its factors has been demonstrated there;
now that meaning which resides in the nominal stem is being defined as subtle. (52.49)
1. "The root *iṣ* [is used] in the sense of 'to see' (*darśana*). 2.

The three verbal roots *vī*, *ṣac*, and *ṣṇu* are to be understood here in their respective order: *vī* in the senses of "motion," "pervasion," "procreation," "beauty," "existence," and "eating"; *ṣac* in the sense of "inherence" (*samavāya*); and *ṣṇu* in the sense of "flowing" (*prasravaṇa*). For this very reason...
In accordance with the two subsequent roots (the second and third), one should note the doubling of the letter *ṣ* even in this root *viṣṇu*. Here, the second root is sometimes read as *saveṣ*,
but that is because [the rule] "and *śamavaiti*" applies there.
It has been set aside because it is inconsistent with the explanatory statements previously mentioned.
(See verses thirty-five and thirty-six, p.
523): "The *nārāḥ* are those belonging to *nara*; that *nara* is Puruṣottama."
It leads one to complete discernment and destroys all darkness.
Therefore, the man is eternal and is not harmed anywhere;
for all things, whether conscious or unconscious, are related to the man. (52–51)
By being subject to His lordship, by being sustained and nourished, likewise by being governed, as well as by being created, entered, and withdrawn; || 52-52 ||
He pervades all beings through his activity; and "nārāḥ" refers to his place of dissolution (ayana), because his nature is defined by them. (52–53)
It is the abode and the refuge of the Nārāṇas, and they are always its refuge;
it is always the supreme goal of those Nārāṇas, who are themselves the Self.
The waters are called *nārāḥ*, and they are his place of resort (*ayana*);
therefore, by these reasons, the Supreme is shown to be named Nārāyaṇa.
Thus has this subtle [teaching] been indicated to you; now hear the supreme [teaching] based on the castes (varṇa).
It is the definition of the Supreme Goal, unimpeded, in the form of the wheel, and the fire that consumes all evils.
Pervasive throughout all scriptures, renowned among the virtuous as Gopana, this path consists of eternal bliss and is the supreme goal for men. || 52-57 ||
This is the meaning; listen now to the supreme [meaning] taught regarding Vāsudeva. (p.
524) The subtle meaning of the Vāsudeva-mantra is as follows: that which is the gross meaning pertaining to action and its factors is indeed what was stated previously. (52–58)
The subtle meaning, which rests upon each individual word, is contained within the mantra known as Vāsudeva;
the word "Bhagavān," taken as a whole, signifies that which is worthy of worship.
The determination of the meaning of the letter *bha*:
It constantly sustains the entire universe, nourishes it as well, supports it, fills it, and indeed gathers it together within itself. (52–60)

The meaning of the letter *ga* is now defined as being subtle and consisting of the threefold Vedic ritual (*trayī-karma*). It is sung by all words and is understood by those seeking liberation (*apavargin*). (52–61)
O Sage, that which understands everything by itself and pervades the entire world, and which is the leader of all objects, is remembered as the meaning of the letter *ga*.
The definition of the *matup* suffix:
He chooses the universe as his own; he exists as the self of sovereignty;
and he increases every desire—therefore, this is declared to be the meaning of "Artha. (52–63)
The definition of the meaning of the word *vāsu*:
It covers (*chādayati*) everything with its own pure nature of knowledge and bliss.
(Verses 35 and 36 are to be consulted.)
