And just as fuel entered by fire becomes identical with it, [so too does the mind become one with the object]. (52.64)
Thus covered by Him, the universe is indeed composed of that alone;
for the universe dwells within Him, and He likewise dwells within it.
The meaning of the word *vāsu* has been indicated, and the "goer" (*gantṛ*) is now fully described.
It is traditionally remembered as *vāḥ* because it extends through all objects like a thread. (52–66)
"He brings forth all existents" and "He creates and impels"—this is declared to be His own true meaning, as He is praised by the virtuous in sacrifices. (52–67)
The definition of the meaning of the word *deva*:
"He shines by his own nature; he sports by himself through the acts of creation and so forth;
and he is always praised by the gods. Thus is the meaning of *deva* declared. (52–68)
The letter *da* is said to signify the giver of all desires, the purifier of all embodied beings, and the protector of all creatures. (52–69)
He is to be worshipped by all and the bearer of the souls of all;
this is declared to be the meaning of the letter *va*. Such is this subtle course.

In the investigation of the meaning of the letter *bha* within the determination of the meaning of the other [letter *a*]: "But the 'other' is not obtainable through syllables; behold its form! It should be known as the constant prior limit (*pūrvāvadhi*) which is called the material cause (*upādāna*). (52.71)

The contemplation of the syllable *ga* is as follows: "The world has a constant material cause" (*dhruvaṃ jagadupādānam iti gakāracintanam*). Regarding the determination of the meaning of the letter *ga*:
it either causes one to know the Veda (*gāṃ vedayati*) through the true scriptures, or one finds it for oneself at the outset (*ādau vindati vā svayam*). (52.72)

O Sage, that deity named Govinda is Saṃkarṣaṇa; this is the determination of the meaning of the letter *va*. Varuṇa encompasses the universe, which consists of both the three Vedas and ritual action. (52–73)
The meaning of "vā" is explained as that which chooses and creates the universe;
the explanation of the meaning of the letter "ta" is that which is emitted and withdrawn, and he who wears a garland is celebrated [as Śiva]. (52–74)
The Lord bears both of these within the interior of the lotus of His own navel;
therefore, Aniruddha is here designated as "Sragdhara" (the Wearer of the Garland).
Thus, the description of the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha) is accomplished by means of these very four syllables. Regarding the meaning of the syllable *va*:
by the syllable *va*, Vāsudeva is described as the support of nectar (*amṛta*).
By his form, the primordial deity is proclaimed as Saṃkarṣaṇa;
he who is the Lord Vāsudeva, the eternal support of liberation. (52.77)
The meaning of the syllable *sa* is established as "He alone is Saṃkarṣaṇa. Now, the meaning of the syllable *su* is explained:
"He who, being eternal, first brought forth the world and action. (52–78)
That Soma has risen; by him Pradyumna, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), is [manifested].
Here, Uddāma and Udaya are proclaimed as Saṃkarṣaṇa. (52.79)
For in the state of Saṃkarṣaṇa, the manifestation of Hari is complete;
that which consists of Vāsudeva is declared to be Saṃkarṣaṇa. (52–80)
It is now explained that Pradyumna is also he [Kṛṣṇa] himself; thus the meaning of the syllable *su* is determined. Next, the meaning of the syllable *da* is determined:
"He by whom, the Great Soul reclining upon the waters, granted space. (52.81)

For the sake of the increase of both the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), he who has granted space within the interior of his own navel-lotus for the purpose of the individual soul (*dāsya*) is proclaimed as Aniruddha. (52–82)
By the syllable *ekāra*, Pradyumna, the source of the universe, is proclaimed; he who is of the nature of Saṃkarṣaṇa is celebrated as Pradyumna. (52–83)
"That he is Aniruddha"—in this way, the meaning of the letter *da* is determined.
The determination of the meaning of the letter *va* follows; thus, through these three syllables, the supreme identity with the [three] manifestations (*vyūha*) is declared. (52–84)
Furthermore, it is stated by way of conclusion:
"In brief, the supreme reality has been shown to you in that which is called Vāsudeva.
Now, in this *Jitanta*, listen to my exposition of the entire meaning. (52.85)
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Meaning of the Mantras of Viṣṇu and Others," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
Chapter Fifty-Three, titled "An Exposition on the Meaning of the Mantra Known as Jitantā," beginning from verse 3402:
Meditated upon even once, it swiftly destroys a multitude of sins numbering many tens of millions.
We meditate upon that divine splendor of the god Sudarśana.

Ahibudhnya states that, in defining the gross meaning of the first quarter [of the mantra] beginning with "mantra," the two meanings of the root *ji*— namely, brilliance (*aujjvalya*) and non-obstruction (*avighāta*)— are the causes for bowing (*namana*).
Brilliance and lack of obstruction are said to be the meanings of the root *ji*;
both of these serve as the motivators for the act of bowing by one who bows. (53-1)
The state of being produced by the six qualities beginning with knowledge belongs to those two; indeed, both of them are born from knowledge, power, strength, and so forth.
Because he is replete with the qualities of knowledge and the rest, the Blessed One alone is to be honored.
A great ocean of the powers of knowledge, strength, sovereignty, heroism, and splendor.
The Blessed One alone, the Soul of the Universe, is intended to be praised as infinite.
This very point is established by the term *puṇḍarīkākṣa*, which serves to illuminate the meaning as it has been described. (5.3)
One who is impelled by passion and anger is perceived by the eye alone;
this one, however, because his desires have been fulfilled, is devoid of those various activities. (53.4)
The Lotus-Eyed One (Puṇḍarīkākṣa) is so called because He is serene due to the abandonment of all transformations;
this very term refers to both characteristics: His being the adversary of all that is to be abandoned and His being a mine of auspicious qualities.
Liberation from defects such as passion and the fulfillment of virtuous qualities. || 53-5 ||
The term *puṇḍarīkākṣa* is used to designate Puruṣottama;
it is this very word *puṇḍarīkākṣa* that defines the first manifestation (*vyūha*) known as Vāsudeva. (53–6)
Having addressed the lotus-eyed one for that very reason, Brahmā, looking at himself and seeing [the Lord] as infinite, says: "Victory is yours! (53.7)
Thus, O Sage, the gross [body] born of association has been described; now hear also about the subtle one.
In the determination of the subtle meaning, the term "Puṇḍarīkākṣa" (the Lotus-eyed One) reveals the Lord's state of being unassailable by time.
For the city called Kāla consumes the Puṇḍarīka. || 53-8 ||
Because it is external and therefore unperceived by that [consciousness], the proof of this is established following an exposition of the threefold nature of time:
"Time is threefold—gross, subtle, and supreme—but not within the Supreme Self. (53.9)
One should perform immersion in Vāsudeva, the Supreme Brahman;
time is gross when measured by units such as lava, and subtle when it defines the essential principles.
A supreme time, which pervades the activities of the manifestations (vyūhas), is now described.
(p. 530) Regarding the manifestation of the distinction of Paravāsudeva from the three manifestations: "The three manifestations are always measured by time. (53.11)
But the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva is not subject to time even by means of a military array;
rather, the determination of the "array of time" (kāla-vyūha) is made only with reference to the three arrays.
Because he is honored by time and is immeasurable, he is called the one of immeasurable splendor.
Regarding the term *puṇḍarīkākṣa*, it establishes the Lord’s eternal possession of infinite glory:
"The lotus (*puṇḍarīka*) is the supreme abode, eternal, imperishable, and undecaying. (53.13)
Because He dwells eternally within that [lotus], He is called Puṇḍarīkākṣa (the Lotus-eyed). Furthermore, it serves to demonstrate that He is established in His own majesty:
"The lotus is the supreme abode; He shines in His own majesty. (53.14)
The God established in his own majesty is called Puṇḍarīkākṣa;
therefore, he is proclaimed by the name Vāsudeva, [identical] with the designation Puṇḍarīkākṣa.
This subtle meaning of the word Puṇḍarīkākṣa has been declared. Now, having begun the investigation of its supreme sense, listen to the ultimate meaning of "Puṇḍarīkākṣa. (53.16)
The Determination of the Meaning of the Syllable *Pa* (1): Hari is the supreme purifier, liberated from defects such as passion (*rāga*).
Here, this should be understood: the syllable *pa*, the syllable *u*, the syllable *ṇa*, the syllable *ḍa*, and the syllable *rī*.

Having divided the letters constituting the word *puṇḍarīkākṣa*— namely the letter *ka*, the letter *ā*, and the letter *kṣa*— into eight parts, the supreme meaning known as the "Other" (*para*), which is established as having the nature of being immeasurable and so forth, is explained in sequence by four and a half verses beginning with the words "attachment and so forth" (*rāgādi*).
"It is demonstrated" means:
[The following is] the determination of the meaning of the letter *u*: "Because its nature is eternally manifest (*nityodita*), its arising is known as unrestrained (*uddāma*). (53.17)
The determination of the meaning of the letter *ṇa*:
because it precedes the triad of arrays (*vyūha*), it is recited as the primary one.
The determination of the meaning of the letter *ḍa*.
He whose unimpeded prowess is remembered for bringing about the attainment of both the pure and impure paths. (53.18)
The definition of the meaning of the letter *repha* preceded by the vowel *ī*:
Since [the syllable *rī*] supports the entire world, from Saṃkarṣaṇa down to the earth, as its substratum, and itself pervades it to the very end; [therefore it is so called]. (53.19)
The determination of the meaning of the letter *ka* together with its vowel *ā*:
Bliss (*ānanda*), being independent, is itself the supreme primordial nature (*parā prakṛti*).
The determination of the meaning of the letter *kṣa*.
Of this [universe], which consists of both pure and impure, and whose nature is both conscious and unconscious. || 53-20 ||

The end of a class [of consonants] is recited as the "end of the class" (*vargānta*), representing the ultimate limit; thus, the style consisting of phonemes known as *parā* has been demonstrated to you, showing that the meaning of the word *puṇḍarīkākṣa* cannot be fully expressed even after a long period of time. || 53-21 ||
Even in tens of thousands of years, it is clearly not possible to describe this directly;
(p. 532) [this is] the determination of the gross meaning of the second quarter of the mantra: "She who is known as the Creator of the Universe, the Attractor, and the Auspicious Wind. (53.22)
The gross [nature of reality] has been described as arising from the conjunction of action and its factors;
now, however, listen to me as I explain the subtle meaning, the subtle reality. (53.23)
Regarding the term *viśvabhāvana*, its meaning as referring to the cause of all is as follows:
"The Lord, who perpetually brings forth the universe—consisting of both sentient and insentient forms—preceded by Pradyumna, is called Viśvabhāvana. (53.24)

Because he employs his causality for the sake of omniscience, he clearly brings the universe into being and knows it exactly as it is; thus he is designated as "the Creator of the Universe" (Viśvabhāvana) by those most skilled in words, and is called "Omniscient" (Sarvajña). (53.25)
Having attained that which eternally bears the nature of the second manifestation (vyūha) known as Saṃkarṣaṇa, the universe indeed comes into being from that;
thus is the mighty Baladeva designated as Viśvabhāvana.
The universe was without a protector, for all things other than the Protector were themselves unprotected; then the Lord himself manifested as the Protector.
As soon as he had arisen, the entire universe indeed came into being by itself.
He is designated as the "Creator of the Universe" because he gazes upon it as its Lord;
his status as the supreme support of all is vast, since he himself is the substratum of the universe during its manifestation. (53.28)
Since the universe, like a tilaka mark or a mole, abides within him, he himself becomes Viśālākṣa (the Wide-Eyed One) by virtue of being the vast substratum. (53.29)
"Manifesting the universe as that [Self], you are called Viśvabhāvana, the Creator of the Universe.
Thus, O Viśvabhāvana, this subtle meaning has been declared to you in brief. (53.30)
Now, listen as I speak concerning the ultimate meaning;
this is the exposition of the meaning of the letter *va* preceded by the letter *i*.
(1) But this [fire], ignited from the support of nectar, has Vāsudeva and the others as its stages. || 53-31 ||
The determination of the meaning of the letter Śa:
Śaṅkara [bestows] [liberation] upon all embodied beings through the instruction of perfect knowledge.
The determination of the meaning of the second letter Va.
Since he is recited as Varāha, he is the best day among days.

Saṃkarṣaṇa is truly declared to be the day of Vāsudeva; he is the one who bestows success upon all beings, the very first of the gods, and the expounder of the meaning of the letter *bha* together with the vowel *ā*. (53.33)

1. Here is the application: having divided the phonemes situated in the word *viśvabhāvana* into seven parts as follows—the letter *va* preceded by the letter *i*, the letter *śa*, the second *va*, the letter *bha*, the letter *ā*, the third *va*, and the letter *na*.

The objective reality designated as "other," which is established through their immeasurable nature and so forth, is demonstrated in sequence by the five and a half verses beginning with "Because it is the support of the nectar" (amṛtādhārataḥ). [p.
534] This is the demonstration of how the letter *bha* intends to bestow the accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Because it bestows perfection upon living beings through the cultivation of pure actions arising from various authentic scriptures,
it is therefore called "the Giver of Perfection" (Siddhida).

The demonstration of the two qualities intended by the term "Ādi"—namely, being the first and being a deity—is as follows: He is the primordial source of the gods who possess the nature of both manifestation and withdrawal;
and he shines forth clearly as the beginning. Therefore, he is called Ādideva. (53.35)
It veils all darkness and reveals that Imperishable; He is Varuṇa, abiding in the immeasurable, and He is considered by the wise to be the Path. (53.36)
"The Supreme One consisting of phonemes has the meaning 'the creator of the universe' (viśvabhāvana)";
this indicates that the gross meaning of the third quarter of the mantra has already been determined.
Now, listen as I explain the meaning of the word *hṛṣīkeśa*. (53.37)
The meaning produced by the connection between action and its factors was explained previously;
now, listen to this subtle analysis of the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). (53.38)

In the sevenfold description of the meaning of the term *hṛṣīkeśa*, the first explanation— that it refers to being the stimulator of knowledge— is illustrated by the verse: "Having destroyed the darkness [of ignorance] and the enemy Madhu through wisdom..."
The form manifested by the Blessed One establishes the existence of the *sattva*. (53.39)
The state of being Hṛṣīkeśa (the Lord of the senses) of the Īśa has been described by the wise as being,
through the means of purifying knowledge, characterized by being the cause of joy; thus, it refers to the manifestation known as Pradyumna.
"Having purified it, he gladdens [the disciple] with the thought, 'The Lord is Knowledge. (53.40)
This state of being Hṛṣīkeśa is indeed proclaimed as Pradyumna-hood;
it is the state of being the supreme controller of the organs of perception.
The organ of perception is the *hṛṣīka*, and He is its internal controller. (53–41)
This indeed is declared to be the state of Pradyumna as Hṛṣīkeśa; his supremacy consists in being identical with the universe.
The sense objects are called the *hṛṣīkas*, which consist of both primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and its evolutes (*prākṛta*). (53–42)
For they gladden all living beings, and their Lord is the Teacher of the World;
for this state of being identical with the world arises from the inspiration of being identical with Him.
The Lord is the supreme deity who is the locus of joy caused by the sport consisting of creation and so forth;
it is evident that the Lord rejoices through that sport which takes the form of creation.
Thus, his status as Hṛṣīkeśa and his divinity are clearly established. (53–44)
He is the supreme locus of sovereignty, heroism, beauty, and virtue;
through his unchanging nature, he is the one whose senses are joyful and whose form is heroic.
By virtue of his absolute independence, he is the Lord eternally engaged in the acts of creation and so forth. (53–45)
The state of possessing sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) and valor (*vīrya*) as one's essential nature is called *hṛṣīkeśatva*.

The term "world" (*jagat*) intends the state of being the sovereign over all sentient beings; here, *hṛṣī* is designated as knowledge, and the *hṛṣīkas* are those whose nature is consciousness. (53.46)
Because it is mobile, its form is the world; its Lord is the Master of the worlds.
Thus has this subtle [form] been described, which rests upon the nominal stem. (53–47)
The commencement of the exposition for the sake of others:
Now, listen to my supreme meaning which relies upon the phonemes; [this is] the exposition of the meaning of the letter *ha*.
(1) It sustains every living being by means of its nature as the essence of pure dharma. || 53-48 ||
The determination of the meaning of the syllable *ṛ*:
it is called "Truth" (*satya*) because from it both the manifest (*sat*) and the unmanifest (*tyat*) arise.
Next, the determination of the meaning of the syllable *ṣa*, which has the vowel *ī* as its head.
Through the application of his illusory power, he sustains the sun in the sky by means of a marvelous feat.
An exposition on the meaning of the letter *ka* preceded by the letter *e*:

[She who is] *karālā*, the womb of the world, of terrible form, and composed of darkness (*tamomayī*). Here, the construction is as follows: the letter *ha*, the letter *ṛ*, and the letter *ṣa* with the letter *ī* as its head.

The letter *ka* has the letter *e* as its head; the letter *śa* [follows]. Having thus divided the letters situated in the word *hṛṣīkeśa* into five parts, the meaning designated as "supreme" (para), which is established through its state of being immeasurable (*aprameya*) and so forth, causes [the world] to breathe, and so on—this is shown sequentially by means of two and a half verses.
It is shown as follows: (p. 537) "He pacifies [the afflictions] while abiding in the immeasurable"—this is the state based on the phonemes, which defines the meaning of the letter *śa*. (53.50)
O great sage, this threefold meaning has been declared regarding Hṛṣīkeśa;
now listen to the explanation of the gross meaning of the fourth quarter of the mantra, which is threefold, O daughter of the Great Puruṣa. (53–51)

Having drawn out [the word] "jitaṃ" (conquered), one should say "jayasva" (be victorious) here, or "jaya" (be victorious). Then, "jitaṃ te" (victory be to you) or "namaste'stu" (salutations be to you)—both of these are the words used here.
In Aniruddha, who is the immediate presiding witness of the world consisting of both sentient and insentient beings, victory is indeed expressed in the form of prostration. (53)
This expression "Victory to You" (jitaṃ te) indicates supreme lordship;
how could such an intimate salutation be appropriate for one who is most exalted? (53-54)
By whichever exceedingly lofty form he approaches, that [form] and its second and third [successors]—these two are the objects of salutation therein. (53–55)

In order to illuminate that the Blessed One Aniruddha, who acts for the welfare of the world, possesses two aspects, there [are placed] the salutation and the homage regarding the subject matter. (53–56)
The meaning produced by action and its factors has been described in its gross form.
Now, listen to the description of the subtle meaning—that which resides in the nominal stem (prātipadika); consider that to be the subtle. (53–57)
(p. 538) Examination of the meaning of the syllable *ma*:
It measures the manifold reality consisting of the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*).
Examination of the meaning of the syllable *hā*.
Then that entire [world] retreats and enters within by means of the inner self. || 53-58 ||
Now, it brings to life the entire meaning of the collection [of syllables] "Mahat," and thus it is honored in each respective context;
because it is greater than the great, it is etymologically defined as "the Great" (Mahān). || 53–59 ||
The definition of the meaning of the syllable *pu*:
it nourishes, it abides, it remains unmanifest, and it arises again and again.
This is the definition of the meaning of the syllable *ru*.
It proclaims the scripture of manifold meaning and is itself proclaimed in various forms.
He accepts the worship offered and, being propitiated, bestows the fruit; he brings an end to sins and is honored by various people. (53–61) [Exposition on the meaning of the letter *ṣa*] (1)
The determination of the meaning of the word *puruṣa* as it arises from its constituent parts:
it destroys [suffering] at the end of action (*karmānte*) and is likewise served by many (*purubhiḥ*).
Here, two verbal roots should be understood: *ṣo* in the sense of "ending" (*antakarman*) and *ṣaṇ* in the sense of "gathering" or "enjoyment" (*saṃbhakti*).
He lies within the city; he creates the city; he rests within the many beings. || 53-62 ||
An exposition on the meaning of the syllable *pū* preceded by the letter *ra*:
it sustains the entire universe and wards off all darkness.
An exposition on the meaning of the syllables *va* and *ja*.
It protects all those who have taken refuge in it, and it also conquers even that which consists of darkness.
Birth clearly casts those who hate [the Dharma] into cruel wombs;
yet he who is ancient, being truly that which was designated by the term "primordial" (pūrvaja), is born again in those very same wombs.
He is the first-born of all the gods, the primordial unborn one from whose body [Brahmā] was born;
for his first-born son was Brahmā, who was fashioned at the beginning of the kalpa.
The former lives have been fully described; since they pursue [their goals] before you, he himself causes those former ones to manifest in their own forms. (53–66)
The definition of the meaning of the state of a Great Being:
greatness consists in independence in the performance of all states and actions;
that which is indivisible from [all] persons is his "Great Being-hood. (53–67)
And this very [power] is that splendor; it is declared to be this power.
This is a form derived from the verbal root *van*, meaning "to request" (*yācane*).
It is that which exists in non-differentiation from the Puruṣas.
This very state of being unceasing is also suchness, the state of the Blessed One. (53-68)
And such is its nature as the cause of stability, origination, dissolution, and protection; thus has this subtle [nature], based on each step, been explained to you in brief. (53–69)
The commencement of the exposition for the sake of others:
Now, listen to my supreme meaning based on the letters; this is the exposition of the meaning of the letter *ma*.
The crusher of all the wicked ones, possessed of immeasurable prowess.
The determination of the meaning of the syllable *hā*:
He is eternally beneficial toward his enemies, the protector of all embodied beings, the manifest path for those engaged in action, arising from the rituals of the three Vedas. (53–71)
An investigation into the meaning of the syllable *pa* preceded by the syllable *u*;
Padmanābha, reclining upon the waters, the source of the vast manifestation of the worlds.
An investigation into the meaning of such a *repha* (the letter *ra*).
The support of all worlds without exception, the locus for the arising and persistence of their respective effects.
The determination of the meaning of the syllables *ṣa* and *pa*:
In Śvetadvīpa, he is Nṛsiṃha; among those who consume oblations, he is Agni in form; among all the gods, he is Bhāskara; and for the virtuous, he is the supreme purifier. (53–73)
The determination of the meaning of the letter *ū*:
the support for various kinds of wisdom in accomplishing what is to be done.
The determination of the meaning of the second *repha*.
The powerful lord of all worlds, the fire of time at the end of the aeon.
The determination of the meaning of the letters *va* and *ja*:
He who is the Boar (*varāha*) is remembered by the virtuous as the one who raised up the earth and the destroyer of rebirth;
he is the unconquered (*ajita*) by gods, demons, and others, the primordial ancestor of the Great Puruṣa. (53–75)
Thus, in this lineage of great beings, there is a style based on phonemes;
this great mantra named *Jitanta* indicates the intended meaning of the primary great mantra and possesses manifold great significance.
It describes the eternal God in the form of a wheel and in various forms.
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Meaning of the Mantra Known as Jitantā," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
From the beginning, verse number 3478:
The fifty-fourth chapter, titled "An Exposition on the Meaning of the Nārasiṃha Anuṣṭubh Mantra."
Meditated upon even once, it swiftly destroys millions of floods of sins;
we meditate upon that divine splendor of the Lord Sudarśana.
With seven verses, the greatness of the mantra is described by Ahirbudhnya: "Thus, the great mantra named Jitantā has been declared to you in brief."
Now, O Nārada, hear from me the truth concerning the Nārasiṃha [incarnation].

This great mantra of Nṛsiṃha is the means for accomplishing various kinds of fruits pertaining to this world and the next; it is most wonderful and the provider of enjoyments belonging to the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial realms. (54–2)
He is the one who wards off the three kinds of states consisting of internal forms and the like; likewise, he is the crusher of Rākṣasas, Daityas, and Dānavas.
Even by the followers of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, Vedānta, and Pāśupata, this [Vedānta] must necessarily be relied upon:
"O great sage, this alone is the supreme knowledge of the Sāṃkhyas; this is the foundational step for yogins of restrained self. (54.4)
This indeed is the singular path of the high-souled Sāttvatas;
this is the essence of the end of the three Vedas; this is the Pāśupata doctrine. (54.5)
Out of a desire for the welfare of all sentient beings, this was revealed by Saṃkarṣaṇa at the beginning of the Kalpa:
"In the past, when this world had been created in its various forms, Saṃkarṣaṇa proclaimed this supreme knowledge for the benefit of all living beings. (54–6)
Even for Brahmā, Rudra, and the others, the attainment of this mantra from Saṃkarṣaṇa required great exertion.
In ancient times, Brahmā, having performed severe penance, learned it from him;
I studied it from him, and from me the divine great sages have learned it.

In the determination of the gross object, preceded by the knowledge of its being subordinate (*śeṣatva*), there is the description of the surrender of both the self and what belongs to the self to the Blessed Lord; this is called bowing (*namana*), and it is remembered as the state of becoming humble (*nīcībhāva*).
Indeed, the state of being subordinate to another is precisely what constitutes one's status as a *śeṣa* (subordinate).
Having brought oneself into the state of being a remnant (śeṣatā), the knower of mantras, by means of the words "I bow," offers his own self to Him. (54.9)
The representation of sentiments such as the Furious (raudra) through words like "ugra" and others found in the mantras is as follows:
the Furious sentiment is declared to be "ugra" due to an excess of wrath;
the Heroic sentiment, arising from an excess of energy, is expressed by the word "vīra. (54-10)
He is *bhayānaka* (the terrifying) because he is the cause of extreme fear through the four extraordinary sounds beginning with "Mahāviṣṇu" and others, which are themselves formidable (*bhīṣaṇa*).
O Sage, he speaks of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) and the auspicious words of the mantra; he also speaks of the state beyond death and of the wondrous and terrifying. (54.12)
The extraction of the true nature of the self (*ātman*) as being essentially subordinate to the Lord through the word "I" (*aham*):
"The extraction of the self as 'I' is by means of the self that belongs to the Lord.
Furthermore, there is the demonstration of the specific application of the *rasas*, such as the Furious (*raudra*), which are denoted by words like "Ugra" and others.
The fierce god, with the intent to destroy his enemies, was a hero seeking the destruction of the hosts of gods.
He is Mahāviṣṇu, blazing indeed, and also Sarvatomukha;
he is the wondrous Nṛsiṃha, perceived by those who have attained perfection in yoga.
The god Bhīṣaṇa was designated for the destruction of the hosts of minor Rākṣasas;
he was gazed upon by Lakṣmī with auspicious eyes, whose outer corners were curved with joy.
He is the death of even the deaths of the sages through his terrifying and wondrous yoga;
such is this gross object produced by the conjunction of action and its factors. (54.16)
An investigation into subtle meanings:
understand this subtle meaning which rests upon nominal stems; [followed by] an investigation into the meanings of formidable words.
It emits the entire universe and itself devours what has been emitted.
An examination of the meaning of the word *vīra*:
it conquers (*vīrayati*) every state of being and also delights (*ramayati*) them in manifold ways.
By the word *mahat*, there is the indication of being devoid of the three kinds of limitation.
Because it is devoid of limitations such as time and space, it is remembered as "Great" (mahān). || 54-18 ||

Furthermore, there is a ninefold demonstration of the etymological derivation of the word *mahat*: (1) "The Great One (*mahān*) is so called because he is magnified (*mahīyate*), or because he excretes (*mehati*), or because he deludes (*muhyati*), or because he rains (*miheḥ*); or because he thinks (*manute*), or because he abandons (*sajahāti*), or because he leaves me behind (*māṃ jihīte*). (54.19)
Because everything is measured within it, or rather, because it does not abandon the entire world,
its manifestation occurs in due order;
it is glorified in the supreme ether and is thus defined as "Mahān" (the Great).
This great one performs the act of giving; he bestows what is desired. He deludes [the world] by means of his own activities; thus the God is remembered as Mahān.
He indeed excretes his own vigor into the waters as semen; thus he is called "Mahān" (the Great).
By virtue of his eternal union with his own self consisting of knowledge, he is "Mahān. (54.22)
He abandons the various states of being which they know as the six states; he leaves behind that goddess who is considered to be *meti*, and she approaches him. (54.23)
That divine couple, eternally embraced, [arises] from *mahan* (the Great).
Here, these seven verbal roots (*dhātu*) are intended to be understood: *maha* in the sense of worship (*pūjā*), belonging to the *bhvādi* class;

*miha* in the sense of sprinkling (*secana*), belonging to the *bhvādi* class; *muha* in the sense of confusion of mind (*vaicittya*), belonging to the *divādi* class; *manu* in the sense of understanding (*avabodhana*), belonging to the *tanādi* class; and *ohāk*...

The root *tyaj* belongs to the *juhoty-ādi* class; *ohāṅ* (in the sense of "going") belongs to the *juhoty-ādi* class; *mā* (in the sense of "measuring") belongs to the *adadi* class. Here, regarding the root *miha* in the sense of "sprinkling," sprinkling means "mixing. By this, the consistency of the text is established that the root *mih* has the act of giving as its meaning. Although there are nine [roots] for the sake of their utility in the ninefold etymological derivations...

Although the elements (*dhātu*) were already required, it should be understood that the number nine is completed because the root *mih* and the root *hā* are repeated twice due to a difference in their intended meaning.
(p. 546) "In this [receptacle], the entire universe is contained, like a jujube fruit in a bowl. (54.24)

The Great One does not abandon that which exists outside, nor does He leave it within the body; therefore, He discerns the meaning of the word Viṣṇu in this world and moves through both the existent and the non-existent. (54.25)
(2) He pervades all enjoyments and bestows them upon living beings himself;
with all individual souls dependent upon him, he is praised within by his own self through the primordial sound (svarātman). 54-26.

Thus those who know the true nature of words and their meanings declare Viṣṇu to be the God. This is the definition of the meaning condensed in the term "Mahāviṣṇu": because he enters the great cycle of worldly existence while being born, he is called "Great" (Mahān). (54.27)
The wise declare this God to be Mahāviṣṇu; He is the blazing manifestation of sound and meaning, eternally present in the hearts of yogins and in the supreme state of the seers. (54.28)
And because the sun, the moon, and fire—this supreme triad of splendors—shine forth spontaneously within the sacrificial canopies of the Brahmins; (54.29)
Having entered within, it causes [the world] to blaze; having descended, it blazes forth as well.
Blazing by means of its own nature as the essence of knowledge, it alone devours the universe.
Thus they call that Harimedhas blazing on all sides.
(1) The root *vi-cir* means "separation" (*pṛthagbhāve*).
(2) The root *vi-ṣḷ* means "pervasion" (*vyāptau*).

3. *Harimedhāḥ* refers to one whose resolve (*saṃkalpa*) removes the evils (*durita*) residing [in others]; the meaning is that he is distinguished by an unfailing resolve directed toward destroying the evils residing in those who have taken refuge in him, which constitute obstacles to their own attainment [of Him].
(547) The definition of the term *sarvatomukha* (all-facing): Power (*śakti*) is declared to be the "face" (*mukha*), which is situated on all sides of it. || 54.31 ||
They call him the one whose face is turned in every direction, the eternal possessor of all powers.
Regarding the definition of the term *Nṛsiṃha*: he destroys (*han*) and slays (*hinasti*) the bondage of men; thus he is *Nṛsiṃha*. (54.32)
The definition of the meaning of the word *bhīṣaṇa*:
He bestows fear (*bhiyam sanoti*) upon the wicked; therefore, he is called *bhīṣaṇa*.
The definition of the meaning of the word *bhadra*.
The sun bestows prosperity and dispels the worldly existence of the virtuous.
He causes the terrible existence—this cycle of saṃsāra constantly filled with suffering—to dissolve.
Regarding the definition of the term "death of death": ignorance is declared to be death, and death is that which takes away the vital breaths. (54.34)
Death is declared to be *saṃsāra* (transmigration) for them, because Hari is their death.

First, regarding the word "death" (*mṛtyu*) as referring to the triad beginning with ignorance (*ajñāna*), the etymological explanation is shown: "That by which one abandons the intellect is called death; it is said to be ignorance. (54.35)
The established position is that "mṛtyu" (death) is so called because it extends death to living beings;
since it consists of a continuous succession of deaths, saṃsāra is called "mṛtyu. (54.36)

The second instance of the word "death" (mṛtyu) has as its purport the destruction of the triad beginning with ignorance (ajñāna), which was previously denoted by the first instance of the word "death"; this capacity for destruction is here indicated as being limited by the subsequent death.
(p. 548) *Nāśakatvam ihoddiṣṭaṃ mitam uttaramṛtyunā*.
The description of the fourfold meaning of the word "I" (ahaṃ): "He goes toward Hari, he attains Him here in his true nature; such is he. (54.37)
For consciousness is, by its very nature, entirely full bliss;
moreover, it is inherently undiminished in all respects, including knowledge, power, and so forth. (54.38)
Or rather, this [Self] may be immeasurable by day, since everything transcends time;
or else, this living being (jīva) is measured within the day, and he is called the "I-principle" (ahamartha).
The day is to be known as Saṃkarṣaṇa; in him the entire individual soul (jīva) is situated.
This is the determination of the intended meaning of the formidable and terrifying words, in order to demonstrate the meaning of the mantra according to the path of Sāṃkhya.
By the two words "ugra" and "bhīṣaṇa," the unmanifest form is expressed. (54.40)
That which is fierce, exceedingly terrible, formidable, and fear-inducing—
that unmanifest should be fully known as the very form of the Blessed One.
An investigation into the meaning intended by the word "blazing":
By the word "blazing" (jvalantam), the nature of the individual soul (jīva) is expressed.
Consciousness is declared to be the blazing; the conscious agent thereof is the Blazer (Jvalana). (54.42)
He is called "blazing" because his Vedic rites are not yet completed; having observed everywhere the nature of worldly existence and the defects arising from it, [he remains thus]. (54.43)
When one who is detached knows the supreme Hari in every respect, then all cognitive activity of that knower comes to an end. (54.44)
Therefore, he who is described as being immersed in primordial nature (prakṛti) while still conscious, though wandering in saṃsāra and burning with afflictions, is also called a Bhagavān. (54.45)
That which impels this world of sentient and insentient beings in its various ways—
Time, who is the very form of the Lord— is designated by the word "Vīra. (54.46)
The determination of the intended meaning of the term *Mahāviṣṇu*: The pervasion of those three principles is expressed by the word *Viṣṇu*;
furthermore, [the term *Mahā* denotes] being unstained even within that pervasion, as well as that which is superior to it. (54–47)
Greatness and venerability are described by the word "mahat.
The meaning intended by the term "sarvatomukha" (facing all directions) is explained as the state of possessing all powers; it is by the word "sarvatomukha" that omnipotence is proclaimed. (54–48)
The Lord possesses omniscience as well as the status of being the creator of all;
the investigation into the intended meaning of the word "Bhadra" (Auspicious) expresses, by means of that word, the Lord's eternal freedom from defects. (54–49)
The determination of the intended meaning of the term *nṛsiṃha*:
likewise, by the word *nṛsiṃha*, the state of being the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*) is expressed.
The determination of the intended meaning of the term *mṛtyumṛtyu*.
Its capacity to bestow liberation arises from the wind that slays death. (54–50)

The determination of the intended meaning of the word "I" is as follows: that perfection which is achieved through *prasaṃkhyāna* over a long period of time—that very state of being beyond primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is directly described by the word "I. (54–51)

All natural activity, such as "he injures" or "he goes," is expressed by the word *ahaṃ* (I) when it denotes its agent; that which is other than this is what is denoted by the term *ahaṃpada* (the "I-word"). (54–52)
This unconditioned reflective awareness, which persists even at the point of death of the body and vital breath, attains the status of the "I"; that is the unadorned living soul (jīva). || 54-53 ||

One should thus contemplate the Self through the investigation of the intended meaning of the word "I bow" (namāmi); it is that by which one becomes spontaneously humble. Just as a river [becomes humble] in the ocean, so too is humility [in the Divine] a state of being submerged.
Thus, this subtle meaning pertaining to the Mantra system has been declared to you as it stands upon the path of Sāṃkhya.
Those who know the reality of that thorough discernment enter the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Now, behold from me His form as He abides on the path of Yoga.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Meaning of the Nārasiṃha Anuṣṭubh Mantra," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
From the beginning, verse number 3533:
The fifty-fifth chapter, titled "An Exposition on the Meaning of the Nārasiṃha Anuṣṭubh Mantra."
Meditated upon even once, it swiftly destroys the flood of tens of millions of births;
we meditate upon that divine splendor of the Lord Sudarśana.
The promise to determine the meaning of the mantra according to the system of Yoga: Ahirbudhnya says— “Just as the wise practitioners of Yoga explain this mantra...”
"O Sage, it should be spoken by you in that manner; listen to me as I speak it. (55-1)
The definition of the meaning of the term *ugra*: he is called *ugra* because he has arisen from wrath (*krudh*) and because of his obstruction of the [sensual] instruments.
The definition of the meaning of the term *vīra*.
By whom [the channels] are opened, the *īrā* and the winds residing within the body are conquered. || 55-2 ||
That hero has arisen through yogic practices by those who have reached the further shore of the knowledge of the tantras;
he is one who has conquered his senses and his breath, who blazes within on all sides, and who defines the radiant nature of word and meaning. (55.3)
Because he is free from all limitations of the senses, he blazes forth, spreading everywhere.
Hari, who consists of all knowledge, is designated as "all-facing" (sarvatomukha), for he is the definition of the meaning of the word "all-facing. (55.4)
The definition of the meaning of the word *bhīṣaṇa*:
*Bhā* is said to be perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*); its impelling is *īṣaṇa*.
He who impels knowledge is called *bheṣaṇa*, and the Lord, the creator of the universe, is called *bhīṣaṇa*. (55–5)
The indication that the meaning of the term "Death-of-Death" (mṛtyumṛtyu) has been previously stated:
"Mahāviṣṇu and Nṛsiṃha, and Death-of-Death, as before. This is the definition of the combined meaning of the sentence.
He who has conquered the senses is established as the vital breath (samīra), the very form of the living soul (jīva). || 55-6 ||
They know him as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), who is all-pervading, venerable, the perfect inspirer of the intellects, and the liberator from saṃsāra. || 55-7 ||
"I bow to that God"—such is the instruction for yoga.

In the exposition of the meaning of the mantra according to the Pāśupata doctrine, the meaning of the word *ugra* is as follows: he who is to be propitiated by fierce vows (*ugravrata*) is described by the word *ugra*. (55–8)
The definition of the meaning of the word *vīra*:
the quality of being worthy of worship by those who have mastered [the teachings] is described by the word *vīra*.
The definition of the meaning of the word *sarvatomukha*.
The prior non-existence of the three impurities is designated by the term "all-facing" (sarvatomukha). || 55-9 ||
The definition of the meaning of the word *jvalat* (blazing):
the density of the first [element] is described by the word *jvalat*.
The definition of the meaning of the word *bhīṣaṇa* (terrifying).
But the noose, which consists of the five objects of sense, is indicated by the word *bhī*. || 55-10 ||
It frightens, it tears asunder, and it clearly cuts the bond of the bound soul;
thus, this word "bhīṣaṇa" (the terrifying) denotes the cutter of the bonds of the bound soul. (55.11)
The definition of the meaning of the term "Death-of-Death" (mṛtyumṛtyu); the fact that the Lord’s quality of being the bringer of auspiciousness is expressed by the word "Death-of-Death";
and the indication that the meaning of the subsequent term has already been demonstrated previously.
Mahāviṣṇu and Nṛsiṃha have already been shown previously.
The determination of the meaning of the condensed statement:

[He is] eternally beloved by those who delight in fierce vows, worshipped by those devoted to fierce vows; untouched by the three impurities, a mass of consciousness, and the shatterer of bonds. (55.13)
"I bow to Him whom they call Śiva, Viṣṇu, the Great One, the Supreme Person"—this is the meaning recorded in the Pāśupata [tradition]. (55.14)

(p. 554) An indication that the meaning has already been determined in accordance with the doctrine of the three Vedas: "That which is to be known through the path of the three Vedas has already been determined.
The determination of the meaning of the mantra according to the Sāttvata doctrine.
With vigilance, grasp this meaning, which is to be realized by the Sātvatas.
The word *ugra* refers clearly to the manifestation known as Saṃkarṣaṇa;
for he emits the stainless scripture, delights [the world] by emitting it, and at the end, he swallows that scripture—thus is Ugra remembered as Saṃkarṣaṇa. (55.16)
Setting aside the interpretation that the word "vīra" refers to the military array (vyūha) named Pradyumna, he impels the triad [of qualities] by means of passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas);
he makes that Vidyā heroic in both the creation of the learned and the creation of men. (55.17)
He exerts himself even against the honey of darkness, and he applies his stainless action to the performance of the meaning of the scriptures. (55.18)
Therefore, they call the primordial Pradyumna the Hero and the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
[Regarding] the term "Mahāviṣṇu," it refers to the manifestation (vyūha) named Aniruddha:
"He becomes great through his activities and is unrestrained (aniruddha) in every respect. (55.19)
By means of one, three, or four efforts, those former ones were of limited conduct;
and because their task was limited, their power was restricted. (55.20)
It should be understood that this was established in the previous chapter by twenty-three and a half verses, beginning from the seventeenth verse up to the first half of the fortieth verse.
In the Aniruddha-tattva, however, activities are taught that are beyond numbering;
indeed, the effects such as creation, maintenance, and so forth, are immeasurable. (55.21)
That power which has Him as its object, that pervasion, and that state of Viṣṇuhood—
these belong to that fourth manifestation (turyavyūha) of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, who is himself unobstructed.
Therefore, he is called Mahāviṣṇu and Aniruddha by the wise.
The blazing of the word refers to the manifestation as Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others;
its expansion within the midst of the cosmic egg is declared to be "blazing. (55-23)
Regarding what they call the "incarnation" (avatāra) which is the manifestation of the power of Hari-meghas:
by the word "sarvatomukha," there is an indication that among the incarnations, this represents the ultimate limit of accessibility, characterized by birth in various forms of existence.
By the term "facing in all directions," the entry into various wombs is meant. || 55-24 ||
Even at the stage of manifestation (*avatāra*), the word *bhadra* signifies the absence of connection with anything to be abandoned;
its auspiciousness (*bhadratva*) therein consists precisely in its not relinquishing its own essential nature.
The word *bhīṣaṇa* signifies the bestowing of liberation.
The terrifying nature of the bonds of cyclic existence is considered their fear. (55.25)
That [state] is taught as being attainable through mere consciousness (vijñāna) along with its modes;
it is [derived from] the verbal root *mṛ* (to die), as in *anta-karman* (the act of ending).
By the term "death of death" (*mṛtyumṛtyu*), the quality of being an adversary to that which is to be abandoned—expressed by the word *bhadra*—is indicated.
That awakening which consists in the opposition to what is to be abandoned belongs to Brahman at all times. (55.26)
And that [power] is declared to be innate by the term "the death of death.
Regarding the word *Nṛsiṃha*, its meaning consists of a twofold pervasion: having bound the *nṛs* (men/selves) within and having concealed them, and also having surrounded them on all sides. (55-27)
That state of that deity which is called Puruṣottamatā is expressed by the word Nṛsiṃha; this very thing is stated to be the meaning of the sentence.
Having manifested himself in a threefold array in the forms of Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others,
he remains as the all-pervading Lord, facing every direction, for the sake of accomplishing the various effects dependent upon each.
It blazes within the belly of existence in various forms of manifestation;
blazing thus, it becomes indeed auspicious and even more auspicious.

Thus, as soon as it is understood, that which is terrifying and brings about the destruction of bondage becomes the adversary of death, since it is the death of death itself, whose very nature is to be abandoned. (55.31)

I [bow to] that Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), who is easily accessible to men through the knowledge of the manifestation of his cosmic array, and who stands pervading this entire universe both internally and externally. || 55-32 ||
"I contemplate Nṛsiṃha through all the senses as my very self.
Thus has the goal of the Sāttvata doctrine been briefly illustrated for you. (55.33)
(557) Listen now to that subtle and manifold meaning:
first, in the description of the supreme goal, it is stated that the term *ugra* refers to the manifestation (*vyūha*) known as Saṃkarṣaṇa.
The support of all worlds without exception, the destroyer of the disease of saṃsāra.
The first manifestation of Viṣṇu, known by the name Saṃkarṣaṇa, is of unrestrained emergence; it is designated as Vaiṣṇava and is characterized by fierce colors. (55.35)
Its proof is that the universe shines forth therein like a mole on the skin,
and because one destroys disease through the instruction of the divine scripture. (55.36)
That unbridled, irresistible, and radiant manifestation of Viṣṇu—

herein lies the secret: the description of the supreme meaning of the Nārasiṃha Anuṣṭubh mantra consists in the fact that the syllables of the mantra are intended for the manifestation of the Vyūhas and Vibhavas, which are established as being of the nature of the Immeasurable (Aprameya) and so forth.
An illustration: For instance, in an *anuṣṭubh* verse there are eleven words. Among them, the first word ends in the nominative case and expresses the agent (*kartṛ-kāraka*).
The tenth word ends in the third person singular and expresses the action of bowing (*namana-kriyā*). The remaining nine words end in the accusative case singular.

The words are those which convey specific objects that have become the objects of the act of bowing. Among them, the first three words refer, respectively, to the triad of manifestations (vyūha) known as Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha.
The group of six words beginning with "jvalat" [refers] to that which was set forth at the conclusion of the fifth chapter.

It establishes, as appropriate, thirty-nine manifestations beginning with Padmanābha and ending with Pātālaśayana. Therein, by means of the remainder of the chapter beginning with "Listen now to the supreme," [it teaches] the nature of the *vyūha* of Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others— [the forms] Ugra, Vīra, Mahā-...

The meanings of the words "Viṣṇu" and so forth are now demonstrated. Because there is much to be said, the fact that words such as "jvalat" (blazing) refer to Padmanābha and others will be shown in a separate chapter commenced later.
In this regard, the purport of these three and a half verses beginning with "the support of all worlds" is as follows:
By the letters *u*, *ga*, and *ra* situated in the fierce word (*ugrapada*), the three qualities (*guṇatraya*) are intended in reverse order:
by the letter *ra*, the state of being the support of all worlds; by the letter *ga*, the destruction of the disease of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra-gada*);
and by the letter *u*, the nature of arising characterized by its unrestrained intensity. [This is] by means of the letters *ra* and the others.

This is because, by bringing to mind other synonymous terms such as "the support of all worlds" which are co-referential with [the word *ra*] itself, it is possible to bring to mind the aforementioned qualities through those means.
Furthermore, the fact that words such as "the support of all worlds" are synonyms for the phoneme *ra* has been explained in detail.

In the seventeenth [chapter]: "Udaye" means rising and being unrestrained, as well as being unimpeded. Thus, Viṣṇu’s first manifestation (*prathamodaya*), which is unimpeded and adorned with qualities such as being the substratum of the entire world, is indeed Saṃkarṣaṇa; he alone [is denoted] by the syllables that are the components of the word *ugra*.
Regarding the term "designated" (*samuddiṣṭa*): in this very manner, the comprehension of the meaning in the case of the words *vīra* and so forth should also be inferred.
Therefore, the Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa is the one designated by the word *ugra*. (55.37)
By the word "vīra" (hero), the manifestation of Pradyumna is established;
he is the form of the support of nectar, possessed of *māyā*, and from him comes fire.
The lotus-eyed Pradyumna is thus declared by the term "vīra. (55.38)
The establishment of that [truth] is the nectar, which is the Dharma of the Blessed One; its support is the locus of reliance.
This is the determination of the meaning of the sentence as a whole.
For Pradyumna, who takes refuge in the Dharma, is the sustainer of the True Dharma. || 55-39 ||
Since knowledge awakens one from ignorance through illusion, it burns away the defect of ignorance consisting of darkness, just as fire consumes [fuel]. (55.40)
Therefore, the Lord Pradyumna is celebrated by the epithet Vīravara;
the manifestation of Aniruddha is proclaimed by the term Mahāviṣṇu.
Time (Kāla) and Primordial Matter (Pradhāna) are their support, and Vital Breath (Prāṇa) has always been their foundation. (55–41)
And constantly concealing those two while choosing all possible courses of action, he gradually nourishes the human embryo through successive years. (55.42)
Taking the form of fire in this world and becoming the Sun himself,
he is the granter of fearlessness to the universe, Vaikuṇṭha, and the unimpeded world.
(p. 559) Mahāviṣṇu, the self-governing supervisor, has been described;
his manifestation is Puṣkara, which, in the form of Time, bears [the world] born from his navel. (55.44)
And the inner Person, as well as the Pradhāna residing within it, is designated by the terms "Time" and "Pradhāna" without distinction. (55.45)
Causing the triad of Sāṃkhya, Time, and the Living Being to breathe through time,
he is designated by the color of the vital breath as Gopana, known by that name.
The goals (gatis) are said to be effects; and by desiring to choose them, he is described by the one whose color is like Varuṇa, for that indeed is his state of non-obstruction (aniruddhatā).

Nourishing the embryo within the womb for a thousand years— consisting of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the eightfold subtle body (*anuṣṭakātmaka*)— the Lord, praised as the ocean of light, [remains] in the science of time.
In the divine creation, such as that of Agni, Sūrya, and others, according to the science of medicine (vaidyaka),
he himself assumes their respective names through his entry into each of those deities.
The Lord himself is proclaimed to have the color of the rising sun;
he pervades everything from time down to the earth, consisting of both the sentient and the insentient. (55–50)
That which has arisen from the ocean of worlds is variegated by the limbs of the worlds;
he who always grants fearlessness to it by the destruction of its wicked ones.
And he who remained unimpeded in the undertaking of each respective task, the presiding overseer who, having entered into all beings, restrains them; || 55-52 ||
"This [Lord] is described by the color of the Teacher of Vaikuṇṭha, who bestows fearlessness.
Thus have the emanations (vyūhas) been indicated by the triad beginning with Ugra; hereafter, the meaning as defined by Jvalat and the others is proclaimed. (55–53)
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Meaning of the Nārasiṃha Anuṣṭubh Mantra," in the Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā, a secret doctrine within the Śrī Pāñcarātra Tantra.
From the beginning, verse number 3586:
The fifty-sixth chapter, titled "An Exposition on the Meaning of the Nārasiṃha Anuṣṭubh Mantra."
Meditated upon even once, it swiftly destroys the flood of tens of millions of births;
we meditate upon that divine splendor of the Lord Sudarśana.
The description of how words such as "jvalat" (the blazing one) and others refer to the thirty-nine incarnations beginning with Padmanābha,
by Ahirbudhnya:
The majestic wheel of deities, blazing and described by the primordial syllable—listen attentively as it is described by various [masters] in their respective ways. (56-1)
Among the eleven incarnations intended by the word *jvalat*, (1) the letter *ja* refers to the first incarnation named Padmanābha; for it is said:
"The incarnation of Viṣṇu which is Padmanābha is of great glory."
He is described by some as "the unconquered" (Ajita) because he has not been conquered by anyone anywhere. || 56-2 ||
The letter *va* refers to the twentieth incarnation known as Kāntātmāmṛtadhāraka; he is the Sustainer of Nectar (*amṛtadhāraka*) by virtue of being the syllable that supports nectar.
1. Herein follows the sequence for the division of syllables corresponding to each respective incarnation: the letter *ja*, the letter *va*.
The letter *va* followed by the letter *ā*, the letter *la*, again the letter *la*, again the letter *la*, the letter *na*, the letter *ta*,
again the letter *ta*, again the letter *ta*, and the suffix *am*; thus, by these eleven phonemes which are the components of the word "Jvalat" (Blazing).
Regarding the intention to describe the eleven incarnations beginning with Padmanābha:
it should be understood that the enumeration of these respective incarnations according to their specific numbers here follows the sequence stated in the fifth chapter.
The letter *ā* following *va* refers to the fourteenth incarnation known as the One Reclining on the Ocean;
in that very context, he is the Ocean-Recliner and Varuṇa, because he is immeasurable. (56.3)
The letter *la* refers to the fourth incarnation known as Śaktyātmā; for the Lord of the Earth (Dhareśa) has stated that Śaktīśa is indeed the Vaiṣṇavī power (*śakti*),
under another name of that very same [deity].
The two incarnations known as Hari and Kṛṣṇa—the thirty-third and thirty-fourth—have been declared: Hari is designated as Vibudha, while Kṛṣṇa is the Lord of Puruṣa. (56.4)
The Lord of Men is described by the caste known as *vibudha*;
both of those gods are said to consist of the essence of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
The letter *na* refers to the twelve incarnations known as the *dharmas*.
For that eternal Dharma, which is the path to heaven and liberation, is proclaimed by the Lord as the northern path of Dhareśa. (56–6)

The letter *ta* refers to the third incarnation known as Ananta; for the Blessed One who is recited as Ananta possesses the mark of the *tāla*, and that deity, the upholder of the earth, is described by the mark of the *tāla*. (56–7)
By means of another synonym for that very [Kūrma], it refers to the two [fifteenth and sixteenth] incarnations known as the presiding deity of the Kūrma-vidyā:
"The Lokamālās are said to be garlands; the wearer of the garland (sragdhara) is called Kūrma."
The Virāj-vidyā has been proclaimed by the virtuous, and Vairāja is its presiding lord.
Those two deities are proclaimed by the names Vairāja and Sragdhara;
the letters *a* and *ma*, which are components of the suffix *am*,
signify the twenty-second incarnation known as Kālanemi and Ghna.
By means of time swallowed up by the Immeasurable One, the Supreme Person [attains his goal]. || 56-9 ||
It is said that the Time which destroys Kālanemi is difficult to overcome.
Among the ten incarnations intended by the term "all-facing" (*sarvatomukha*), the letter *sa* refers to the eighteenth incarnation known as the "Stealing of the Nectar" (*pīyuṣaharaṇa*).
It is the immeasurable, the supreme, the immortal, and the imperishable.
It describes the bringing of the nectar by the lotus-eyed Puruṣa;
through another name for him, it refers to his nineteenth incarnation known as Śrīpati. That very same eternal satisfaction is fully pervaded by the Immeasurable One (Viṣṇu). (56.11)
Śrī speaks to the Lord of Devas, the Lord of Śrī; she is declared to be *tṛpti* (satisfaction).
The letter *va* together with the *repha* (*vra*) refers to the sixteenth incarnation known as Varāha, by virtue of being the collection of Varāhas who support the entire universe. (56–12)
The Boar (Varāha) is celebrated as the support of the entire world.

Herein is the sequence of the division of its syllables: the letter *sa*, again the letter *sa*, the letter *va* with the letter *ra*, again the letter *va* preceded by the letter *a*, the letter *ta*, the diphthong *o*, and again the diphthong *o*.
Furthermore, there is the letter *o* headed by *ma*; the letter *kha* preceded by *u* and headed by *ma*;
and again the letter *kha*. Thus, by these ten syllables which are the components of the word *sarvatomukha*, [the mantra is formed].
The intention is to describe the ten incarnations beginning with the "seizure of the nectar" (pīyūṣaharaṇa). (p.
564) By means of another designation for that very letter *va* preceded by the letter *a*, it refers to the thirty-ninth incarnation known as "lying upon the netherworld" (pātālaśayana).
And from the syllable Varuṇa, which is pervaded by the immeasurable. || 56-13 ||
The Blessed One, the God of gods, is declared to be the one who reclines in the netherworld (pātāla).
Regarding the letter *ta*, it refers to the thirteenth incarnation known as Vāgīśvara.
The goddess Sraṅvāk has been proclaimed by the lords of sages as she who creates and sustains the universe. (56–14)
Vāgīśa is expressed by the second syllable of the *sragdharā* meter. Regarding the letter *o*, it refers to the thirtieth incarnation known as Trivikrama:
"That god who was the leader of Bala strode across the earth three times. (56–15)
Hari is celebrated by that color as "the Stepmaker" (Vikramin).
Through another synonym for that very same [color], it refers to the eighth incarnation known as Viśvarūpa. For the Lord is he who sports with his own universal form. (56–16)
That god is Viśvarūpa; he is described by the Lord as such.
By means of another designation for that very same deity whose head is the letter *ma*, his status as the eleventh incarnation known as Vaḍavāmukha is established.
Overwhelmed by the rice-offering, the superior color was crushed. || 56-17 ||
He speaks of Aurva, the mare’s mouth, the god of gods who consumes the waters;
the preparation for that is the "odana" (rice-mash), and water is designated as the "prasū" (mother/source) of the odana. || 56-18 ||
1. Here, the state of being "second" is in relation to the letter *ja* situated in the word *jvalat*.
2. In the term *ota*, the suffix *kta* has the sense of the agent (*kartari*). (p.
565) That deity, crushing the water by drinking it, is the "Crusher of the Rice-Porridge" (*odanamardana*).
The letter *kha*, preceded by *u* and topped with *ma*, refers to the twenty-ninth incarnation known as Vāmanadeha:
"For that syllable which is the Dwarf-bodied one is the crusher of Uddāma and Udaya. (56.19)
Vāmana speaks very clearly to Bali, who has requested the earth as a petitioner:
"For Vāmana indeed crushes his vast undertaking, his exalted rise, and his pervasiveness. (56.20)

By means of another synonym for that very [letter], it refers to the thirty-seventh incarnation known as Vedavit; that same letter, being the essence of the Vedas, expresses Hari as Vedavit among the nine incarnations intended by the word Nṛsiṃha, specifically through the letter *na*.
The two incarnations known as Nara and Nārāyaṇa, the thirty-first and thirty-second, are derived from the syllables *nara* and *nārāyaṇa*:
"Nara and Nārāyaṇa indeed [arose] from the syllables *nara* and *nārāyaṇa*. (56.21)
The letter *ṛ* signifies the twenty-third incarnation known as the Abduction of the Pārijāta Tree:
"He who is with Satyā is Satya; he is the Great One who carried away the Pārijāta. He was described by Satyārṇa while carrying Satyā seated upon his lap. (56.22)

1. Herein is the sequence of the division of phonemes: the letter *na*, again the letter *na*, the letter *ṛ*, the aggregate of the four phonemes consisting of *ma*, *na*, *ṛ*, and *sa*, the letter *i*, again the letter *i*, the letter *ṅa*, the letter *ha*, and the letter *ma* which is a constituent of the suffix; thus it is.
By means of the nine phonemes that constitute the word *nṛsiṃha*, there is the intention to express the group of nine incarnations beginning with Nara and Nārāyaṇa. (p.
566) [The collection of the four phonemes consisting of *ma*, *na*, *ṛ*, and *sa*...]
That which has as its ultimate goal the twenty-first incarnation known as Rāhujit;
for that which follows the "dwarf-bodied" (kharva) is indeed Mardana, joined with the Path (pathā);
beyond that is Aṅkuśa, and beyond that is Soma—thus from these four syllables. (56-23)
The hook that restrains Soma as he moves along his path is called Rāhu;
the deity who crushes him is designated as Rāhujit (the Conqueror of Rāhu). 56-24.
The letter *i* has the significance of the two incarnations known as Paraśurāma and Śrīrāma, the thirty-fifth and thirty-sixth; O Nārada, the two Rāmas are indicated by the syllable *rā*.
(2) Regarding the letter *ṅa*, its reference to the tenth incarnation known as Kroḍātman is stated: "The Blessed One is celebrated by Ekadaṃṣṭra as Kroḍātman. || 56-25 ||
The letter *ha* signifies the ninth incarnation known as Vihaṅgama; Janārdana, in the form of a swan (*haṃsa*), comes together with the Sun.
Furthermore, this letter *ma* constitutes the final constituent part of the first half of the mantra.

In this context, [the word] is supplied by virtue of the power of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*satti*), and semantic compatibility (*yogyatā*), in accordance with the comprehension of the meaning. For this very reason, in the root text, this letter *ma* is specified as being "after the letter *kha*" in the phrase *khavadehāt paraḥ*.
Furthermore, it should be noted here that there are two possible derivations for the word *siṃha*, established according to the rules of grammatical science (*śabdānuśāsana*).

For example, from the root *sic* in the sense of "to sprinkle," by the Uṇādi rule *siṃceḥ saṃjñāyāṃ hanumau kaśca*, when the suffix *kap* is applied, the augment *num* is added, and the final letter *c* of the root is replaced by *h*, the form *siṃha* is produced; this is one [derivation].

Another [explanation] maintains that, since the *pṛṣodarādi* group is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*), the word *siṃha* is included therein; thus, from the root *hiṃs* (meaning "to injure") with the suffix *ac* (by *pacādyac*), the form *siṃha* is established through the transposition of the positions of the letters *ha* and *sa*. Both of these [views]— [The text continues: ...are also [rejected].

Having accepted this [etymology], such a distinction has generally been adopted in the mantra-śāstras, namely that the fifth letter of the *ka*-group is pronounced in place of the *anusvāra* which is a constituent of the word "siṃha.
Therefore, here, in accordance with the limits of our own system, it is precisely the letter *ṅa* [that is intended] in the word "siṃha."
The word *ekadaṃṣṭra* is employed with the intention of making [the meaning] understood:
"That Lord of Gods, the Bird, is described by means of the color of the sun. (56.26)
Regarding the letter *ma*, which is a constituent of the suffix (*pratyaya*), its referent is the thirty-eighth incarnation known as Kalki:
"He who, named Kalki, subdues the Dasyus born at the end of the Yuga in the Tiṣya age—he is celebrated for his subduing [of enemies] while standing above the sun. (56.27)
Among the four descents intended by the terrifying sound [of the syllable *bhī*], the letter *bha* refers to the second descent known as Dhruva:
"O Great Sage, the deity Dhruva is designated by the syllable *dhruva*."
The letter *ī* signifies the twenty-seventh incarnation, known as Nyagrodhaśāyin;
having assumed a form composed of *māyā*, [he rested] upon a radiant leaf of the banyan tree. (56.28)
He who lies in the form of Kānta is described by the letter of Māyā (the letter *m*). The letter *ṣa* refers to the seventeenth incarnation known as Narasiṃha;
indeed, Nṛsiṃha, the God of gods, is described by the syllable *nṛsiṃha*. (56–29)
The letter *ṇa* refers to the fifth incarnation known as Madhusūdana:
"Having previously slain Madhu, he who crushed the primary [obstacle] of Brahmā, relying on the strength of his own arms, granted fearlessness to Viriñca. (56.30)
For that Madhusūdana was addressed by the god with the ocean of fearlessness (*abhayadārṇa*).
Herein is the sequence of the division of phonemes: the letter *bha*, the letter *ī*, the letter *ṣa*, and the letter *ṇa*;
thus it is.
By the four syllables that constitute the word *bhīṣaṇa*, there is the intended expression of the four descents beginning with Dhruva. (p.
568) Regarding the three descents intended by the word *bhadra*, the syllable *bha* refers to the seventh descent known as Kapila.
He bestows the supreme, divine accomplishment consisting of perfect discernment.
The Lord Kapila is proclaimed by means of the syllable *si* (the giver of perfection).
As for the syllable *da*, it refers to the twenty-sixth incarnation known as Dattātreya;
indeed, the Blessed One Dattātreya is described by the syllable *dat*. (56–32)

The letter *ra* is intended to signify the twenty-fifth incarnation known as Śāntātmā; he is praised by that very letter because he is the fire of destruction for the defects [of the world]. This refers to the two incarnations expressed by the term "death of death" (*mṛtyumṛtyu*).
First, the word "Death" (mṛtyu) refers to the twenty-eighth incarnation known by the names Ekaśṛṅga and Tanu, which are synonyms for the Fish (Matsya).
"Time is declared to be Time; Pradhāna is the supreme Prakṛti. (56.33)
The male principle residing therein is the Abode of Truth (Ṛtadhāman), who is the Vairāja and possesses four states;
he who, while sustaining the world within the body, is called Śaṅkha and Mīna. (56.34)
The God whose body has a single horn is described by the colors of death;

he is the primary one, whose form is truth, the Vairāja who causes the world to shine, and who is the referent of the second term "death" (mṛtyu) as the twenty-fourth incarnation known as Lokanātha. (56.35)
The Lord of Gods, the Protector of the World, the Great Sovereign, who possesses four states of existence—
[it should be understood that] by the three syllables *bha*, *da*, and *ra* in the word *Bhadra*, the intention is to signify the three incarnations beginning with Kapila.
It is quite clear that by the two occurrences of the word "mṛtyu," two incarnations are intended. Thus, by the word *jvalat*, eleven incarnations are indicated; by the word *sarvatomukha*, ten;
by the word *nṛsiṃha*, nine; by the word *bhīṣaṇa*, four; and by the word *bhadra*, three.
By the term *mṛtyumṛtyu*, two [deities] are indicated; thus, it has been explained that the six words beginning with *jvalat* refer to thirty-nine descents. (p.
569) "The one designated by the letter of death (*mṛtyu*) is even beyond the previous world. (56.36)

Thus, the supreme *rīti* based on phonemes has been demonstrated to you. Listen once more, O best of sages, to the description of another greatness of the mantra through the remainder of this chapter. (56-37)
This [mantra], when recited in reverse syllable by syllable, is called the Vaikuṇṭha weapon;
this same [mantra], when recited in reverse letter by letter, is known as the Nārāyaṇa weapon.
That which consists of the vowels in reverse order, possessing the form of a *saṃhitā* word, is the great weapon of Nṛsiṃha known as the "saw of claws. (56.39)
Varuṇa, who is free from measurement and established as the fire of time, is likewise immeasurable; such is the third syllable that has been proclaimed. (56.40)
The first [syllable] is "sūkṣmasthaḥ," the second is "sūkṣmaḥ," and "saṃsthitaḥ" is the fire of time (kālapāvaka).
"Varuṇaḥ" is the pair of subtle [elements]; this is declared as the seventh syllable. (56.41)
"Sūkṣmastha, gopana, paścāt, varuṇa, bhuvanāśraya, varajā, and āra—this is declared to be the Nārasiṃha weapon. (56.42)
This nine-syllable [mantra] is preeminent; therein, that which is produced in reverse order is the weapon-mantra (*astra*), while the syllables beginning with *nārasiṃha* are highly praised. (56.43)
In that regard, due to the reversal of the vowels, the weapon-mantra (astra) consists of the letters beginning with *tvatima* and ending with *hā*.
It is all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*), the support of nectar (*sāmṛtādhāra*), and it is secret (*gopana*); moreover, that mantra consists of two syllables.
In that regard, regarding the reversal of vowels, Gopana is the protector of the virtuous.
Whatever weapon has been proclaimed everywhere in reverse order,
its pacification is proclaimed in each instance by means of the direct (anuloma) order.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Meaning of the Nārasiṃha Anuṣṭubh Mantra," in the Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā, a secret doctrine within the venerable Pāñcarātra Tantra.
From the beginning, verse number 3631:
The fifty-seventh chapter, titled "An Exposition on the Meaning of the Jyotiścakra Mantra.
Meditated upon even once, it swiftly destroys a multitude of sins numbering many millions.
We meditate upon that divine splendor of the god Sudarśana.
First, in the detailed exposition of the meaning of the Gāyatrī, Ahirbudhnya establishes that the word "tat" (that) refers to the Sudarśana discus, which is of the nature of the Lord’s volition:
ahirbudhnyaḥ— [text follows]
As for the triad of lights previously demonstrated in the circle of lights:
that light which is named Sāvitra is called by the name Sāvitrī. (57-1)
Listen attentively as I correctly explain its commentary;
that which was described as "volition" (saṃkalpa) is called Sudarśana. (57.2)
That prosperity of the Great Power of Viṣṇu, which is born from a ten-millionth part [of her essence], she expands and extends through states that consist of both the pure and the impure. || 57-3 ||
At the time of reabsorption, He indeed protects her again;
He protects her in each respective place through His sustaining nature within the portion of manifestation.
Furthermore, as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and again by way of those respective meanings,
[this is explained] in the twenty-third chapter by twenty-five verses beginning from the second half of the forty-fourth verse up to the first half of the sixty-ninth verse.
This wheel of light has been illustrated by means of verses;
therefore, the mental resolve directed toward it is indeed called the supreme Vaiṣṇava [meditation]. (57.5)

The word *savitṛ* refers to the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) as characterized by qualities such as being the cause of the universe and the bestower of enjoyment and liberation; for He impels all activities and brings forth the entire world.
The word *avatīrṇa* is derived from the root *av-tṛ*, meaning "to go" or "beauty," and from the root *tṛ*, meaning "to give. (57-6)
For he has gone everywhere, protecting all; he is supreme, beloved for his six qualities, and the giver of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; thus he is etymologically defined as Savitṛ. (57–7)

The word *vareṇya* has the sense of being an object of worship; it is derived from *varaiḥ neyam* (to be led by the excellent ones), thus *vareṇya*. Alternatively, *vara* is said to mean "proclaimers," so *vareṇya* means that which is to be chosen (*varaṇīya*) by them. Or else, it is that which leads to the Supreme (*vara*). || 57–8 ||

The word *bharga* refers to the specific quality of the Sudarśana discus intended by that [word] "that" (*tat*): "Bharga is declared to be splendor (*tejas*), power (*prabhāva*), and the nature of the agent;
it supports this entire world and also sustains the lords. (57–9)
It delights all that [is experienced], bestows the desired object, leads even to its destruction, and completely severs bondage. (57.10)
It burns away all suffering and likewise consumes time;
therefore, they know the wondrous *saṃkalpa* (volition) of Viṣṇu as the supreme *bharga*.
p. 573) The word *deva* refers to the Supreme Self, characterized by qualities such as luminosity (*dyotana*).
Illuminating all states of being, shining forth eternally by itself, it purifies all ignorance and the entire world. (57.12)
Therefore, all this is woven therein like a thread through a gem;
from here, O Worthy of Praise, the entire expanse of space is stretched out.
"Devah" refers to Viṣṇu, the eternal Supreme Self.
The phrase "dhīmahi" has the sense of being intent upon a specific knowledge consisting of worship;
here, "dhī" means knowledge, reflection, and likewise meditative cultivation. (57–14)
Having first ascertained the meaning of the third quarter, the collective meaning of the entire *gāyatrī* is ascertained:
"Dhīḥ" refers to activities preceded by intelligence, while "pracodana" refers to the act of impelling.
He who is the all-powerful Savitṛ and the god who consists of pure consciousness; || 57-15 ||
And he who is the omniscient Lord, who impels each and every thought, the imperishable cause of the acts of creation, maintenance, dissolution, and protection; || 57-16 ||
We worship the resolve of that god as the name Bharga;
such is the meaning of the Gāyatrī when it is singing for the sake of protection. (57-17)
A brief description of the greatness of the Gāyatrī:
One who is disciplined in both twilights attains supreme Brahminhood;
for a practitioner, it is mastered in just one month through a thousand recitations performed externally. (57–18)
The three imperishable Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛtis), which are fulfilled by the syllable Oṃ, protect one from all great evil and from every kind of harm. (57.19)

This triad—consisting of the three-footed [Gāyatrī] and the statement "this is it"—is supremely purifying. Following an exposition on the essential nature of the three *vyāhṛtis*, there is a concise illumination of their meaning:
"That existence which belongs to all beings is the supreme and inferior power of Viṣṇu. (57.20)
Having herself become the power of being (*bhavatī*), she is designated as "Bhūḥ," and she herself becomes this entire world for as far as this world extends. (57.21)
