She is called Bhū by the wise, for she protects the world; she constantly brings forth for the virtuous that which is more excellent, namely the enjoyments known as liberation. (57.22)
That [fire] is described by the wise as the sacrificial ladle (sruva), and from it arises the Vyāhṛti consisting of speech;
this is but a mere indication of the directions regarding the weapons, such as the Brahmaśiras, which are hidden within the Gāyatrī mantra.
The Brahmadaṇḍa weapon [is formed] foot by foot; "tat" is the Ṛc in reverse order. (57.23)
The missile named Brahmaśiras is recited word by word;
the Brāhma missile consists of its syllables produced in reverse order according to their vowels.
It is proclaimed as the Subrahmāstra, the destroyer of all other weapons; Ānanda is Varuṇa, and he who possesses that [Ānanda] is Varuṇa, who has four states of being.
The third is Sāprameya; likewise, there is Vyāpaka residing in Śaṅkha.
Also Sānanda and Varuṇa, and Sāprameya who possesses the four states of existence. || 57-26 ||

The supreme seven-syllable weapon-mantra of the god Śaṅkha, which is always [present], is declared to be superior even to the Brāhma-mantra; it is produced from the reversal of its own vowels. (57.27)
But that bliss alone is remembered as the divine single syllable (ekākṣara).
Such is the extent of the distinction shown for this Ṛgvedic verse of Sāvitrī.
In the determination of the meaning of the *triṣṭubh* verse beginning with "jātavedase," there is a description of the meanings of the words *jātavedas* and *soma*.
Listen now to the meaning of this *triṣṭubh* verse beginning with "jātavedasaḥ."
For he who always knows everything that has arisen within every single being, [is a knower of the Self]. || 57-29 ||
Consciousness, which is born and perfectly established by its own nature, always possesses existence as its Veda—a great power characterized by bliss and vibration. (57.30)
That Goddess, the refuge of the worlds, has eternally manifested;
the Veda is said to be discernment (vicāraṇa), and discernment is manifold action (vividhā kriyā). || 57-31 ||
The manifestation of activity belonging to that Viṣṇu is his state of being the creator of all;
he is the omniscient, the omnipotent, and the maker of all, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). || 57-32 ||
Jātavedas is designated as the Self, and Soma is proclaimed [to be that same Self];
for, under the influence of ignorance, it is constantly born while residing within all wombs. (57.33)
The phrase "sunavāma" (let us press [the Soma]) has as its purpose the induction of the fitness for being subordinate to the Lord within the bound soul (*baddhātman*).
Here, that induction of fitness is expressed by the root *su* (to press).
To state that this induction of fitness consists in the discrimination between the self and the primordial matter (*prakṛti*), the intended meaning is [as follows]:
In the example accessible through the word *soma*, there is instruction on the distinction that the term *soma* refers specifically to the juice produced by pressing. (57.34)
The sacrifice can only be performed with Soma that has become *rasa* (essence).
This meaning of the sentence arising from the preceding quarter-verse contains an implicit simile. (57.35)
The application of a point learned from an illustration to the subject under discussion:
"Just as they press the Soma for Jātavedas at the sacrifice, so the Sage, desiring to give himself, offers his own self to the Supreme Self. (57.36)

Through discriminative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*), one distinguishes [the Self] by its own nature from the body, the senses, the mind, the vital breath, and the qualities (*guṇa*), which arise from the causes of equilibrium and disequilibrium. (57.37)

Having thus distinguished that the fruit for one who sacrifices with the self as the oblation— as described— is the manifestation of the eightfold qualities consisting in the realization of one's own true nature, [the Lord] gave himself to this Jātavedas.
Abiding in that, having become one-minded with it, he then perceives through his own [nature].
By means of this alternative formulation, it is indicated that the very meaning of the word *namaḥ* is intended here in the first quarter [of the verse]:
"This is precisely the meaning of the word *namaḥ*, shown here by way of another method."

"Understand from me the meaning of the second quarter [of this chapter], which demonstrates how the Supreme Person effects the removal of bondage— that is, the connection with *prakṛti* which obstructs one's own attainment. (57.39)
He who behaves like an enemy is indeed called an *arātīya*;
that is declared to be bondage, which has its basis in false knowledge. (57.40)
His existence is known through the Veda; his attachment to the qualities is beginningless.
That eternal Jātavedas [Fire] desired to accept Soma as his son. (57.41)

Let it itself burn away that existence of bondage which is its opposite; having bound that existence consisting of attachment to the qualities (*guṇas*) with great firmness, the latter half of the verse establishes the previously stated meaning by means of an illustration. (57.42)
He carries us across all the difficult points of the principles that are to be abandoned.
[This is] the justification for the word *agni*, occurring in the latter part of the compound, as referring to the Supreme Person:
"And he is described here too by the word *agni* as Jātavedas. (57.43)
The word *agni* (fire) is etymologically defined as that which leads (*nayati*) the entire world, having come near it, into its own acceptance (*aṅgīkāram*). 57.44.
The fire that leads the individual soul approaching its own self to its own supreme state—
that Jātavedas carries us across all difficulties.
Regarding the fourth quarter of the verse which focuses on the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), the meaning of the sentence is described here: "The illustration is the great ocean named Sindhu;
just as a navigator would ferry a man standing in a boat across it by means of that boat. (57.46)
From the pair of words beginning with *durita*, in the sense of "crossing over," we have *duritātyaya*.
*Durita* is said to be misfortune (*dauḥsthya*) arising from wind, rain, and so forth. (57–47)
"He is described as one who, having repeatedly transcended all evils, has completely cast off every misfortune such as wind, rain, and the like. (57.48)
Just as a sailor carries a man standing on a boat across the ocean by means of that boat, so too is the application of this analogy to the subject at hand:
"In this way, the Blessed One, Agni Jātavedas, is Hari himself. (57.49)
Avoiding all evil—the mass of afflictions that obstructs liberation—and every difficult path, one should cross over to the sequence of reality. (57.50)
In this matter, based on the analogy of the boat, the means alone is the sphere of action for the person; however, the other task belongs to Hari, just as it does to the boatman. (57–51)
In this mantra, there is a brief indication of the nature of the hidden weapons beginning with Pāvaka; that which is recited word by word in reverse order is called the Pāvaka weapon.
That Āgneya [section] concerning Jātavedas is established quarter by quarter, according to its syllables.
This [mantra], when recited in reverse syllable by syllable, is declared to be extremely fiery (atyāgneya).
It consists of four movements (caturgati), is immeasurable, and possesses its own vitality; furthermore, it has four movements. (57–53)
The two subtle ones are immeasurable; the fourfold course is immeasurable.
The fourfold course is immeasurable, as are Varāha and Śaṅkha. (57.54)
One should meditate upon the immeasurable mass as unified within the *piṇḍa*;
that immeasurable fourfold state is the primordial deity, the fourfold state. (57–55)
This [verse] is the reverse of the latter half; now hear that which arises from the first half:
"Bliss alone, joined with the two subtle [energies], and from the immeasurable. (57–56)
One should remember the four states of existence, the immeasurable Varāha, and Śaṅkha; and one should contemplate the immeasurable Piṇḍastha as unified with the three.
Caturgati, Sādideva, Sānanda, and likewise Varuṇa—this is the arrangement of those born in the eastern half, beginning with Caturgati and Sādideva. (57–58)
The two *hana*s, the armor (*varma*), the weapon (*sāstra*), and likewise the wife of Agni (*agnijāyā*) at the end;
this is known as the fifteen-syllable mantra, consisting of vowels in reverse order. (57–59)

One should know that the three-syllable mantra ending with the eight-syllable *hanat* consists of the vowel produced in reverse order; furthermore, it shall consist of two phonemes and occupy the upper position.
Furthermore, hear again of their forms in the first half, which consists of a single vowel: Aprameya, then Sānanda, and Varuṇa; this mantra consists of two syllables. (57–61)
Ānanda, that which is the single *trivarṇaka* formed by combining [the previous three] in the first half, this Ānanda alone is traditionally known as its reverse order. (57–62)
These two [verses] are in reverse order and consist of all-encompassing peace and well-being.
(p. 580) Thus, this manner of the *triṣṭubh* meter has been shown to you in brief. (57–63)

In the explanation of the meaning of the *anuṣṭubh* verse beginning with "triyambakam," the term *triyambaka* was stated to refer to the Supreme Person endowed with the powers of knowledge and action;
now, listen to the supreme, purifying method of this *anuṣṭubh*.
Desire, declaration, and action—these three are the mothers of the world. || 57-64 ||
He in whom there exist the three powerful powers that bring about the world—knowledge, will, and action—is to be known as Tryambaka (the Three-Eyed One). || 57-65 ||
The definition of the meaning of the word "yajāmahe" (we sacrifice):
the root *yaji* is the relinquishing of a substance with reference to a certain deity.
The definition of the meaning of the word "sugandhi" (fragrant).
He who possesses a beautiful fragrance is called "sugandhi" (fragrant). || 57-66 ||
Everything that indicates excellence is called "fragrant" (sugandhi),
for it perfumes all principles with its own splendor when it is offered as an oblation.
That which perfumes by means of its penetration and transforms everything into its own nature—namely, all the elements such as earth and the rest, including smell and the other qualities. (57–68)
He under whose control the beautiful [senses] abide, that ruling deity is known as Sugandhi; he is the self of knowledge, the knower of all, and the subduer of all.
An Exposition on the Meaning of the Term *Puṣṭivardhana*:
Prosperity (*puṣṭi*) is declared to be manifestation (*bhūti*), which consists of both the existent and the non-existent;
it is the power (*śakti*) of Viṣṇu, composed of Viṣṇu himself. He (Viṣṇu) increases that [power] by his own self. (57–70)
Having brought it forth through volition and expanded it in various forms,
and having maintained and restrained it, he then withdraws it again.
Therefore, that Blessed One Viṣṇu is described as the "Increaser of Prosperity" (Puṣṭivardhana);
by means of describing the meaning of the words, it is demonstrated that the first half [of the Veda] is intent upon the offering of great oblations to the Blessed One.
It consists of will, knowledge, and action; it is called Śobhana and is beloved by the world.
He whose sovereignty is made known by his own form, who is pure, consisting of pure consciousness,
supreme, the Lord of all worlds, the Puruṣa with lotus-like eyes.
"Having aimed at our own deity, we shall sacrifice the supreme substance called 'one's own self' (svātman)"—such is the meaning of the first part of the mantra. (57–74)
The explanation of the meaning of the second half [of the verse]:

The word "death" (mṛtyu), which has been etymologically defined here in the context of defining the death of death, refers today to one who has renounced both self and what belongs to the self within the Supreme Self, the Divine. (57–75)
May I be liberated from death and from cyclic existence, that great ocean of manifold sufferings,
just as a ripe cucumber is released from its bond without effort.
"Just as he is liberated from death, may I likewise be released from bondage; having performed this renunciation, he hopes for stability in me, the Immortal. (57–77)
From that immortal Brahman, to whomsoever I have given myself, may I never be released from him; may my state be one of security.

The meaning of the *anuṣṭubh* verses has been declared as follows: "The auspicious state consisting of Brahman is proclaimed [in this mantra], demonstrating that, according to the intended purport (*tātparya*), the fruit characterized by the seeker’s attainment of similarity with Brahman is what is meant to be expressed."
That which was explained as the triad of lights is indeed this triad of meters.
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Meaning of the Mantras of the Jyotiścakra," in the Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā, a secret doctrine within the Śrī Pāñcarātra Tantra.
From the beginning, verse 3710: The fifty-eighth chapter, titled "An Exposition on the Meaning of the Pañcahotṛ Mantras.
Even a single meditation [upon Him] swiftly destroys a multitude of sins numbering in the tens of millions.
We meditate upon that divine splendor of the god Sudarśana.
Ahirbudhnya:
(1) The Daśahotṛ, the Caturhotṛ, and likewise the Pañcahotṛ; the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ and the Saptahotṛ—these are declared to be the five Hotṛs. || 58-1 ||

In this regard, the following should be noted: in the twenty-third chapter, after the description of the wheel of light (*jyotiścakra*) with its hundred spokes, the wheel of Brahman (*brahmacakra*) was described.
Therein, the meaning of the mantras of the wheel of light was explained by means of the preceding chapter.
Now, the description of the meaning of the mantras of the Brahma-cakra, which follows in sequence, is introduced here.

Within that Brahma-cakra, many mantras are contained: the five *hotṛ*s together with the planets (*sagrahāḥ pañcahotāraḥ*), the ritual materials (*saṃbhārāḥ*), the wives of the gods (*devapatnyaḥ*), the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇāḥ*), the hearts (*hṛdayāni*), and the hundred *rudras* (*śatarudrāṇi*).
Such are these [mantras].

Among them, the first five anuvākas, beginning with "Consciousness is the ladle" (*cittiḥ sruk*), which are recited in the third prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, are [to be used] respectively by the Daśahotṛ and the others.
These are intended by five terms, because they designate the sacrificial implements characterized by the numbers ten and so forth, respectively.
The sixth section, "Speech is the Hotṛ," is another Ṣaḍḍhotṛ formula. Although [the text says] "sūryaṃ te... [and so on].

In the fourth section, "The Eye" (*cakṣuḥ*), the implements for the oblation are not expounded; nevertheless, because they are expounded in the other four sections as well, such usage occurs due to their preponderance according to the principle of creation (*sṛṣṭinyāya*). For this very reason, it has been said by the poets as well: "A single flaw is submerged in a confluence of virtues, like [the dark spot] of the moon."

"Like a mark upon rays. These five, beginning with the *daśahotṛ*, are designated by the two names *caturhotṛ*. Where these two words appear in the singular number, they primarily designate only the second and third sections (*anuvāka*) as previously described; however, where...

These two [terms] end in the plural; therein, by the principle of the inherence of gender (*liṅgasamavāyanyāya*), they function metaphorically (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*) to denote the collection [of mantras] beginning with the *daśahotr*. And this being the case, by that very same principle, it would follow that the words *daśahotṛ*, *ṣaḍḍhotṛ*, and *saptahotṛ* would also denote their respective collections.
Their absence [in other texts] is established; rather, it is the words *caturhotṛ* and *pañcahotṛ* themselves that convey them.

This has been explained in detail in the second and third chapters of the second book of the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, and is thus easily understood from that source. Likewise, regarding those very mantras...
The manifold excellence of these [mantras], such as their being the cause of the creation of the world,

and the specific applications of each according to their role as means for attaining various fruits, have been elaborated upon in that very [work] and are not further detailed here. In that regard, these mantras are [to be understood] individually:

They consist of three parts: the first part explains the means for the oblation (*homa*); the second part, however, is the section on the *graha* (libation) devoid of the *svāhākāra*; and the third part is the *svāhākāra* itself. In that regard, within the first section (*anuvāka*) consisting of fifteen sentences, beginning with "The mind is the ladle" (*cittiḥ sruc*), there are ten sentences.
The first part [consists of] the preceding [verses]; the subsequent ones constitute the *graha* portion. At the end is the utterance of *svāhā*.
In the second anuvāka, which consists of ten sentences beginning with "Pṛthivī is the Hotṛ," the first part consists of four sentences; the remainder is the *graha*. At the end...

The *svāhākāra* (the utterance "Svāhā"). In the third anuvāka, consisting of eight sentences, beginning with "Agni is the Hotṛ," the first half consists of the first portion; the second half is the *graha*; at the end is the *svāhākāra*. In the fourth anuvāka, consisting of nine sentences, beginning with "The Sun is your eye," the first six sentences constitute the first portion; the latter [portion]...

The *graha* [offering] is followed at the end by the utterance of *svāhā*. In the fifth section (*anuvāka*), which consists of thirteen sentences beginning with "The Mahāhaviḥ Hotṛ," the division into six sentences and so forth is as before.
The sixth section is similar to the fourth section.

Regarding the cause for the application of the term "graha" (cup/drawing) in the latter part of all these mantras, it is stated in the first section of the second chapter of the second book of the *Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa*:
"Prajāpati desired, 'May I create offspring. He beheld this Daśahotṛ [formula]. Him..."

Having mentally impelled [the creation], he offered oblations into a clump of *darbha* grass. Thereupon, indeed, he created offspring. Once created, they departed from him. He seized them with a *graha* (an offering-ladle or vessel). That is why the *graha* is called a *graha*. Thus it has been explained. The meaning therein is as follows: once upon a time, Prajāpati performed the creation of offspring.

Desiring [progeny], he examined the means for it in the Vedas and directly realized the mantra known as the *daśahotṛ*. Having uttered that mantra mentally, he offered clarified butter (*ājya*) into a clump of *darbha* grass at a certain spot. Then, by the power of that oblation, he created the progeny he had desired. Those created beings—
Devoid of affection for this Prajāpati, the subjects departed.

And that Prajāpati, having acquired the power through the recitation of the portions of the *grahas* as previously described, took back the subjects who had fled. Therefore, because it is the means for seizing (*grahaṇa*) the subjects, the *graha* is so called.

"Accomplished" (niṣpanna): this is the basis for the application of the word *graha* within the portion concerning the cups (*graha*) included in the *daśahotṛ* mantra. In the four subsequent sections (*anuvāka*), that basis is, respectively, the state of being the means for taking up the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the *cāturmāsya*, the *paśubandha*, and the *jyotiṣṭoma*.
This should be understood as it has been elaborated in that very second section (anuvāka).

Thus, Āpastamba has demonstrated the rules for the practical application (*prayoga*) of these mantras—which are intended by either the term *caturhotṛ* or *pañcahotṛ*—as follows: "These are the *caturhotṛ*s..."
Where they serve the purpose of oblation (*homa*), they should be employed with the planets (*sagraha*) and accompanied by the exclamation *svāhā* (*sasvāhākāra*);
where they do not serve the purpose of oblation, they are without planets and without the *svāhā* exclamation, and so forth.

Therefore, in this context, these [mantras], which have been assigned in the twenty-third [chapter] as constituent parts of the Brahma-wheel machine (*brahmacakrayantra*), [are to be understood accordingly].

Since it might follow that mantras—being devoid of the *graha* portions because they do not serve as offerings (*ahomārthatva*)—should be excluded from being parts of the yantra, an exception (*pratiprasava*) is made right there by the statement: "Outside this wheel, the five *hotṛ*s are remembered together with their *grahas*. Thus, these [mantras] are indeed used together with the *grahas* when drawing the yantra.
Regarding "viniyoga": the fifty-eighth chapter is commenced for the purpose of determining the meaning of those mantras. (p.
584) That austerity consisting of knowledge belonging to Viṣṇu, who desired to create the universe...
That volition (saṃkalpa) is defined by the Hotṛ priests in the form of ritual action (kratu). || 58-2 ||
Even now, applying himself to the investigation of each [topic], this yogi indeed performs those various auspicious sacrifices consisting of knowledge (jñānamaya). (58.3)
An indication of the specific mantras intended by the terms *daśahotr* and so forth: (1) "Consciousness is the ladle; the *daśahotr* is this cause of the *agnihotra*.
That which begins with 'the earth' is declared the *caturhotr*. (58–4)
(2) He is the source of both the New Moon and the Full Moon sacrifices; (3) he is Agnihotṛ and Pañcahotṛ, and he originates from the Cāturmāsya rites. 58–5.
The Sūrya-hoṭṛ and that Gārhapatya-hoṭṛ are the cause of the animal sacrifice;
these two are determined as the Ṣaḍḍhoṭṛs in the Veda by the best of sages. (58–6)

(5) (The Mahāhavis and the Saptahotṛ are the causes of the Jyotiṣṭoma. 1. As for the authority for the Daśahotṛ mantra being the cause of the Agnihotra: "Having drawn [the butter] with that [mantra], one should offer the Agnihotra; thus one offers it as something already born."
This is the Śruti (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, 2.2.1).

2. As for the authority for the Caturhotṛ-mantra being the cause of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, [it is stated]: "Prajāpati desired, 'May I create the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. He [created] this..."
"He beheld the Caturhotṛ [offering]. Having pursued it with his mind, he offered it in the Āhavanīya fire.

From that, indeed, he brought forth the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.2.1)—this is the Śruti. Likewise, here too, he desired, "May I create the Cāturmāsya sacrifices," and he [beheld] this...

"He beheld the Pañcahotṛ; having pursued it with his mind, he offered it in the Āhavanīya fire. From that, indeed, he created the Cāturmāsya sacrifices"—this Śruti, recited in that very context, should be understood as the authoritative source.

Likewise, in this case as well, the following scriptural passage (*śruti*) cited in that very context should be understood: "He desired, 'May I create the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*). He perceived this *Ṣaḍḍhotṛ* [offering]. Having recited it mentally, he offered it into the *Āhavanīya* fire. From that, indeed, he created the animal sacrifice."

Although this half-verse is not found in all extant Mātṛkā manuscripts, it has been inserted here by me through my own inference; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of incompleteness. Furthermore, the authority for the Saptahotṛ-mantra being the cause of the Jyotiṣṭoma is the scriptural statement: "He desired, 'May I create the Soma-sacrifice.'"
"He beheld this Saptahotṛ [formula]; having pursued it with his mind, he offered it in the Āhavanīya fire. Thereby, indeed, he brought forth the Soma sacrifice"—this is the Śruti to be understood.
(p. 586) Now follows the promise to describe the meaning of the aforementioned mantras.
Now, O Nārada, listen as the meaning of the Daśahotṛ and the others is described.

First, in the determination of the meaning of the Daśahotṛ mantras, there is the presentation of the meanings of the terms beginning with *citti*: "Citta" is known as the intellect (*buddhi*), which is the cause of determination;
"ahaṃkāra," however, is the mind (*manas*), which is the cause of self-conceit (*abhimāna*). (58–8)
The faculty called mind (manas) is the cause of conceptualization and discursive thought;
that which is called speech (vāk) is the uttered voice, taking the form of "let it be so. (58–59)
*Ādhītam* is indeed the directing of speech, which is called study (*adhyayana*);
*ketaḥ* is declared to be knowledge, the comprehension of that which is recited. (58.10)

That which is cognized, which is to be uttered, and which falls within the scope of definitive determination—that is declared to be the organ of speech; and Sarasvatī is that which is manifested by it. (58.11)
He who protects that speech by speaking it well is called the Lord of Speech (vākyapati).
That which is said to be the cause for the engagement in utterance is effort (prayatna). (58–12)
That breath is the *sāman*, which is said to be the excellence of its utterance.
This is the demonstration of the grounds for the designations such as "Ten Hotṛs" (*daśahotr*);
the names "Ten Hotṛs" and so forth are designations for the implements of the sacrifice. (58–13)
Due to the distinction between action and manifestation, the power of the Blessed One is twofold for Viṣṇu, who acts as the sole refuge of the world and possesses all powers—
that divine Vaiṣṇavī energy which follows after all states of being. (58.14)
One part of that [Lord Hari] is called action (*kriyā*), which consists of His instruments for performing deeds;
another part of Him is known as manifestation (*vibhūti*), and it is perceived here as the world. (58.15)

The nature of action as being of the form of volition (saṃkalpa) and its status as an instrument for purposeful activity is stated as follows: "Volition is declared to be Viṣṇu’s instrument for purposeful activity;
and action is the determination of that volition," and so forth.
The phrase beginning with "so be it" (evam astu) and ending with the word "thus" (iti) is called the conclusion (vākyānta). || 58-16 ||
The function of the intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), and mind (manas) with respect to sound is intended here;
it is declared to be threefold. Thus it has been stated by you, O Stabdha. || 58-17 ||

The definition of sacrificial implements such as the *sruk* ladle, as stated in the passage beginning with "citti," extending from the intellect (*buddhi*) up to the final cognition (*miti*), consists of both the form of the substrate and its function,
within the extensive sacrifice known as the "Arrangement of the Universe" belonging to Harimedhas. (58.18)

Through the state of being the *sruk* and the *ājya*, and by virtue of the nature of the fire as the *upavaktṛ*, the Brahman priest is remembered as the *upavaktṛ*; the granting of permission (*anujñā*) is remembered as the proclamation (*pravacana*). (58–19)
The word known as that which is to be uttered is called "Agni";
the act of uttering it, when studied, is sung of as "Barhis. (58-20)
The effort that is his cause is called the vital breath (prāṇa), which is said to be the oblation;
speech uttered is the altar, and the bearer is sung as the Hotṛ priest. (58.21)
That which is the equality of the chanting is *sāman*, and he is called the *adhvaryu*.
This is the injunction for the knowledge of the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice known as the "Arrangement of the Universe" (*jagadvidhāna*), as it has been described;
thus, the "Arrangement of the Universe" is endowed with ten instruments. (58–22)
Whatever Vaiṣṇava sacrifice has been performed, one should contemplate it today while uttering some common or Vedic speech. (58.23)
Having attained the state of a Vaiṣṇava, one should contemplate this mantra;
by means of defining its essential meaning,
the focus on the offering of oneself as the oblation to the planetary portion is made clear.
"O Vācaspati, O Vidhi, O Nāman"—thus its meaning is stated. || 58-24 ||
Speech is indeed the supreme power of Viṣṇu, consisting of the Brahman of sound;
its lord is Vācaspati, and he is called Vidhi because he ordains (vidadhāti). || 58-25 ||
Because it bends everything toward itself, it is called *nāman*;
O Blessed One, we shall worship that Name, which is synonymous with the state of total prostration.
"And may you, O Ordainer, grant us a mind that is inclined [toward you].
The Sage speaks this very thing again as the surrender of one's own self. (58.27)
The determination that the Blessed One alone is the recipient of the fruit arising from the offering of one's own self as an oblation is as follows:
"May that Vācaspati, mentioned previously, drink Soma—resembling the juice of the Soma plant—which is his own essence, as if it were offered by me to him in a sacrifice. (58.28)

Having drunk that which is appropriate for a state of dependence characterized by being subordinate to that which defines its own nature, may He bestow upon us that very *nṛmṇa* (strength/wealth) which He has bestowed;
that *nṛmṇa*, whose form is His grace, is to be meditated upon by men. (58.29)

The removal of the suspicion that the offering of oneself as an oblation might be for one's own sake is expressed by "svāhā," which is the renunciation of one's own self; thus it becomes a "svāhuta" (well-offered).
In the Caturhotṛ-mantra as well, it is precisely the sacrifice previously described that is presented through a different formulation.
And this very sacrifice is intended here as the fourfold *caturhotṛ*. (58.30)
Demonstrating that the words *pṛthivī*, *dyu*, and *rudra* refer to *prakṛti*, *puruṣa*, and *kāla* respectively:
"That *pṛthivī* which consists of the expansion of the universe is known as *prakṛti*;
*puruṣa* is declared to be *dyu*, for he shines by means of his own consciousness. (58.31)
He obstructs those two at the time of dissolution and causes them to flow forth at the time of emergence;
thus Time is called Rudra, the uniter and the disuniter.
The word *Bṛhaspati* refers to the Blessed Lord by virtue of His being the Lord of Śrī:
"That Power is designated as *Bṛhat* (the Great), from which everything is nourished (*bṛṃhayate*).
Janārdana, the God of gods, is the Lord (*pati*) of that [Power]; thus He is Bṛhaspati. (58.33)
In the determination of the meaning of the term *vācovīrya* within the context of the planetary divisions (*grahabhāga*), it is demonstrated that it refers to the Lord’s exertion toward creation:
"The vitality of speech is breath; the supreme exertion of Viṣṇu is creation."
By the term "most fully gathered" (*saṃbhṛtatama*), there is the intention to express that the effort of creation has as its object all things;
and it is most fully gathered precisely because its object is all things. (58.34)

By the principle that "the vital breath is the oblation," it is intended here as well that the very same vital breath mentioned previously is the oblation; thus, the vital breath is accepted as the oblation in this context.
This demonstrates that the remainder of the mantra is devoted to the prayer for the bliss consisting of the great essence of servitude (*dāsya*).
"You, who are Vācaspati himself, shall be invited and honored today. (58.35)
Therefore, for this sacrificer, bestow today the desirable, the excellent, and the bliss of heaven;
prepare it so that he may drink the Soma as before. (58.36)
The final sentence of the mantra is intent upon the prayer for the cessation of obstacles:
"May the Unborn Indra, bestowing nourishment (*irā*), produce me today as one fit for sensory power and for the capacity to attain Brahman. (58.37)
An Exposition on the Meaning of the Pañcahotṛ Mantra:
This [sacrifice] designated as the Caturhotṛ is now declared to be the Pañcahotṛ.
Agni, who was previously described, is celebrated as that Hotṛ. (58–38)
The two Aśvins are the life-breath of knowledge, for they pervade the entire world;
the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ are proclaimed as the two Adhvaryus. || 58-39 ||

Tvaṣṭṛ is designated as Saṃkalpa (volition), since all that is to be fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ [proceeds from it]; Maitrī (friendliness) is designated as Mitra, and compassion belongs to Harimedhas (Viṣṇu). || 58-40 ||
The application of the portion of the *graha* as a means for the self-sacrifice (*ātmayāga*) is as follows:
(p. 591) this mantra beginning with "Soma" is prescribed for that sacrifice.
In that context, there is a distinction between the meanings of the words *soma* and *śukra*, which appear both in the genitive and in the nominative cases.
The two words ending in the genitive case, *soma* and *śukra*, denote the essence of the creeper (*latāsāra*). || 58-41 ||
The other two words containing the term "self" (*ātman*) are stated to be the reason for the preceding [statement]: namely,

that the individual soul (*jīva*), intended by the word *soma* in the nominative case, is superior to the essence of the creeper (*latāsāra*), which is intended by the word *soma* in the genitive case.
This Soma is the life-force of Soma; he is the leader even of the vital breaths. 58-42.
For even if Soma were praised with hymns, he would not please Puruṣottama as much as the individual soul (jīva) when offered as a sacrifice to the Self; indeed, it is superior to that. (58.43)

The justification for that is as follows: the mortal Soma is indeed highly praised, whereas you are immortal and consist of consciousness. This demonstrates the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the term *śukra* when it refers to the individual soul (*jīva*).
It is called *śukra* because of its excessive flow and also because it is the seed of the world. || 58-44 ||
In that context as well, this application of the name of the individual soul has been previously explained;
furthermore, the address "Indra" is an invocation of the Blessed One,
and the address "Indra" is also the recognition of the god Harimedhas.
The term *vātāpi* refers to the Lord’s excellence in the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) characterized by pervasiveness;
for it is said that he is called *vātāpi* because he is pervasive (*vyāpin*) through his own activity (*kriyā*) by means of the wind (*vāta*). (p. 592)
The activity of the source of the world is creation, which is inconceivable and preceded by pervasion.
There is no state whatsoever that is beyond its range.

The term *havanaśrut* signifies one who is intent on taking pleasure in hearing the invocation within his own domain; thus he is called *havanaśrut*, for he hears the invocation with reverence. (58.47)

By means of determining the intended meaning of the two verses beginning with "śrātā," this demonstrates that in all souls whatsoever, there exists the state of servitude (dāsya) produced by the qualities of the Blessed Lord:
"O Indra, O Supreme Ruler, You are the maker who hears our invocation."
These Soma-offerings, supported by their qualities, are our very selves. || 58-48 ||
"May it be well-offered; may this be a well-sacrificed oblation; this indeed is the supreme offering.
Now follows the determination of the meaning of the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ-mantra.
This Pañcahotṛ has been declared; now the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ is being recited. (58–49)

Today, Viṣṇu has attained the state of the sacrificer, the sacrificial animal, the existent being, the self made into an oblation, together with the body and senses, and accompanied by the prepared offering.
He procreates, he delights, he performs sacrifice, and he is described;
the Sun enters this Viṣṇu, who is the cause of visual cognition.
Vāta is the consciousness of that which possesses motion; its movement is declared to be pervasion.
Thus, that shining one is the god Dyaus, whose charioteer is discernment (vijñāna). || 58-52 ||
Looking inward, he is proclaimed as the intermediate space;
bringing all together through the vital breaths, he is the sacrifice by virtue of being the object of worship. (58–53)
The earth, the power of Viṣṇu, expanding by its own splendor, is the fivefold constituent; the vital breath is said to be the back and the head-limb. (58–54)
The self is said to be the internal organ; and the bodies, which exist without beginning or end, are its external limbs. Furthermore, the "grasper" (graha) is now described.
Vācaspati is designated as the Lord of Speech; the Vaiṣṇava power is indeed the act of speech.
That very power is called the sacrificial ladle (juhū), while the vital breath (prāṇa) is proclaimed as the Hotṛ priest and the oblation (āhuti). || 58-59 ||
The gods are said to have increased by assuming various forms such as bodies and so forth;
"erayasva" means impel, for impelling is considered to be the act of *eraṇa*. (58–57)
An Explanation of the Meaning of Another Ṣaḍḍhotṛ Mantra (1):

Now, O Nārada, listen to the determination of another Ṣaḍḍhotṛ. Initiation (*dīkṣā*) is the mental resolve (*mānasa-saṃkalpa*), while the state of speech (*vāg-avasthā*) is known as speech (*vāk*). 58–58.
The waters are said to be Viṣṇu’s compassion; his mind is called desire. Asceticism is designated as discernment, while the Potṛ priest is considered the Abhigara.

1. The *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* mantra is of two kinds: one consists of the fourth *anuvāka*, beginning with "The sun is your eye" (*sūryaṃ te cakṣuḥ*), and the other consists of the sixth *anuvāka*, beginning with "Speech is the hotṛ" (*vāgghotā*). Since the Brāhmaṇa specifies, "Speech is the hotṛ of the six hotṛs," it is that [second one] which is used in the *cāturhotra-cayana*.

It is to be employed [in that context]. However, for the other [type of person], there is an application in the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), because a rule is seen in the *Hotṛ-brāhmaṇa-kāṇḍa*: "One who intends to sacrifice with the animal sacrifice should offer the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula mentally into the *āhavanīya* fire. Thus, in the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), there is an established option.

It should be understood that although the two *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* mantras have been applied separately, because they are both applied together at the *brahmacakra*, an explanation of both types has been provided here.
(p. 594) The determination of the meaning of the *saptahotṛ* mantra.
The wise have declared that the seven hotṛ-priests are the "Great Oblation" (mahāhavis);
the mind is called the oblation, and it is here said that the mind is the oblation.
Its greatness is proclaimed as its vastness of scope;
effort is declared to be the oblation, and here the vital breath (prāṇa) is said to be the oblation. (58–61)
Truthfulness is non-perversion, as well as constant application; splendor and energy are proclaimed here, while its eternity and infallibility are likewise [proclaimed]. (58–62)

In this context, *manas* is said to be *mati*; its non-falling away (from its object) is as described previously. Furthermore, *anādhṛṣya* and *apradhṛṣya* characterize its power (*śakti*) and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).
Potar and Maitrāvaruṇa are traditionally known here as the two Abhigars;
because it is not a matter of great exertion, it is described as "Ayāsya" (the Effortless). || 58-64 ||
The determination of the portions of the planets:
because it takes away or receives worship here, it is described as "Hṛt" (the Heart).
The lineage of disciples and teachers is called the "Daivya-tantu" (the Divine Thread). 58–65.
"Manu is said to be the thread [of creation], representing the prosperity of the lineage of the virtuous.
Heaven and Earth are the parents; these two parents are the lords of the sacred tradition (*śruti*).
O Sage, this section concerning the Hotṛ priests has thus been explained to you in brief. (58–66)
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Meaning of the Pañcahotṛ Mantras," in the Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā, a secret doctrine within the Śrī Pāñcarātra Tantra.
Chapter Fifty-nine, titled "An Exposition on the Meaning of the Puruṣasūkta, Śrīsūkta, and Vārāha Mantras," with a total of 3,776 verses from the beginning.
Meditated upon even once, it swiftly destroys the flood of tens of millions of births;
we meditate upon that divine splendor of the Lord Sudarśana.
In the determination of the causes for defining the meaning of the mantras beginning with the *saṃbhāras* contained within the Brahma-wheel,
Ahirbudhnya says:
"The *saṃbhāras*, the wives of the gods, the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and the hearts."
"Rudras and Brahmas"—this is established by the following scriptural citation. (59-1)

1. In the preceding chapter, the group of officiating priests (*hotṛvarga*), together with the *grahas*, has been explained. Now, the explanation of the *saṃbhāras* and other elements has reached its proper occasion. Nevertheless, because those of keen intellect can understand their meaning through the mere recitation (*nigada*) itself, and for fear of making the treatise too voluminous, they [the *saṃbhāras*, etc. are not treated here.
The intention of the first verse is that the commentary is now being commenced.

Here, we shall demonstrate merely the essential nature of the categories such as the "requisites" (*saṃbhāra*) for the sake of the convenience of those seeking to understand. To explain: the six categories beginning with the requisites are designations for specific types of mantras.

In this context, the eighth section (anuvāka) of the third chapter of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, consisting of twenty-one statements beginning with "Agni by means of the Yajus-formulas," is called the *saṃbhārayajus*; for [it consists of] those materials to be gathered as constituent parts of the sacrifice.
Because the *yajus* stoma and others are recited in that same section (*anuvāka*),
the ninth section consisting of twenty-six sentences beginning with "Senā is Indra’s" is called the "Wives of the Gods" (*devapatnyaḥ*); for it says, "Ūk and Sūnṛtā are the wives of the gods."

Because we observe the application of the indicative marks of the mantras: the tenth section (*anuvāka*), consisting of forty-nine sentences beginning with "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ" (*devasya tvā savituḥ prasave*), is the mantra for receiving the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā-pratigraha-mantra*),
as evidenced by the indicative marks of such mantras as "May King Varuṇa lead you, O goddess Dakṣiṇā, to Agni for gold" (*rājā tvā varuṇo nayatu devi dakṣiṇe'gnaye hiraṇyam*).
By the word "heart" (*hṛdaya*), the collection of mantras known as the *Pañcahotṛ-hṛdaya* is intended.

That consists of one hundred and twenty-eight statements, beginning with the eleventh anuvāka: "He has fully known gold, the dharma, and Vena. This refers to the secret meaning intended by the word "heart."

Because this section serves as its basis, it is designated by the word "Heart" (hṛdaya). For the five Hotṛ-mantras beginning with "Consciousness is the ladle" (cittiḥ sruc) have their heart— their secret essence,
the reality that is the nature of the Supreme Self— clearly and clearly expounded by this section.

For this very reason, this Anuvāka consists of five parts. Among them, the first part—beginning with "Gold is Dharma" (*suvarṇaṃ dharmaḥ*) and ending with "He is the mental self of men" (*sa mānasīna ātmā janānām*)—consists of fourteen sentences.
[The second part] begins with "Consciousness is the ladle" (*cittiḥ sruc*) and consists of the Supreme Self, who is the heart of the Daśahotṛ...

The second part, consisting of twelve sentences beginning with "The revealer of reality" (*tattvaprakāśakaḥ*) and ending with "the sages have discerned Brahmā, Indra, Agni, and the foundation of the world," etc., elucidates the Supreme Person who is the heart of the *caturhotṛ* mantras, beginning with "The Earth is the Hotṛ. [One] hundred...

The third part consists of twelve sentences beginning with "niyutaḥ" and ending with "tena kḷpto'mṛtenāham asmi"; it establishes the essential nature of the Blessed Lord, who is the heart of the Pañcahotṛ-mantras beginning with "agnir hotā. It continues from "suvarṇaṃ kośam" up to "śatadhā carantam."
This fourth section, consisting of twelve sentences beginning with "Vāgghotā" (Speech is the Hotṛ),
elucidates the specific nature of the Supreme Person who is the essence of the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ-mantras.
It comprises seventy-eight sentences, ending with the concluding portion of the Anuvāka beginning with "Indro rājā jagato ya īśe" (Indra is the king who rules over the world).

The fifth part, beginning with "Mahāhavirhotā," elucidates the specific nature of the Blessed Lord Śrīpati, who is the heart of the Saptahotṛ-mantras. Since the nature of the Blessed Lord is already established by one part alone, there would be no purpose in establishing it again through another part.

However, any doubt as to the purpose [of the subsequent sections] must be dispelled by the fact that each succeeding portion is intended to describe the nature of the Lord as qualified by specific attributes not previously apprehended in the preceding portions. Thus, this entire section (anuvāka) is intended to be designated by the word "heart" (hṛdaya). The Rudras are the Śatarudrīya...

The *saṃjñaka* mantras are those recited in the eleven sections (*anuvākas*) of the fifth chapter of the fourth book of the *Taittirīya-saṃhitā*, beginning with "Obeisance to you, O Rudra" (*namaste rudra*) and ending with "I place you in my jaw" (*taṃ vo jambhe dadhāmi*). These are the *brahmāṇi*, characterized by the marks of Brahman (*brahmaliṅga*).
Which hymns? Those beginning with "brahma jajñānam" and others, which are well known in the eighth anuvāka of the eighth prapāṭhaka of the second aṣṭaka of the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa.
(p. 596) For the benefit of the world, [the author] intends to determine the meaning of the Puruṣasūkta and the Śrīsūkta.
Regarding the description of the manifestation of Lakṣmī from the Supreme Person:
"The Puruṣasūkta arose in ancient times from the Supreme Being;
and for the welfare of the world, the Śrīsūkta emerged from Lakṣmī. (59.2)
A demonstration of the differences of opinion regarding the number of verses in the Puruṣasūkta:
"That Puruṣasūkta is said to have various divisions and recensions;
some [hold it to] have four verses, while others [hold it to] have five, six, or seven. (59-3)
Furthermore, some recite sixteen verses, while others recite eighteen; indeed, the *puruṣasūkta* is studied with variations according to each individual Vedic school. (59.4)
The Puruṣa-sūkta demonstrates the object of knowledge it sets forth:
the sacrifice of the Puruṣa, which is the cause of the origin of the entire world, the bestower of heaven and liberation, and which is both divine and human, is expounded in this hymn. (59–5)
The first four verses possess the quality of discerning the essential nature of the fourfold self consisting of Vāsudeva and the others;
therein, the fourfold self is discerned by means of these initial four verses.
Among those, the first mantra establishes the first manifestation (*vyūha*) known as Vāsudeva, who is adorned with the status of being the Lord of Lakṣmī:
"He who is the Supreme, the lotus-eyed, the eternal Supreme Self. (59–6)
And that Lakṣmī, who is the source of the worlds and possesses those attributes, is the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva himself, as he is presented by the first [syllable]. (59–7)
In order to explain the meaning of each word of the mantra, the demonstration that the term *sahasraśīrṣa* refers to the Lord of Śrī is as follows:
"She who has a thousand [rays] moving together with Him, having attained a state of co-existence."
Śrī is the supreme power, whose very form consists of the six perfections in their entirety.
He who is both detached and yet attached, who is eternally present and the refuge of all—
thus is the Blessed One celebrated as "the Thousand-headed."
The word *puruṣa* refers to the state of having attained all desires, because he is full; he is eternally called *puruṣa* from the root *pṛ*, meaning "to fill.
(p. 598) [This applies also] to the word *sahasrākṣa*.

The root *aś* (to reach) signifies the excellence of the bound self characterized by the quality of thousandfoldness; or else, it is derived from *aś* (to eat), *aj* (to drive), or *añc* (to move). (6.10)
The Person (puruṣa) who is omnipresent and rests upon primordial nature (prakṛti) is designated as Akṣa.
The word "sahasrapāt" refers to his being distinguished by the quality of having a thousandfold nature;
and because the root *pad* has the sense of transformation (*pariṇāma*), he is thus etymologically defined as "Pāda. (59–11)
Prakṛti is declared to be the primordial nature (prakṛti), and she is eternally transformative.
Regarding the demonstration of the grounds for the application of the term "thousand" (hasra) to both Prakṛti and Puruṣa:
among the six qualities (guṇas), that which is power (śakti) is called "thousand" (hasra). || 59-12 ||
Pradhāna and Puruṣa are eternal in her creation and emanation;
at the end, they are likewise remembered as having resorted to her for a thousandfold duration.
The conclusion regarding the distinction between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* in Vāsudeva:
"He who is unmanifested as a thousand puruṣas, the thousand-eyed, the thousand-footed.
This is by way of defining the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*) of the latter half [of the verse].
The demonstration of the quality of being unlimited with respect to its cause and its supremacy is established by the verse itself: "He, having encompassed the earth on all sides... (59.14).
The entire universe that has passed away exists as various states of being;
for the measure of the cause is indeed present in its effect, just as the nature of milk persists in the production of curd.

In some cases, the effect exists within the continuous series of causes; indeed, the measure of the effect is already present in the cause, just as the specific form is absent from a lump of beeswax. (59.16)
It is not so; for the Blessed One, even when creation or dissolution occurs, there is no such thing as a fixed limit to the extent of effects. Thus, he is described as "the ground" (bhūmi). (59.17)
"Acquired in the Blessed Lady," meaning consisting of both pure and impure [elements];
the earth is the material cause of the world, and it is here called the power of the ground (bhūmi-śakti). || 59-18 ||
That which is the distinction between the pure and the impure, and the state of time, the person, and primordial nature— he,
having pervaded the earth on all sides, supports it with his own splendor.
By means of his own volitional nature, at the times of both manifestation and dissolution,
he stood transcending even ten finger-breadths.

The infinity of the Cause is taught by means of the ten fingers. Now, the second mantra is explained as being devoted to the second manifestation (vyūha) named Saṃkarṣaṇa; thus, the state of Saṃkarṣaṇa, which is the cause of the world, is described. (59–21)
This entire universe, consisting of the forms of the past and the future, was indeed originally nothing but the Puruṣa himself when he first desired to create. (59.22)
The demonstration that the word "puruṣa" occurring in the mantra refers to Saṃkarṣaṇa:
"The Puruṣa flows forth clearly through the application of perfect knowledge;
therefore, Saṃkarṣaṇa is proclaimed as 'Puruṣa'. (59.23)
With the second half [of the verse], there is the demonstration that Saṃkarṣaṇa is the bestower of liberation based on his status as the instructor of knowledge:
"Bearing the universe, consisting of both conscious and unconscious elements, like a mole upon the body..."
Saṃkarṣaṇa arises; he is thus spoken of again.
Furthermore, the meaning of the phrase "the Lord of immortality" is stated as follows:
by means of *anna* (food), which is the object of enjoyment consisting of both *prakṛti* and its evolutes (*prākṛta*). || 59-25 ||

By means of its insentient aspect—which, though integrated with time, assumes various forms and modalities—the individual soul (jīvātman), which is the conscious aspect, ascends [to higher states]. (59.26)

When one who previously had no connection with oneself here [in this world] becomes connected through the influence of former association, and when various bonds have been destroyed through contact with virtuous qualities; || 59-27 ||
Immortality is the manifestation of one's own true nature, which is also known by the name "liberation";
its presiding deity is Saṃkarṣaṇa, the Lord, because he bestows the knowledge [of it]. (59.28)
The exposition of the third mantra as referring to the third manifestation (vyūha) named Pradyumna:
"Then, by the third [mantra], Viṣṇu is called Saṃkarṣaṇa, out of a desire to favor those whose consciousness is scorched by the fire of saṃsāra. (59.29)
Such is the greatness of this Viṣṇu, whose nature is Saṃkarṣaṇa: that he has sustained the universe as its primordial unfolding.
The Puruṣa Pradyumna is superior even to him by virtue of his beneficence.
The superiority of Pradyumna is established by the word "Puruṣa" occurring in the mantra: "He who creates many forms, both Prakṛti and Puruṣa, is Puruṣa. (59.31)
His superiority is described through his efforts for the benefit of the entire world.
In the fourth verse of the hymn, "tripād ūrdhva udait," it is established that the fourth mantra refers to the fourth manifestation (vyūha) named Aniruddha. || 59-32 ||
The Lord, being immeasurable and unobstructed, is thus described.
[Now follows] the demonstration that the word "puruṣa" occurring in the mantra has as its referent the Unobstructed One (Aniruddha):
"In the past, he sat, causing all living beings to perform their duties. (59.33)
Worshipped through ritual action, he bestows fruits upon persons;
therefore, Aniruddha is designated as "Puruṣa. (59.34)
This city was previously existing; from that city it arose upwards, beyond the Beyond.
The meaning expressed here is that it was not perceived by [the self] in that state. (59-35)
One quarter of Him alone here consists of the conscious and unconscious;
His pervasion exists as the inner ruler through the will to govern each respective thing. (59.36)
This very point is elucidated here by the verse beginning with "viṣvaṅ":
having become pervasive (viṣvaṅ) on all sides, he strode forth and entered into manifoldness. (59.37)
Both the conscious and the unconscious have been declared as having food and being without food;
therefore she is called Virāj, and Virāj is known by the name Parā (the Supreme).

Hiraṇyagarbha, the soul of the universe, is here called Puruṣa. This concludes the meaning of the Puruṣasūkta, preceded by the statement that the meaning of the remaining fourteen mantras is to be understood from common worldly knowledge.
But the remainder is established from worldly convention; thus, this [system] is well-spoken in such a manner. (59.39)
This is a very brief indication of the meaning of the Śrīsūkta, which has been described in detail in another tantra.
The Śrīsūkta [beginning with] "hiraṇyavarṇām" has been elaborated elsewhere.
*Varṇa* denotes form (*rūpa*); *varṇa* is said to be excellent (*vara*). (59–40)
She whose color is established as both beneficial and beautiful—that goddess Hiraṇyavarṇā is the Śrī-śakti, the supreme nectar. (59.41)
This very hymn is said to be a couple marked by the Supreme;
because they are mutually blended at the beginning, they are the mutual manifestors of one another. (59.42)

For one who is established in the two aforementioned hymns according to the prescribed rule, the attainment of liberation is the certain fruit: "Restrained, with regulated diet, devoted, and with senses controlled, by worshipping these two hymns, one goes to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. (59.43)
Regarding the mantra of Varāha, it is stated that its gross meaning is to be known from common worldly experience: "The mantra named Vārāha is indeed declared to be in the Atyaṣṭi meter;
its associative mudrā is already known to you from the world. (59.44)
Listen now from me to the concise definition of its subtle meaning, term by term,
concerning that eternal form of his which was manifested in the Boar and other incarnations. (59.45)
The Blessed One, assuming the form of a boar, was intent upon lifting up the earth.
Saṃsāra is declared to be night, while liberation (mokṣa) is remembered as the excellent day. (59.46)
He is designated as having the form of a boar because of his defining of the "excellent day" (varāha).
His defining of that very [day] for the sake of others consists in being the support of the entire world and in providing protection at all times. (59.47)

The primary purpose of this treatise is to establish the supreme deity by first expounding upon the nature, form, qualities, and majesty of Brahman, who is the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe.
Wherever the creator of the maintenance, origin, and dissolution of beings is contemplated, there Viṣṇu is contemplated through his essential nature, qualities, and majesty. (60.2)

That [scripture] which, primarily, establishes the nature, form, qualities, and majesty of Lakṣmī— who is the very embodiment of the power of the Lord’s will— is reckoned as Śakti; she is both the attribute and the substratum of Viṣṇu.
Like the moonlight of the cool-rayed one, it follows both existence and non-existence.
Neither different nor of another form, consisting of knowledge, bliss, and action, she abides as the great manifestation, changeless and stainless. (60.4)
Free from attachment and non-attachment, possessing right discernment, full yet empty, bearing the truth;

she is the nature of both closing and opening [the eyes], characterized by existence and non-existence. (60.6)

That Lakṣmī, who is contemplated there by virtue of her essential nature, qualities, and majesty, is that Power (Śakti) whose form consists of both the manifested and the unmanifested, and who is designated as the "twofold power. (60.7)
That power of Viṣṇu, which consists of the universe and possesses both pure and impure natures, is clearly contemplated therein through its own essential forms, qualities, and majesties. (60.8)
Where prosperity is contemplated and where the agent of manifestation resides,

The power whose form is creative imagination is known by the name Sudarśanaparā.
That lotus-born [goddess] is the creative power of the Sustainer of the World, wherein she is contemplated;

Wherein the nature of having form and the nature of being formless, as well as their distinction as pure and impure, are clearly contemplated as belonging to the power of Viṣṇu whose essence is action. (60.11)

he who begins with the letter *ña*, who dwells in the center of the lotus of the letter *ña*, and who has made his presence manifest through the letter *ña*. || 28 ||
The nine letters beginning with *ṭa* are:

Ṭaṅkadhārī (Bearer of the Chisel), Ṭaṅkavapuḥ (Chisel-bodied), Ṭaṅkasaṃhārakārakaḥ (Maker of the Destruction by Chisel), Ṭaṅkacchinnasuvarṇābhaḥ (Resembling Gold Cut by a Chisel), and Ṭaṅkāradhanurujjvalaḥ (Radiant with a Bow of Iron). || 29 ||
Having a form like the fire of a thunderclap, rich with the sound of the thunderclap, filled with the fame of the thunderclap, he increases the bliss of the thunderclap. || 30 ||
The nineteen names beginning with the letter Ḍa are:

the destroyer of the collection of hypocrisy, the increaser of the lineage of hypocrisy, the wearer of hypocrisy, the one whose heart is hypocrisy, and the one intent upon punishing hypocrisy. || 31 ||

The sustainer of the *ḍimba*, the creator of the *ḍimba*, the *ḍimba* itself, he who is intent on destroying the *ḍimba*, the remover of the sins of the *ḍimba*, and whose lotus feet are honored by the *ḍimba*. || 32 ||

He who destroys the host of demons with his raised hand, who is intent on meditation upon the *ḍamaru* drum, who is the destroyer arising from the *ḍamaru*, and who is the joy arising from the *ḍamaru*. || 33 ||
Dwelling in the midst of a pomegranate grove, fond of pomegranate flowers, satisfied with pomegranate fruits, yet devoid of pomegranate fruits. || 34 ||

The eight [deities] beginning with the letter *ḍha* possess bodies as enchanting as the *ḍhakkā* drum; they shine forth with the sound of the *ḍhakkā*, are devoted to playing the *ḍhakkā*, and are intent upon holding the *ḍhakkā*. (35)
He is perfected by the seed-syllable *ḍha*, he is rich with the letter *ḍha*;
his abode is in the center of *ḍha*, and his intestines are fashioned from *ḍha*.
He whose abode is the seed-syllable *ṇa*, who is radiant with garments marked by the syllable *ṇa*;
whose limbs are exceedingly profound due to the syllable *ṇa*, and who is fond of propitiating the syllable *ṇa*. (37)

He whose eyes are tremulous begins with the fourteen letters starting with *ta*; he is the great abductor of Taralākṣī, the enemy who destroyed the demon Tāraka; he is enriched by necklaces radiant with gems, and he delights the fickle heart. || 38 ||
He was served by the demon Tāraka and honored by the demon Tāraka;
his lotus-heart was satisfied by the hymn of praise from the horse-faced one (Hayagrīva).
The glorious one with the face of a horse, praised by those with the faces of horses;
he who is covered by a mass of darkness, yet the crusher of the continuity of darkness.

The dispeller of darkness, the one reclining upon the waters, the increaser of darkness, Hara; he who dwells in the midst of the four letters beginning with *tha*, and who is adorned by the excellent letter *tha*. || 41 ||
Endowed with the seed-syllable *tha* and possessing a beautiful abode of the syllable *tha*, he is the bearer of the ten [deities] beginning with *da*:
Darabhṛt, Darasārākṣa, Darahṛt, and Daravañcaka. (42)
He possesses the luster of a blooming lotus, is adorned with a beautiful discus,
is intent upon gathering curds, and bears a fame as white as curd.
He is devoted to the worship of curd-rice and is the maker of the *dadhivāmana* sweetmeat;
he consists of twenty-four syllables beginning with the letter *dha*, is the wielder of the bow, dear to wealth, auspicious, and honored as equal to the Lord of Wealth. || 44 ||
Dhara, who delights in protecting the earth; the bestower of abundance in wealth and grain;
Dhanañjaya, the presiding lord of grains; Dhanada, who is himself devoid of wealth. || 45 ||
He was perfected in the acquisition of wealth, his mind was esteemed for its riches,
he was devoted to the forest of the king of wealth (Kubera), and he bore the glory of the sovereign of wealth.
The one who brought away the king of wealth, he who is praised by the king of wealth;
the performer of dharma, the increaser of dharma, the possessor of dharma, he who is extolled by Dharmasena. || 47 ||
The King of Dharma (Yama), unattached to wealth, whose praise is fashioned by those who know the Dharma,
[is described] through sixteen [verses] beginning with the letter 'Na'—
[he who is] dependent on the forest of the king of men, and who is devoted to the king of men. 48.
His virtues were praised by the king of men, and he was as radiant as a king of men;
he was as noble as a fresh lotus, and his eyes were like fresh lotuses.
He whose food is the fresh lotus, who is as red as a fresh lotus,
who wears garments of fresh gold, and who is intent on compassion for his new Lord.
He is the sound of the hymn to the nine lords, possessing a form identical to the nine lords;
he is honored by the eye of the *nālikā* and adorned with rows of *nālikā* flowers. (51)
Situated in the center of the movement of the *nālikā*, seated upon the *nālikā* posture, he who delights in the eighteen syllables beginning with the letter *pa*,
whose eyes are like the white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*), and who removes the intoxication of pride. || 52 ||
He who is praised by the sage Puṇḍarīka, whose splendor is like that of a friend of Puṇḍarīka, who is beautiful with the luster of a white lotus, and whose face resembles a white lotus. || 53 ||
Honored by the lotus-eyed one, devoted to compassion for the lotus-like [suffering beings],
supreme, possessing the body that is the goal of the highest, the supreme bliss, higher than the highest.
He who generates supreme bliss, who is dearer than even the finest food, who is as noble as the hand of Puṣkarākṣa, who is Puṣkarākṣa himself, and who bestows auspiciousness. || 55 ||
Accompanied by a multitude of lotuses and joined with the humming of bees,
he is then praised with nine syllables beginning with the letter *pha* ending in *phaṭ*, situated in the midst of the syllable *phaṭ*.

He whose younger brother was destroyed by the sound "phaṭ," who is seated upon the "phaṭ" syllable, who subsists on fruits, whose fruit is praised, and who makes a festival of the worship of fruits. || 57 ||

Delighting in the bestowing of fruits, his mind is completely filled with the attainment of fruits; he begins with the letter *ba*, possesses sixteen [forms], is the praise of strength (*bala*), the support of strength, and the one who brings joy to Balabhadra. (58)
The powerful one, the taker of strength, the crusher of enemies who rival in strength;
the giver of strength, the upholder of strength, whose body shines with power. || 59 ||
The powerful one who bestows strength upon the weak, the destroyer of the demon Bala, skilled in the protection of strength, and the giver of joy to those possessed of strength. || 60 ||

With a heart full of power, consecrated for the withdrawal of that power, he is the Lord of Existence (Bhavapati) who bestows the continuity of existence; he is praised by many as the twenty-four letters beginning with the letter 'Bha'. || 61 ||
He is the destroyer of worldly existence, the remover of worldly existence, and intent upon the stabilization of worldly existence;
he is skilled in protecting from worldly existence and the cause of satisfaction within worldly existence. || 62 ||

The cutter of the ocean of existence, the bestower of happiness upon the sea of existence, the giver of auspiciousness, the one with an auspicious heart, and the one who relies upon auspicious deeds. || 63 ||
His body is anointed with auspicious glory; he is consecrated for the bestowing of auspicious fortune;
he is fond of auspicious trees; he is indeed auspicious, the destroyer of the forest of inauspiciousness.
He whose voice is the essence of auspicious glory, who is adorned by an auspicious mandala, whose feet are praised by Bharadvāja, and who is the refuge of Bharadvāja. || 65 ||
Delighting in the hermitage of Bharadvāja, he is the bestower of compassion upon Bharadvāja;
he possesses the luster of fifty-three emeralds beginning with the letter 'Ma', and his feet shine like emerald.
He whose noble deeds are as dark as emerald, adorned with garments of emerald-blue silk,
who wanders through groves of mango trees, and who delights the people born from the mango tree.
The joyous mango-tree of bliss, beautiful with the delight of the mango;
the mandala, the sovereign of the mandala, the soul of the mandala, the perfect mandala. (68)
Maṇḍeśa, whose circle is the end of the circle, who is worshipped by the circle,
who is purified by the circle, who is the enclosure of the circle, and who is the dense mass.
He who abides in the mandala, the foremost of those within the mandala, marked by the ornaments of the mandala;
the destroyer of the Madhu demon, whose speech is as sweet as honey. || 70 ||
He is devoted to the offering of honey, the glory of Madhumangala,
the conqueror of the gods, the bee, the sweet one, and the lord of sweetness.
The destroyer of the demon Madhu, the one who brings about the lineage of Madhu, exceedingly beautiful in the month of Madhu, and resplendent during the spring season. || 72 ||
Nourished by honey, honey-bodied, honey-drinker, honey-protector;
sweet, of sweet form, adorned with sweet garments. || 73 ||
The Lord of Madhurānagarī, the destroyer of the demon Madhu, who is devoted to sweet food and is skillful in bestowing sweet joy. || 74 ||
He whose lotus-eyes are sweet, who is united with the Lord of Madhura, who is skillful in the bliss of sweetness, and who is joined with the enemy of Madhu. || 75 ||
Shining with sweet ornaments, adorned with sweet armlets, resting in the forest of the king of beasts, and graced by a circle of deer. || 76 ||
He who respects the deer, the lord of deer, the enemy of deer, the tearer asunder;
the ten names beginning with the letter *ya*:
He who is fond of sacrifice, whose body is sacrifice, and whose mind is fully delighted by sacrifice.
Devoted to the continuity of sacrifice, busied with the preparations for sacrifice, he was the sacrifice itself, the locus of sacrifice, and eager to accomplish sacrifice. (78)
He whose dwelling is in the sacrificial hall, who is honored by sacrifices, and whose food is consecrated by sacrifice;
he who possesses twenty consonants beginning with *ra*, the lord of mercury (*rasendra*), endowed with essence (*rasa*), the king of essences, and eager for essence.
He is endowed with aesthetic flavor (rasa), the bearer of flavor, clothed in flavor, and a mine of flavor.
He is the conqueror of flavor, the most excellent of flavors, and is delighted by the king of flavors.
He is intent on the essence of aesthetic flavor (rasa), his prowess consists of the gift of rasa;
he is the king of rasa, the bearer of rasa, the lord of rasa, and the beloved of rasa. || 81 ||
The leader of the letter *ra*, the abode of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), resplendent with an abundance of *rasa*;
he who delights in the eight letters beginning with *la*, and who is worthy of the *lavaṅga* flower. || 82 ||
Standing in the midst of a clove forest, longing for the clove blossoms,
he was entwined by rows of creepers and honored by the nectar of the vines.

Adorned with creepers and graced by the tilaka mark of the beautiful-bodied woman, his lotus-feet are praised by heroes; beginning with the letter 'va', he possesses seventeen [qualities] and is eager for a majestic gait. (84)
Situated in the center of the leaf of Virāj, served by the essence of Virāj, he is the giver of boons, endowed with excellence, and most exalted. || 85 ||
The praise of the excellent one, the ever-increasing, the bearer of excellence, and the source of excellence;
he who delights in the granting of boons, the most eminent, and who is intensely eager to bestow boons. (86)
With a heart tender from granting boons, accompanied by his excellent elephant,
his lotus feet praised by Śāradā, he bears the fame of the autumnal lotus; [he is the one whose name begins with] twenty-five letters starting with 'Śa'.
He whose eyes are like autumn lotuses, who is served by the presiding deity of autumn, who dwells upon the seat of Śāradā, and who is praised by the Lord of Autumn. 88.
The subduer of Śāradāvāsa, resplendent in Śāradāvāsa;
he whose power is praised by Indra, and whose prowess is equal to that of Indra. || 89 ||
Possessing sovereignty equal to that of Śatakratu, he removes the intoxication of Śatakratu;
the glorious one bears the bow and arrows, and his majesty arises from the arrow. || 90 ||
The glory of his fame was as white as an autumn arrow; his eyes were like the lotuses of autumn;
he was perfected through union with the autumn season; and he was adorned by a circle of arrows.
Transcending arrows, yet bearing arrows, he is ever eager to cherish his arrows;
his form is identical to that of the source of arrows, and he is skilled in combat with arrows.
He delights in Śarabṛndāvana; his prowess is esteemed by the arrows (or by Śara); he begins with the letter *ṣa*; he consists of sixteen syllables;
he is a six-footed being; he has the form of a bee; and he is served by swarms of bees.
Sweet with the form of a six-footed bee, he is the six-footed one, exalted by the six-footed;
he is praised by the Vedas with their six limbs and is rich in the words of those six limbs. || 94 ||
He whose abode is the poetry of the six lotuses, whose splendor is fashioned by the six points, who dwells in the midst of the six points, and who is made pure by the six points. (95)

He who is being praised by the six traditions, who abides within the interior of the six traditions, who is surrounded by the auspiciousness of the six powers, and who has made the six wheels his crest-ornament. (96)
The twenty [names] beginning with *sa* are:
Sāra, Sārasa, Raktāṅga, Sārasārasalocana, Sāradīpti, Sāratanu, and Sārasākṣakarapriya. || 97 ||
The lamp of the essence, the compassion of the essence, the blazing one who causes the growth of the essence of the forest,
the subduer of the essence of the deer, and the one whose earrings are fashioned from the essence.
He dwells in the forest of Sārasa; he is rich with the cries of cranes;
he is fond of essential songs; he is the essence; he is most learned among cranes. 99.
He is the protector of the virtuous, ever-delighting, and the teacher who bestows eternal bliss;
his feet are worshipped by true physicians, and his mind is radiant with the wisdom of a true physician.
He whose name begins with the letter *ha*; he who has sixty-four [forms];
the conqueror of Hari; the chariot of Hari; he who is devoted to the service of Hari;
he who has the color of Hari; he who moves like Hari; he who is on the back of Hari; he who is affectionate toward Hari. || 101 ||
He is yellow-hued, a praiser of Hari, and devoted to meditation on Hari;
he is like Hari in destroying at the end of an eon, and is resplendent with the essence of Hari.
His limbs were anointed with yellow sandalwood paste; he was esteemed by the mind of Hari;
he was devoted to the compassion of Hari; and he was eager to liberate the swan. || 103 ||
He who grants fearlessness to the sons of Hari, he who is honored by those equal to the sons of Hari, he who is present through the meditation on Hari, and he who bestows joy upon Hari. || 104 ||
The king of weapons, the wielder of weapons, praised as the leader of weapons;
the weapon that is Hari, whose body is the weapon, the destroyer of weapons, and the increaser of weapons. || 105 ||

The destroyer of weapons, the one who engages in combat with weapons, the one adorned with weapons; the giver of weapons, the one devoted to weapons, and the one who sets forth the path of weapons. || 106 ||
He is complete with a continuous stream of weapons, adorned with a circle of weapons;
he is devoted to the gift of weapons and is embellished by all formidable weapons. || 107 ||
He who has the form of a swan, the gait of a swan, whose majesty is praised by swans;
he who delights in the path of the swans, the protector of swans, and the leader of swans. || 108 ||
His body is the object of the swan’s gaze; he is delighted by the song of the swans;
he is the conqueror of the swan; he is the lord of the swans; he moves with the swan; his vehicle is the swan. || 109 ||
Born from a swan, moving with the gait of a swan, well-honored by the king of swans;
possessing the speed of a swan, bearing a swan, and having a body as beautiful as a swan. || 110 ||
With a body as beautiful as a swan, his mind associated with the swan;
he who knows the essence of the true nature of the swan, his mind bowed to the swan. || 111 ||
His power is praised by the swans; he is intent on protecting Hari;
his majesty is extolled by the swans; and his prowess is like that of Hara’s son. || 112 ||

The twelve names beginning with the letter *kṣa* are: Born from the ocean of milk, permeated by the nature of milk, united with the Lord of the milk-ocean, and resplendent with the fame of milk. (113)
The destroyer of the night’s end, honored by the lords of the night, united with the sovereign of the night, and one who has made the night a festival. || 114 ||
Content with the consecration of milk, desiring the drinking of milk, devoted to food consisting of milk and ghee, and using a cosmetic paste produced from milk. (115)
Thus has been declared this divine proclamation of the fruit, which destroys all sins,
brings about the destruction of all enemies, and bestows all prosperity. 116.
It generates all good fortune, brings about all auspiciousness, pacifies all poverty, and destroys all calamities. || 117 ||
It is the secret that brings about all peace, wards off all diseases, removes the most stubborn seizures caused by planetary spirits, and dispels all suffering. || 118 ||
Those men here who recite the thousand divine names of the Lord of the Cakrarāja and the names of the King of Weapons—for them all prosperities come to pass; of this there is no doubt. (119)
Thus ends the *Śrīsudarśanasahasranāmastotra* within the *Ahirbudhnyasaṃhitā*, a secret doctrine (*tantrarahasya*) in the form of a dialogue between Vyāsa and Nārada.
(1) 1. In the enumeration of the names as they have been stated, their total number is sixty-one.

It does not exceed five hundred. In this regard, is the term "Thousand Names" used figuratively for these very [five hundred] names, or is the count of one thousand names incomplete due to omissions of text here and there? By a more powerful means of proof...

Without [the assumption of] the figurative nature of the term *sahasranāma*, the inappropriateness of such an assumption suggests the necessity of a textual omission (*granthalopa*), which occurred by chance between two manuscript collections brought from different regions that were compared with one another while their mutual contents remained unknown.
The mention of "not being made of silver," however, precludes the suspicion that there might have been an omission of a textual passage.
